pages.markdown:
# Pull request review threads across patchsets

A review thread is pinned to a path, a side (`old`/`new`) and a line range of
the diff the reviewer saw. When the pull is updated, lines shift or disappear.
Threads therefore carry a signed anchor ([encryption](../encryption.md)) so
every client can show them on the right lines or mark them as moved or
outdated. Part of [Design decisions](README.md).

## The anchor

Line-anchored events (`line-comment`, `thread-comment`) may carry:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `patchset` | The head commit the reviewer's diff was cut against (empty for a portable patch-backed pull) |
| `anchorLines` | The exact text of the commented lines on that side, prefix stripped, newline-joined, at most 12 lines |

Both are signed: when present, the signed content appends
`NUL patchset NUL anchorLines` to the existing per-type content under the
unchanged `forkmesh-pull-comment-v1` label. Events without an anchor sign the
same bytes as before. On disk (`.forkmesh/pulls/<n>/NNNN-<type>.md`) they are
front-matter keys `patchset` and `anchorLinesB64` (base64url). Cross-language
vectors live in `desktop/tests/test_crypto.cpp` and `app/tests/test_crypto.py`.

## Placement

Desktop (`PullReviewModel.cpp`) and web (`06-repo-content.js`) apply the same
rule:

1. **Same patchset**: the thread is *current* at its lines.
2. **Text search**: otherwise, find `anchorLines` as consecutive lines on the
   same side, nearest the original line. Same line: *current*; elsewhere:
   *moved*; not found: *outdated*.
3. **Patchset only**: a different patchset with no anchor text is *outdated*.
   A diff with no named patchset keeps the thread *current* while the line
   exists.
4. **Legacy** (no anchor): painted where it says while the line exists,
   otherwise *outdated*.

Moved threads show a `Moved` badge and the original lines. Outdated threads are
never painted on a line; they are listed at the top of their file with an
`Outdated` badge. Applying a suggested change uses the current line and refuses
when the thread is outdated. Matching is exact on purpose: a thread is never
shown on code it did not discuss.

## Branch review threads

A branch without a pull request can be reviewed the same way, from the desktop
compare view or the phone apps. Branch threads use the same event types and
anchors and are stored in the `forkmesh/pulls` ledger branch under
`.forkmesh/branch-reviews/<first 24 hex of sha256(branch)>/` with a
`branch.md` naming the branch, so pull loaders never treat them as pulls.
Placement uses anchor text only, because a branch view can include
uncommitted changes.

Signature:
`forkmesh-branch-comment-v2\n<owner/name>\n<type>\n<branch>\n<author>\n<ts>\n<sha256 hex of contentForSigning>`.

Rendering only reads an existing ledger checkout; only posting a comment
creates it.

A phone cannot write Git, so it sends the signed event to
`POST /api/repo/<owner>/<name>/pulls` with `{"branch": "<name>", "event": {...}}`
and no `number`. The relay verifies the v2 signature and queues it in
`pull_inbox` with `number: 0`. The owner's desktop
(`PullStore::applyRemoteBranchEvent`) or a Go mirror (`writeBranchReviewItem`)
drains it into the ledger, skipping event ids already stored. Shared vectors
are pinned in `app/tests/test_branch_review_intake.py`,
`server/intake_test.go` and the iOS and Android test suites.

## Limitations

- The web compare page does not show branch review threads.
- The web places threads against the signed creation diff, so threads written
  against a later desktop head appear moved or outdated there.
- Whitespace-only edits and renames make a thread outdated.

pages.title: Relay, synchronization, and migration
pages.description: Suite version: 1.0.0-rc.1 · Vectors: fold.json, identifiers.json · Part of the ForkMesh protocol suite
pages.markdown:
# Relay, synchronization, and migration

Suite version: `1.0.0-rc.1` · Vectors: `fold.json`, `identifiers.json` ·
Part of the [ForkMesh protocol suite](README.md)

## Roles

- A **source of truth** is a node holding the owner's working repository. It
  signs catalog records and `forkmesh-repostate-v1` attestations.
- A **mirror** is an independently operated HTTPS origin serving a copy. Its
  own attestations prove what it serves, not what the owner published.
- The **relay** (mainnode) routes reads to mirrors, verifies signed
  submissions, and indexes metadata. It never stores repository bytes and is
  never authoritative for collaboration meaning.

## Clone and fetch routing

- **FM-REL-001** MUST — A relay serves a public clone or fetch only from a
  mirror that passes three checks. The mirror has a fresh signed health
  result. Its live advertised refs hash (FM-ID-005) to a state that a source
  of truth in the repository's logical group attested with
  `forkmesh-repostate-v1`. Mirrors are grouped by root commit, falling back to
  name. A source is checked against its current pin plus bounded recent
  history. A mirror's self-attestation never activates a repository. When the
  group has no source-signed pin, routing fails closed.
- **FM-REL-002** MUST — The two requests of a smart-HTTP clone (`info/refs`,
  then `git-upload-pack`) reach the same accepted origin. A relay may retry
  another integrity-matching origin only before any response byte is sent. It
  never splices responses from different origins and never rewrites pack
  data.
- **FM-REL-003** MUST — Receive-pack is refused before any request body is
  read unless FM-AUTH-002 authorizes the request. Both upload-pack and
  receive-pack hide the `refs/forkmesh/` namespace, which holds merge
  anchors and staging refs, and reject wants for object ids that no
  advertised ref reaches.

Protocol negotiation inside Git (protocol v0 or v2) is left to stock Git
clients and servers. The refs digest is always computed from a protocol-v0
advertisement generated for attestation.

## Collaboration log exchange

- **FM-SYNC-001** MUST — A collaboration log is exchanged as one canonical
  envelope per line, separated by LF. A reader splits only on LF and retains
  a stray CR in the record, where it fails as `noncanonical_encoding` rather
  than being normalized into a valid envelope. An importer verifies every
  record and recomputes state; it never trusts an exported snapshot. Export
  sorts unique raw records by SHA-256 of their bytes.
- **FM-SYNC-002** MUST — Folding is a pure function of the policy and the set
  of unique raw records. Permutation, duplication, and delay never change the
  result. The state digest is `sha256:` + hex SHA-256 of the canonical JSON
  state document (`forkmesh-collaboration-state-v1`). Duplicate deliveries are
  counted, not re-applied.
- **FM-SYNC-003** MUST — Beyond FM-SIG-004, a fold enforces six rules:
  - An event whose parents are not all present stays **pending**, with its
    raw bytes retained.
  - A descendant of a rejected event is rejected.
  - The Lamport `clock` is 0 without parents and otherwise one more than the
    greatest parent clock.
  - Two different events signed by one key in the same `sequence` slot are
    **equivocation**; both are excluded and counted.
  - Role authorization follows the pinned policy. Unauthorized events are
    audited but never folded.
  - Concurrent differing scalar writes produce an explicit conflict rather
    than a winner chosen by time, author, or arrival order.

  The complete family rules are normative in
  [Conflict-safe collaboration](../design/conflict-safe-collaboration.md).

A fold over an incomplete set cannot detect omission. A relay that withholds
events is an open threat (TM-008), not a property this suite guarantees.

## Migration and rollback

- **FM-MIG-001** MUST — A repository migration state receipt (FM-ID-006)
  excludes run timestamps, attempt counters, and credentials. Re-running an
  import over unchanged provider data yields the same receipt, and source
  deletions are pruned, not retained as stale objects.
- **FM-MIG-002** MUST — Each legacy collaboration record migrates through an
  importer-signed `create` or `decide` event. That event binds the exact
  legacy record digest and records whether the legacy signature is `valid`,
  `invalid`, or `unavailable`. It never presents the importer's signature as
  the legacy author's. The original bytes are kept alongside the new log.
- **FM-MIG-003** MUST — Rollback proceeds in a fixed order: stop writers
  emitting the newer version first, then roll back readers. Readers keep
  accepting and preserving newer raw envelopes they already hold. No
  implementation down-converts or deletes signed events, because that loses
  causality. Recovery restores policy and NDJSON, re-verifies, and compares
  state digests; corrupt lines stay quarantined while valid objects keep
  folding.

pages.markdown:
# Release binary publishing

Release binaries are never committed to git. A release is two things kept
apart on purpose (how releases reach users is the
[mirroring and distribution](../mirroring.md) pillar; signatures are covered in
[encryption](../encryption.md)):

- **Metadata**: small, signed text committed to the repository and synced
  across the mesh like issues and pull requests.
- **Payloads**: the binary bytes, kept in a content-addressed store (CAS) on
  the node that serves the repository, and fetched by their SHA-256.

A mirror can carry the bytes, but it cannot change them without breaking the
signed hash, and git history never grows by the size of a build.
Part of [Design decisions](README.md).

## Two kinds of release

**Repository releases.** Any repository can publish releases from the web or
the desktop. The manifest's canonical body is built by
`release_manifest_content` in `app/src/releases.py`: repository, tag, the
commit the tag pointed to (`tag_commit`), the commit embedded in the artifact
(`build_commit`, when present), and one line per asset (name, blob SHA-256,
size, content type, OS, architecture, label), sorted. The creator signs
`release_signing_message`:

```text
forkmesh-release-v1\n<repo>\n<tag>\n<author>\n<ts>\n<sha256 of the content>
```

with their Ed25519 identity; `verify_release_manifest` in `app/src/events.py`
checks it. Release name, notes and the prerelease flag are not signed, so they
can be edited without invalidating the release. Download counts are not
signed either.

**ForkMesh's own desktop releases.** Channels under
`.forkmesh/releases/<channel>/` (`latest`, `candidate-<version>`) hold
`SHASUMS256.txt`, `release.json` and `release.json.sig`: a raw 64-byte Ed25519
signature over the exact `release.json` bytes, made with the release publisher
key (not a user identity). `tools/forkmesh-release-publish.sh` writes them;
`www/public/install.sh` and the desktop updater verify them. Operating
instructions are in
[`.forkmesh/releases/README.md`](../../.forkmesh/releases/README.md) and the
developer overview in [`docs/release/README.md`](../release/README.md).

## The content-addressed store

Blob path, relative to the store root (`cas_blob_relpath` in
`app/src/releases.py`):

```text
sha256/<first two hex digits>/<full sha256>/data
```

The served store is `<bare repository>/forkmesh-releases/` on each mirror
(`server/bootstrap.go`, `server/gateway.go`). A local publish without
`--cas-dir` writes to `.forkmesh/release-blobs/`, which `.gitignore` excludes.

## Download

```text
GET /api/repo/<owner>/<repo>/releases/blob/sha256/<sha256>?filename=<asset name>
```

The route is matched in `app/src/urls.py`. The response is immutable and can
be cached forever; the App forwards the request to a node holding the blob.
`filename` only sets the download name and never changes which bytes are
returned. Installers ask the repository recorded in the manifest (`repo`),
because only that node is guaranteed to hold the blob.

## Verification order

1. Authenticate the metadata: the release signature against a trust anchor
   (the publisher key built into `install.sh`, a local PEM, or a digest from
   an authenticated controller).
2. Check that the manifest binds `SHASUMS256.txt` (`checksums_sha256`).
3. Download the blob by hash and check its SHA-256 before installing or
   running it.

Nothing downloaded is executed to decide whether it is trustworthy.

## Related

- `app/src/releases.py`: tag and asset-name validation, CAS layout, canonical
  manifest, `SHASUMS256.txt` generation, semver ordering for `latest`, and the
  re-upload decision for an asset name.
- `app/tests/test_releases.py`
- [Release flow](../release/README.md)

pages.markdown:
# Scoped community trust lists

Status: protocol version 1, candidate. The dependency-free reference resolver
is `app/src/trust_lists.py`. The vectors in
`conformance/trust-lists/v1/vectors.json` bind four independent resolvers to
it byte for byte: the web client (`app/public/trust-lists.js`), the iOS client
(`native/ios/ForkMeshCore/Sources/FMAccount/TrustLists.swift`, tested by
`native/ios/ForkMeshCore/Tests/FMAccountTests/ConformanceTests.swift`), the
Android client
(`native/android/core/src/main/kotlin/com/forkmesh/nativeapp/security/TrustLists.kt`,
tested by
`native/android/core/src/test/kotlin/com/forkmesh/nativeapp/security/TrustListsCryptoTest.kt`),
and the desktop client (`desktop/src/TrustLists.cpp`). The user guide is
[Trust lists](../trust-lists.md). Part of [Design decisions](README.md).

## Goals and non-goals

A trust list is a signed statement that says, for example, "in the `forkmesh`
organization, these keys are security researchers whose advisories I stand
behind". People follow the lists they find useful. ForkMesh does not run a
global list, and no list is followed by default.

- **Reputation is scoped.** Every entry names one role and one repository,
  organization, or community. There is no wildcard or global scope. A follow,
  an include, or a delegation can only narrow scope, never widen it.
- **Nothing essential depends on a list.** Cloning, reading, identity,
  sign-in, pushing, and opening issues or pull requests never consult trust
  lists. A client with no follows behaves exactly as it does today. Lists
  inform ranking, review routing, badges, and moderation queues.
- **Disagreement stays visible.** When followed lists disagree, the result is
  `conflict`. Only the user's local override picks a side.
- **Compromise is recoverable locally.** Equivocation, a forked history, or
  a revocation cuts a list back to its last good version. The client shows
  the list as `recovered` instead of silently following the newest document.

## Documents

Documents are canonical JSON. Every string is printable ASCII other than `"`
and `\`. Object keys are sorted by code point, there is no whitespace, and
integers are at most 2^53−1 in magnitude, with no fractions, exponents, or
`-0`. A receiver accepts a document only when re-encoding its parse
reproduces the received bytes exactly. The restricted alphabet lets every
language write this encoding with a plain sorted-key writer. A raw document
is at most 262,144 UTF-8 bytes.

A document's identifier is `sha256:<hex SHA-256 of the raw bytes>`. Because
the raw bytes include the signature, two documents with the same meaning but
different signatures have different identifiers.

The signed message is the document's `schema` value, a newline, and the
canonical JSON of the document without its `signature` key. Signatures are
Ed25519 over those bytes. The rules of FM-SIG-001 in the
[protocol suite](../protocol/signatures-and-authentication.md#ed25519) apply.
Every resolver also rejects a scalar `S ≥ L` explicitly before calling a
platform verifier. It also rejects non-canonical key encodings (including
x = 0 with the sign bit set), the identity, and small-order and mixed-order
keys. Platform verifiers such as WebCrypto and OpenSSL do not, so the iOS and
Android resolvers use their own strict verifier (`Ed25519.verifyStrict`).
The `forged-weak-keys` vector carries signatures that pass lax verification
for each of those keys. Keys are 43-character and signatures 86-character
unpadded base64url, and both must round-trip.

A list is identified by issuer key and name, not by any single version:

```text
listId = "urn:forkmesh:trust-list:sha256:" ||
         hex(sha256("forkmesh-trust-list-id-v1\n" || issuer || "\n" || name))
```

### List version (`forkmesh-trust-list-v1`)

| Field | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| `issuer` | Signing key of the list owner |
| `name` | Slug `[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]{0,63}` |
| `version` | Integer ≥ 1 |
| `previous` | `null` for version 1; otherwise the document identifier of version − 1 |
| `issuedAt`, `expiresAt` | Milliseconds; `expiresAt > issuedAt`; lifetime at most 400 days |
| `roles` | Sorted, non-empty set of `maintainer`, `moderator`, `mirror-operator`, `organization`, `reviewer`, `security-researcher` |
| `communities` | Sorted, non-empty set of at most 64 scopes, none covered by another |
| `revocationKeys` | Sorted set of at most 4 keys, not including `issuer`, that may revoke later versions |
| `entries` | At most 2,000 `{subject, role, scope, stance, note}` entries, strictly sorted by subject, role, scope |
| `edges` | At most 16 `{kind, issuer, name, roles, communities, expiresAt}` edges, strictly sorted by issuer, name |
| `signature` | By `issuer` |

An entry's `stance` is `trust` or `distrust`. Its `note` is at most 280
characters. Its subject is never the issuer. An entry's role must be one of
the list's roles, and its scope must be covered by the list's communities.

An edge whose `kind` is `include` composes another list and has
`expiresAt: null`. An edge whose `kind` is `delegate` grants another key
authority to publish entries for this list and carries an integer
`expiresAt`. Either way, the edge's roles must be a subset of the list's
roles, its communities must be covered by the list's communities, and it
cannot name its own list.

### Scopes

| Scope | Covers |
| --- | --- |
| `repo:<owner>/<repository>` | That repository |
| `org:<owner>` | Itself and every `repo:<owner>/…` |
| `community:<slug>` | Itself |

Owners match `[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]{0,38}`. Repositories match
`[A-Za-z0-9._-]{1,100}` other than `.` and `..`. The intersection of two
scope sets keeps each member of one set that the other set covers. It then
removes duplicates and any member covered by another member.

### Revocation (`forkmesh-trust-list-revocation-v1`)

`{list, issuer, name, fromVersion, revokedBy, revokedAt, reason, successor}`,
signed by `revokedBy`. `list` must equal the listId of `issuer` and `name`.
`reason` is `compromised`, `malicious`, `retired`, or `superseded`.
`successor` is `null` or `{issuer, name}` of a different list.

A revocation is authorized when `revokedBy` is the issuer, or when a verified
version of the list with `version < fromVersion` names `revokedBy` in
`revocationKeys`. A recovery key committed before a compromise can therefore
revoke everything the attacker publishes. An attacker who adds keys in a
malicious version cannot use them to revoke the versions before it.
Revocations have no expiry. Revocation is monotonic, so no document can undo
one.

### Appeal (`forkmesh-trust-list-appeal-v1`)

`{subject, list, version, role, scope, statement, issuedAt}`, signed by the
`subject` it concerns, with a statement of 1–1,000 characters. Nobody can
appeal on someone else's behalf.

## Verification order

A resolver rejects a document at the first failing step and records
`{documentId, code}`:

1. `too_large`; bracket nesting deeper than 8 outside strings, found by a
   scan before any parser runs, or unparseable JSON: `invalid_json`;
   `noncanonical`; a top level that is not an object, or a `schema` that is
   not a known string: `unsupported_schema`; wrong key set: `invalid_keys`.
2. List version: `invalid_issuer`, `invalid_name`, `invalid_version`,
   `invalid_previous`, `invalid_time`, `invalid_scope` (roles, then
   communities), `invalid_revocation_keys`. Then, entry by entry,
   `invalid_entry`, `entry_outside_scope`, `unsorted_entries`. Then, edge by
   edge, `invalid_edge`, `edge_outside_scope`, `unsorted_edges`. Last,
   `invalid_signature_encoding` and `invalid_signature`.
3. Revocation: `invalid_issuer`, `invalid_name`, `list_mismatch`,
   `invalid_version`, `invalid_revoker`, `invalid_time`, `invalid_reason`,
   `invalid_successor`, then the signature.
4. Appeal: `invalid_subject`, `invalid_list`, `invalid_version`,
   `invalid_scope`, `invalid_statement`, `invalid_time`, then the signature.
5. In context: a list version or appeal whose `issuedAt` is more than
   300,000 ms after the resolver's clock is rejected as `issued_in_future`,
   and an unauthorized revocation as `unauthorized_revoker`.

Duplicate raw documents are counted once.

## Version history

For each list, a resolver considers every verified version it holds:

- two different documents with the same `version` are an **equivocation** at
  that version;
- a document whose `previous` does not equal the identifier of the single
  held document for `version − 1` is a **history fork** at that version;
- an authorized revocation cuts at its `fromVersion`.

The cutoff is the lowest of these versions. The head is the highest held
version below the cutoff that has exactly one document. The list state is:

| State | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `active` | A head exists, it has not expired, and nothing was cut |
| `recovered` | A head exists below a cutoff; `cutoffReasons` says why |
| `expired` | The head's `expiresAt` has passed; older versions are never revived |
| `revoked` | An authorized revocation left no usable version |
| `conflicted` | Equivocation or a fork left no usable version |
| `missing` | The list is followed or referenced, but no verified version is held |

Only `active` and `recovered` lists contribute entries and edges. A
revocation's `successor` is shown to the user and never followed
automatically. A compromised issuer key might have been used to revoke too,
so the user decides.

## Composition and merge

Local inputs are **follows**, `{issuer, name, roles, communities}` where a
`null` narrowing means the list's own scope, and **overrides**,
`{subject, role, scope, stance}` where the stance is `trust`, `distrust`, or
`ignore`. Neither is published or signed. They stay on the device. The client
that stores them validates them before resolving: keys and names use the
document field rules, and each override tuple appears at most once.
Resolvers do not re-validate local input.

1. Each follow starts a walk at its list, scoped to the intersection of the
   list's roles and communities with the follow's narrowing.
2. A walk admits each head entry whose role is in the walk's roles and whose
   scope is covered by the walk's communities.
3. A walk follows each edge. An expired delegation is skipped and counted.
   An edge back to a list already on the path is skipped as a cycle. An edge
   from a path that already holds 4 lists is skipped as depth-limited.
   Otherwise the child walk's scope is the intersection of the current scope,
   the edge's scope, and the child's own scope. The walk stops if that scope
   is empty.
4. Each `(subject, role, scope)` tuple collects at most one source per list,
   the one reached by the shortest path, with ties broken by the
   newline-joined path. Its `stance` is the shared stance of its sources,
   `conflict` when they differ, or `none` when only an override names it.
   `effective` is the override when present, otherwise the stance.
5. A verified appeal attaches to the tuple's assertion when one of that
   assertion's sources is the appealed list. The appeal is `resolved` when the
   list's head is newer than the appealed version and no longer distrusts the
   tuple, and `open` otherwise. Appeals that match no assertion are counted as
   unattached.

The resolution is canonical JSON with `lists` sorted by `listId`,
`assertions` by subject, role, and scope, `sources` by `listId`, `appeals` by
identifier, `rejected` by identifier and code, and `conflicts` by their
canonical JSON. `conflicts` holds `stance` conflicts, noting whether an
override resolved them, plus `equivocation` and `history_fork` records. The
result does not depend on the order of documents, follows, or overrides.

## Telemetry and privacy

`telemetry` holds counts only (documents, rejections by code, lists by state,
assertions, conflicts, overrides, appeals, skipped edges), never keys, list
names or follows. Follows and overrides never leave the device. Clients SHOULD
fetch the whole public bundle, or fetch through a mirror they operate, so a
relay does not learn which lists interest them. Entries name keys, not account
names.

## Threats

| Threat | Mitigation |
| --- | --- |
| Stolen issuer key publishes a malicious version | Recovery key revokes `fromVersion`; followers fall back to the last good version as `recovered` |
| Issuer shows different versions to different followers | Equivocation cuts below the disputed version once both copies meet |
| Rewritten history | `previous` digest chain; a fork cuts the list |
| A list claims global authority | No global scope; entries and edges must stay inside the list's own scope |
| Delegate or included list overreaches | Scope intersection at every hop; delegations expire |
| Attacker revokes with a key added in a malicious version | Only keys named in a version *before* `fromVersion` may revoke |
| Stolen issuer key revokes the whole list | Accepted as a denial of service; the owner publishes a successor under a new key and followers choose to follow it |
| Signature malleability and canonicalization tricks | Byte-exact canonical re-encoding, strict base64url, and explicit `S < L` |
| Resource exhaustion | Size, entry, edge, community, and path-depth limits |
| Silent winner between lists | `conflict` until the user overrides |
| Forged appeals | Appeals must be signed by their subject |

## Rollout

Version 1 is additive: no existing route, table or authorization decision reads
it, and follows and overrides are local, so removing the resolvers is a full
rollback. Any change in meaning needs a new schema string; changing the vectors
means regenerating them with `generate_vectors.py` and passing all four
resolvers. Publishing lists over relays and the authoring and follow UI are not
implemented yet.

pages.description: Suite version: 1.0.0-rc.1 · Vectors: signatures.json, events.json, sessions.json · Part of the ForkMesh protocol suite
pages.markdown:
# Signatures and authentication

Suite version: `1.0.0-rc.1` · Vectors: `signatures.json`, `events.json`,
`sessions.json` · Part of the [ForkMesh protocol suite](README.md)

## Ed25519

- **FM-SIG-001** MUST — Signatures are Ed25519 (RFC 8032, PureEdDSA, no
  context) verified with the cofactorless equation `[S]B = R + [k]A`, where
  `k = SHA-512(R || A || M) mod L`. A verifier rejects:
  - a signature that is not exactly 64 bytes;
  - a scalar `S ≥ L`, so no `S + L` malleability;
  - a point encoding with `y ≥ p`, no square root, or `x = 0` with the sign
    bit set;
  - the identity as the public key;
  - any public key outside the prime-order subgroup (`[L]A ≠ identity`), which
    excludes all small-order and mixed-order keys.

Implementations that wrap a platform verifier (for example WebCrypto) MUST add
the checks their platform omits.

## Domain separation

- **FM-SIG-002** MUST — Every signed message begins with a frozen,
  scheme-specific prefix, and a verifier builds the message itself from the
  fields it will act on. A client-supplied message is never accepted. A
  signature valid under one prefix therefore never verifies under another
  scheme, another version, or a substituted field such as a different HTTP
  method.

### Canonical-string schemes

These follow FM-ENC-007. The fields below come after the prefix line.

| Prefix | Fields | Verified by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `forkmesh-catalog-v1` | owner, name, updatedAt | relay, catalog publish (public records only) |
| `forkmesh-catalog-v2` | recordSha256 | relay, catalog publish |
| `forkmesh-repostate-v1` | owner, repo, stateHash (FM-ID-005), updatedAt | relay, catalog publish and mirror attestations |
| `forkmesh-private-manifest-v1` | owner, name, opaqueRepoId, keyEpoch, manifestHash, updatedAt | relay, private catalog publish |
| `forkmesh-view-v1` | owner, repo, ts | relay, private browse and clone |
| `forkmesh-rotate-v1` | oldPubkey, newPubkey, ts | relay, account key rotation (signed by the old key) |
| `forkmesh-git-push-v1` | owner, repo, method, ts, bodySha256 | relay and mirror gateway, HTTPS receive-pack |

For `forkmesh-catalog-v2`, `recordSha256` is the lowercase hex SHA-256 of the
normalized catalog record minus its descriptive `signature` field. The record
is serialized with sorted keys, no whitespace, and ASCII escaping. The
[published protocol reference](https://forkmesh.com/docs/protocol/#signature-schemes)
lists the remaining legacy schemes (issue, discussion, pull, release, room,
node link). Their field layout is informative until they receive vectors; see
TM-004 in the [threat model](threat-model.md).

### Repository-bound legacy event schemes

This subsection is informative. The v1 strings `forkmesh-issue-event-v1`,
`forkmesh-discussion-event-v1`, `forkmesh-pull-event-v1` and
`forkmesh-pull-comment-v1` bind no repository, so a signed record could be
replayed into another repository. The v2 form inserts the repository on the
second line: `forkmesh-<kind>-v2\n<owner>/<repo>\n` followed by the v1 body
(owner and name lowercased; behind an organization alias either owner is
accepted). Verifiers try v2 first. API intake accepts v1 only until
`EVENT_SIGNATURE_V1_INTAKE_UNTIL_MS` (a constant in each intake file); records
already committed in a repository's own `.forkmesh/` tree stay valid as v1.
All interactive clients sign v2.

## Collaboration envelopes

- **FM-SIG-003** MUST — A collaboration event's signing bytes are
  `"forkmesh-collaboration-event-v1\n"` followed by the canonical JSON of the
  unsigned envelope. The unsigned envelope is the event without `signature`
  and `eventId`, with exactly the keys `schema`, `repository`, `policy`,
  `family`, `object`, `action`, `author`, `sequence`, `clock`, `issuedAt`,
  `parents`, `references`, and `payload`. The author's key signs those bytes.
- **FM-SIG-004** MUST — A receiver rejects an event at the first failing step
  and never lets it influence causality, authorization, or state:
  1. size and canonical parse (FM-ENC-004, FM-ENC-005);
  2. exact key set (`invalid_envelope_keys`), then schema identifier
     (`unsupported_schema`);
  3. field shapes: repository URN, policy digest, known family and action,
     object URN of that family, author and signature encodings, non-negative
     safe integers, sorted duplicate-free `parents` (at most 64), references,
     and payload structure;
  4. event identity (`event_id_mismatch`, FM-ID-004);
  5. for `create` and `decide`, object identity (`object_id_mismatch`,
     FM-ID-003);
  6. repository binding (`wrong_repository`) and policy binding
     (`unknown_policy`) against the pinned policy;
  7. the Ed25519 signature (`invalid_signature`).

  Binding is checked before the signature. A replay into another repository
  is therefore classified as a replay even when its signature is also invalid.

Causality, sequence, equivocation, and authorization rules follow in
[Relay, synchronization, and migration](relay-sync-and-migration.md#collaboration-log-exchange).

## Request authentication

- **FM-AUTH-001** MUST — A time-bound request proof (`view`, `rotate`, and
  `git-push` schemes) is accepted only when its timestamp field is within
  300,000 ms of the verifier's clock in either direction, inclusive. Senders
  write the timestamp as ASCII decimal digits. A verifier rejects a timestamp
  that is not a base-10 integer, and it signs-checks the field text as sent
  (FM-ENC-007). The window limits replay but does not prevent it; see TM-012.
- **FM-AUTH-002** MUST — An HTTPS push is authorized by a signature over
  `forkmesh-git-push-v1`. Before signing and verifying, the owner is trimmed and
  lowercased, the repository trimmed, the method trimmed and uppercased, and
  the body digest trimmed and lowercased. Anything else is rejected: an owner
  that is not a valid account name, a repository that is not a single safe
  path segment, a method other than `GET` or `POST`, a timestamp that is not
  1–16 digits, or a body digest that is not 64 hex digits. The ref
  advertisement `GET` signs the digest of the empty body. When the relay
  streams a pack it has not buffered, it forwards the signed digest, and the
  gateway MUST check the received bytes against it before running
  receive-pack.
- **FM-AUTH-003** MUST — A portable session token is
  `v1.<claim>.<signature>`. `<claim>` is 80–1024 base64url characters of
  ASCII-escaped canonical JSON. `<signature>` is 86 characters and signs
  `"forkmesh-portable-session-v1\n" || <claim>` with the router key. The claim
  has exactly the keys:
  - `type` = `forkmesh.portable-session`;
  - `aud` = `forkmesh-mirror-dashboard`;
  - `v` = 1;
  - integer `iat` and `exp`;
  - `sub`: 32–128 lowercase hex;
  - `name`: an account name;
  - `sid` and `jti`: opaque 16–128 base64url-alphabet strings.

  A verifier rejects, in order: framing (`token_invalid`), encodings
  (`encoding_invalid`), claim shape (`claim_invalid`), time (`not_current`:
  `iat ≤ 0`, `exp ≤ iat`, lifetime over 12 hours, `iat` more than 60 s ahead,
  or `exp` more than 60 s past), a non-canonical claim
  (`claim_noncanonical`), and the signature (`signature_invalid`).
- **FM-AUTH-004** MUST — A catalog publication is signed by a key registered
  to the owner account.
  - When `catalogSigVersion` is 2, `catalogSig` MUST verify
    `forkmesh-catalog-v2`.
  - Otherwise it MUST verify `forkmesh-catalog-v1`, and only for a record
    whose visibility is `public`. Any other visibility is refused with HTTP 426
    `client_upgrade_required` and `requiredCatalogSigVersion: 2` before any
    confidential field is stored.
  - A present `stateSig` MUST verify `forkmesh-repostate-v1`, and a present but
    invalid attestation rejects the whole write.
  - A record whose `updatedAt` is older than the stored record is rejected as
    a rollback.

Inbox submissions (issues, pulls, discussions) prove only that a record was
not altered after signing. They carry no authority. The repository owner's
review and push is the authorization step.

pages.title: Version negotiation
pages.description: Suite version: 1.0.0-rc.1 · Vectors: events.json, identifiers.json, signatures.json, sessions.json · Part of the ForkMesh protocol suite
pages.markdown:
# Version negotiation

Suite version: `1.0.0-rc.1` · Vectors: `events.json`, `identifiers.json`,
`signatures.json`, `sessions.json` · Part of the [ForkMesh protocol
suite](README.md)

ForkMesh has no interactive handshake. Every signed or hashed structure
carries an explicit version identifier, and each receiver selects exactly one
verifier from it:

| Structure | Identifier | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Collaboration event | `forkmesh-collaboration-event-v1` | `schema` field and signing domain |
| Collaboration policy | `forkmesh-collaboration-policy-v1` | `schema` field |
| Collaboration state | `forkmesh-collaboration-state-v1` | `schema` field |
| Canonical-string schemes | `forkmesh-<scheme>-v<N>` | first line of the signed message |
| Catalog publication | `catalogSigVersion` 1 or 2 | request field; selects the scheme |
| Portable session | `v1.` token prefix and claim `v: 1` | token framing and claim |
| Repository migration | `forkmesh-repository-migration-v1`, `forkmesh-repository-migration-state-v1` | job and receipt `schema` |
| Room key proof | `forkmesh-room-key-v2` (v1 only for the compatibility room) | first line of the signed message |

The only advertised negotiation is the catalog upgrade response: HTTP 426
with `{"error": "client_upgrade_required", "requiredCatalogSigVersion": 2}`.
Git protocol v0/v2 negotiation belongs to stock Git.

- **FM-VER-001** MUST — Receivers match version identifiers exactly. They
  reject an unknown or future identifier with the structure's stable code
  (`unsupported_schema`, `invalid_policy`, `token_invalid`, `claim_invalid`),
  never parse it heuristically, and never ignore unknown fields in a signed
  structure.
- **FM-VER-002** MUST NOT — A receiver MUST NOT downgrade. A message that
  fails verification under its declared version is never retried under an
  older version's rules. An older version stays accepted only within its
  published scope: `forkmesh-catalog-v1` only for public records, and
  `forkmesh-room-key-v1` only for the public compatibility room. Because
  prefixes differ, a signature over one version never verifies as another.
- **FM-VER-003** MUST — The bytes an identifier covers are frozen. Any change
  to signed or hashed bytes, field order, normalization, or meaning requires a
  new identifier, and the committed vectors for the existing identifier stay
  unchanged.
- **FM-VER-004** MUST — A new identifier rolls out in a fixed order. First,
  readers that verify and preserve the new identifier deploy. Then writers
  begin emitting it. Readers keep accepting the previous identifier for as
  long as retained history contains it. Rollback reverses the order
  (FM-MIG-003).

pages.title: Chat encryption and public integrations
pages.description: How chat messages are sealed device to device, who can read each kind of conversation, and how apps and webhooks post into it. Part of Security; the overview is on Encryption and…
pages.markdown:
# Chat encryption and public integrations

How chat messages are sealed device to device, who can read each kind of
conversation, and how apps and webhooks post into it. Part of
[Security](README.md); the overview is on
[Encryption and signatures](../encryption.md#end-to-end-encrypted-chat-and-calls).

All chat traffic uses an outer AES-256-GCM room cipher whose passphrase is
derived from the controller's `DATA_KEY`. It protects the wire and retained
storage from third parties, not from the controller operator. On top of it each
conversation has one policy:

| Conversation | Content policy | Who can read it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| World `#general`, public `#` channel | Device-to-device encryption to every device in the room | Anyone who joins the room: guests, and the controller, which can join as a device |
| Private channel or direct message | Device-to-device encryption inside the room cipher | Only the members (the server checks who may join); a private channel's webhook and notice lines are also readable by the server |

Every person's message is sealed and signed by their device, in public rooms
too, so nobody can post, edit or delete as that person. That does not hide
public rooms from the server: they run the open policy, so any device that
joins gets the keys of the messages sealed after it arrived, and the
controller can join as a device. Public channels are controller-readable;
nothing private belongs there. Direct messages, private channels and Cove
invites never travel through a shared room; they use the server's direct and
private rooms, and clients drop such frames if they show up in a shared room.

Apps, webhooks and ForkMesh's own notices are posted unsealed by the server,
in public and private channels alike (never in direct messages), so the server
can read them; clients mark a webhook's line "server-visible". The server marks
each frame it injects, removes that mark from anything a client sends, and
clients show a marked frame as the app or webhook it names, never as a person.
An unmarked, unsealed frame is dropped.
A line a device posts for ForkBot shows as "forkbot · via" the person who
posted it. Making a channel public affects only new messages; making it
private rotates the room key and revokes its incoming webhooks.

Device-to-device encryption uses chat protocol v3, and direct
messages use v4, which adds a per-message ratchet. Every client (web, desktop,
iOS, Android) speaks only these; older v2 frames are ignored. The full
specifications are `docs/app/chat-protocol-v3.md` and
`docs/app/chat-protocol-v4.md` in the ForkMesh repository.

## Device keys

Each installation keeps two kinds of keys on the device (browser storage
wrapped by a non-extractable key where the browser supports it, the desktop
secure store, the iOS keychain, Android Keystore-wrapped storage):

- an **identity key** (Ed25519) for the life of the install, which signs
  everything the device sends;
- **prekeys**, each an X25519 key plus an ML-KEM-768 (post-quantum) key. A new
  prekey is made every 24 hours and its private half is deleted 8 days after it
  was made.

Private keys never leave the device.

## Bundles and new devices

A device announces itself in each room with a signed bundle: its identity key,
its newest prekey, the account it belongs to and the sender id it uses in that
room. Other devices check the signature before using it.

- In every room except direct messages the sender id is the device's own
  Ed25519 node key, and the bundle carries a second signature by that key. A
  bundle without it is dropped, and a key id already seen keeps its sender id,
  so one device cannot speak, edit or delete as another. Browsers keep a
  separate node key for a signed-out visitor and for each account, so a
  guest's messages cannot be linked to the account signed in later.
- The account name in a bundle is only a claim. Clients show it after the
  server confirms that the node key is bound to that account (each device binds
  its key at sign-in); otherwise the sender is shown as a guest.
- Edits, deletes, reactions, stickers and thread replies count only from
  sealed frames, and an edit or delete only from the message's author.

- In a direct message, the server cannot add a key: a bundle that names
  anyone other than the two people in the conversation is dropped, and a second device for an account that already
  has one is **held**: it receives nothing and its messages are not shown until
  you approve it. You see a line in the conversation and a banner with Approve
  and Block.
- Channels and Office rooms accept every validly signed device whose bundle
  is also signed by its node key.

## Sealed messages

For each message the sender picks a random content key and encrypts
the message with AES-256-GCM. For each approved device it then combines a fresh
X25519 exchange with an ML-KEM-768 encapsulation to that device's prekey,
derives a wrapping key with HKDF-SHA256, and wraps the content key. The whole
frame, including every wrapped key, is signed by the sender's identity key and
carries a counter and a timestamp.

A receiving device rejects a frame that:

- is not signed by an approved device;
- claims a sender id other than the one in that device's signed bundle;
- repeats a counter it has already accepted (the relay replaying a frame);
- was not wrapped for one of its kept prekeys.

Relay-held copies are kept for up to 7 days; prekeys live 8, so a message can
still be opened while it is waiting. After a prekey is deleted, nothing sealed
to it can be opened again, even with the device in hand.

## Direct messages: a key for every message

In a direct message each pair of devices runs a ratchet, like Signal's Double
Ratchet. The first message starts it with the same X25519 + ML-KEM-768 exchange
against the other device's prekey; after that every message has its own key,
derived from a chain that only moves forward, and the key is deleted as soon as
the message is opened. Each time the conversation changes direction, both
devices mix in a fresh X25519 exchange and a fresh ML-KEM-768 encapsulation.

- A device stolen today cannot open direct messages it had already received:
  their keys are gone.
- A device that was compromised recovers once the other person replies; against
  a quantum-capable attacker, once its prekey rotates (24 hours).
- A device never encrypts to itself; your own messages stay in your device's
  history, not in a copy the server holds for you.
- If a device loses its ratchet state, it asks the sender to start over and
  the sender re-sends what it still holds.

## Safety numbers

In a direct message, the encryption panel shows a 60-digit safety number and a
QR code. It covers every approved device of both people. Compare the digits
with the other person, or scan their code, then mark the conversation verified.
If an approved device is added or removed the number changes, the verified mark
is cleared and the conversation says so.

## Limits

- The controller still sees who talks to whom, when, and how much, and it can
  drop or delay frames.
- Channels approve every device that presents a valid bundle; only direct
  messages hold new devices. World and public channels are open rooms: anyone
  who joins can read what is said there from then on.
- In channels and Office rooms, forward secrecy is per prekey, not per
  message: a device compromised today exposes the channel messages sealed to
  the prekeys it still holds (up to 8 days). Channels keep this because the web
  reopens their history from the relay on every load.
- In direct messages, the messages sent before the other device first replies
  still rest on its prekey (up to 8 days); Signal adds one-time prekeys for
  these.
- A new device cannot read messages sent before it was approved.
- A modified web client served by a compromised host can read what it shows
  you, as with any web app.
- None of this has had an outside security audit yet.

## Compared with Signal

Direct messages now have per-message forward secrecy, as Signal does. Signal
is still ahead in one way: sealed sender hides who sent a message from Signal's
own server, while the ForkMesh server still knows which two accounts are in a
direct message. That is the next step. ForkMesh adds post-quantum key agreement
at the start of every session and on every ratchet step, a signature on every
frame, holds a new device of a contact until you approve it (Signal warns and
keeps sending), and lets nearby devices chat directly over Wi-Fi or Bluetooth
without a server.

## Implementations

Browser (`app/public/chat-seal.js`, `app/public/chat-mlkem.js`,
`app/public/chat-room-transport.js`, `app/public/chat-frame-auth.js`), desktop (`desktop/src/RoomSeal.{h,cpp}`),
iOS (`FMCrypto/RoomSeal.swift`) and Android (`crypto/RoomSeal.kt`) all open the
shared wire vectors in `conformance/chat/v3/vectors.json`,
`conformance/chat/v3/node-binding.json` and
`conformance/chat/v4/vectors.json`, so a change to key
derivation, signed strings, encoding or frame shape fails the cross-client
tests.

pages.title: Hidden Unicode in user input
pages.description: Every text field on the web, the desktop and both phone apps removes invisible Unicode characters as the user types or pastes, and the app server removes them again from every…
pages.markdown:
# Hidden Unicode in user input

Every text field on the web, the desktop and both phone apps removes
invisible Unicode characters as the user types or pastes, and the app server
removes them again from every parsed request body. One policy,
`forkmesh-hidden-unicode-v1`, is shared by all of them and pinned by
`conformance/hidden-unicode/v1/vectors.json`. Part of
[Security](README.md).

## Why

Invisible characters let text say one thing to a person and another to a
program:

- **Tag characters (U+E0000 to U+E007F)** spell out ASCII that no font draws.
  This "ASCII smuggling" hides instructions for language models in otherwise
  normal text. In 2026 it was used at scale in phishing mail, and it breaks
  agent pipelines that read untrusted text ([The New Stack, September 2026](https://thenewstack.io/?p=22835903)).
- **Variation selectors (U+FE00 to U+FE0F, U+E0100 to U+E01EF)**: there are 256
  of them, one per byte value, so a chain of them after a single emoji can carry
  any payload ([Paul Butler, 2025](https://paulbutler.org/2025/smuggling-arbitrary-data-through-an-emoji/)).
  The same trick reportedly hid an npm loader in 2025.
- **Bidi overrides, embeddings and isolates (U+202A to U+202E, U+2066 to U+2069)**
  reorder what is displayed without changing the logical text. This is the
  "Trojan Source" attack on code review ([Krebs, 2021](https://krebsonsecurity.com/2021/11/trojan-source-bug-threatens-the-security-of-all-code/)).
- **Zero-width and other format characters** (U+200B, U+2060 to U+2064,
  U+FEFF, the soft hyphen, the Hangul fillers) hide binary payloads, split
  words to slip past filters, and make two names that look the same compare
  unequal.

Agents on this platform read issues, chat, pull requests and notes. Nothing a
person cannot see should reach an agent, the database or another user.

## The policy

`app/src/hidden_unicode.py` is the reference. Its rules:

1. **Always removed:**
   - C0 and C1 controls, except tab, line feed and carriage return
   - soft hyphen U+00AD and the combining grapheme joiner U+034F
   - the Hangul fillers U+115F, U+1160, U+3164 and U+FFA0
   - the Khmer inherent vowels U+17B4 and U+17B5
   - the Mongolian free variation selectors and vowel separator (U+180B to U+180F)
   - zero-width space U+200B
   - the bidi embeddings, overrides and isolates
   - U+2060 to U+206F
   - the byte-order mark U+FEFF
   - interlinear annotation (U+FFF9 to U+FFFB)
   - the shorthand and musical format controls
   - every noncharacter and lone surrogate
   - variation selectors U+FE00 to U+FE0D and U+E0100 to U+E01EF
   - tag characters, except the one valid use below
2. **Line and paragraph separators** U+2028 and U+2029 become a newline.
3. **Kept only where real text needs them.** Each rule looks at the character
   before (the last character kept) and the character after.
   - **Emoji presentation selectors** U+FE0E and U+FE0F: kept once after a
     visible character. They are dropped at the start of the text, after
     whitespace, after a joiner, or when repeated.
   - **Zero-width joiner** U+200D: kept between two emoji (this keeps family,
     profession and flag sequences working). Also kept between two letters of
     a script that joins: Arabic, Syriac, the Indic scripts, Tibetan, Myanmar,
     Khmer and Mongolian.
   - **Zero-width non-joiner** U+200C: kept only between letters of those
     joining scripts, as Persian and the Indic scripts need it.
   - **Direction marks** U+200E, U+200F and U+061C: kept only next to a
     right-to-left letter.
   - **Tag characters:** kept only as the subdivision flag sequence. That is
     U+1F3F4, then 2 to 7 tag letters or digits, then the cancel tag (the flags
     of England, Scotland and Wales).

Each rule only removes characters: nothing is added or reordered, and visible
text (accents, CJK, private-use glyphs, visible spaces) is untouched. Stripping
is idempotent.

**Out of scope:** visible abuse such as stacked combining marks
("Zalgo") or look-alike letters (homoglyphs). The policy removes what cannot
be seen.

## Where it runs

| Surface | Code | When |
| --- | --- | --- |
| App server | `app/src/hidden_unicode.py`; `request_bodies.bounded_json_request`, every `json_body` copy, the admin form parsers, `app/host/forkmesh_host/js.py` `Request.json()` / `Request.formData()` | after parsing, before the handler sees the body |
| Web | `www/public/safe-input.js`, loaded by every page next to `analytics.js` | capture-phase `input`, `change` and `compositionend` on inputs, textareas and contenteditable |
| Desktop | `desktop/src/HiddenUnicode.{h,cpp}`, `HiddenUnicodeGuard.{h,cpp}`, installed in `main.cpp` | `QLineEdit` through a validator; `QPlainTextEdit` and `QTextEdit` on each user change |
| iPhone | `native/ios/ForkMeshCore/Sources/FMBase/HiddenUnicode.swift`, `native/ios/ForkMesh/Platform/HiddenUnicodeInputGuard.swift`, installed by `AppDelegate` | every `UITextField` and `UITextView` text change, SwiftUI fields included |
| Android | `native/android/core/.../security/HiddenUnicode.kt`, `app/.../ui/kit/FmSafeInput.kt` | `FmTextField`, `AccountFilledField`, every raw `BasicTextField` / `OutlinedTextField`, and an `InputFilter` on the two `EditText`s |

The desktop guard runs from an application-wide filter on every widget's
`Polish` event, so `guardWidget` checks the widget's type before reading its
`forkmeshHiddenUnicodeGuard` property: a dynamic-property read is a string
search, too costly to run for every label, button and frame.

### Exactness exceptions

Some text has to stay byte for byte:

- **Raw bodies.** The text and byte readers are not touched:
  `bounded_request_text`, `request.text()`, `request.bytes()`. Signature and
  digest checks (ActivityPub inbox, webhooks, federation relay, runner
  leases, hosted Git) therefore still see the exact body. Only parsed values
  are cleaned.
- **Secrets.** On the server, values under keys that name a secret stay
  exact. These are keys containing `password`, `passphrase`, `passcode`,
  `secret`, `token`, `signature`, `ciphertext`, `privatekey` or `sealed`,
  plus the exact keys `sig`, `nonce`, `salt`, `otp`, `totp`, `pin`, `mac`
  and `hmac`. Every client leaves password fields alone too
  (`type=password`, `QLineEdit::Password`, `isSecureTextEntry`,
  `PasswordVisualTransformation`). A password is hashed and never shown, and
  rewriting it would lock out anyone whose saved password already contains
  such a character.
- **Signed source text.** Values under the keys `patch`, `commits`,
  `suggestionPatch` and `anchorLines` stay exact on the server. They are git
  patches, commit mboxes and code lines: their author signs them byte for
  byte and the owner replays them with git. Code may legitimately contain any
  of these characters, and rewriting it breaks the signature and corrupts the
  patch; hidden characters in code are a review concern. Prose fields of the
  same events (`title`, `body`) are still cleaned, so a signed title or
  comment that carries hidden characters is refused (see below).
- **IME composition.** Text is cleaned only once composition ends, so CJK and
  other input methods are not disturbed.
- **Read-only desktop views.** These show text exactly as received. Editable
  desktop editors clean only what the user inserts, and only while the editor
  is the window's focus widget. A file loaded into an editor is therefore not
  rewritten until someone edits it.
- **Undo.** After an undo or redo the desktop leaves the text alone. Undo
  first takes back the cleanup, and a second undo takes back the paste; this
  is the same as autocorrect.
- **Not covered.** The terminal widget passes keystrokes to a shell
  unchanged. End-to-end sealed chat is ciphertext on the server, so only the
  clients clean it.

## Changing the policy

1. Edit `app/src/hidden_unicode.py`.
2. Mirror the change in `safe-input.js`, `HiddenUnicode.cpp`,
   `HiddenUnicode.swift` and `HiddenUnicode.kt`.
3. Add a case to `conformance/hidden-unicode/v1/generate_vectors.py` and run
   it.
4. Copy `vectors.json` to
   `native/android/core/src/test/resources/hidden-unicode/v1/`.
5. Run the checks:
   - `python -m pytest -q app/tests/test_hidden_unicode.py`
   - `forkmesh-hidden-unicode-tests`
   - `swift test --filter HiddenUnicodeTests` in `native/ios/ForkMeshCore`
   - `./gradlew :core:coreTest -Pfilter=HiddenUnicode`

A change that keeps or drops a different set of characters is a new policy
version, so it goes in `v2`.

Write invisible characters in source as numeric code points (`0x200B`,
`chr(0x200B)`). Editing tools can turn a typed `\u200b` escape into the real
invisible character. `test_new_sources_hold_no_literal_hidden_characters`
fails if one slips into the policy files.

## Signed code in pull requests

Cleaning a pull's `patch` and `commits` would fail every pull whose code
holds a listed character (a UTF-8 byte-order mark in a Windows file, a
zero-width space inside a string) with `bad_signature`. `pulls_handler` reads the body once more without cleaning
(`bounded_json_request_with_raw`), verifies the signature over the exact
`patch` and `commits`, keeps them exact, and stores `hiddenUnicode: true` on
the pull when either holds a character this policy removes, so a reviewer and
an agent can be warned instead of the bytes being changed. Prose stays clean:
when the signature only verifies over a title, base or head that cleaning
changed, the server answers 400 `hidden_unicode` with the field names instead
of `bad_signature`.
The `MAX_PULL_BYTES` cap counts the exact `patch` and `commits`, kept
characters included, and code holding a lone surrogate (valid JSON, not
UTF-8) is refused with 400 `pull_invalid`, since it cannot be hashed for the
signature check. Nothing reads `hiddenUnicode` yet: the review pages do not
show the warning.

pages.title: Host-mode agent boundaries
pages.description: What a desktop coding agent can read, execute and reach for each provider and mode, which secrets it can see, what limits its network, how injected instructions are handled, and…
pages.markdown:
# Host-mode agent boundaries

What a desktop coding agent can read, execute and reach for each provider and
mode, which secrets it can see, what limits its network, how injected
instructions are handled, and what limits spend. Each claim is proven by a
named check. Part of [Security](README.md); the wider attacker model is in
the [threat model](../protocol/threat-model.md).

## Run the checks

```sh
cmake -S desktop -B desktop/build -G Ninja
cmake --build desktop/build --target forkmesh-agent-boundary-tests \
  forkmesh-codex-tests forkmesh-vm-runtime-tests forkmesh-agent-access-tests \
  forkmesh-agent-transport-tests
desktop/build/forkmesh-agent-boundary-tests
```

[`desktop/tests/test_agent_host_boundaries.cpp`](../../desktop/tests/test_agent_host_boundaries.cpp) prints one `PASS`/`FAIL` line
per check. It runs in a temporary `HOME` and XDG tree, drops `FORKMESH_HOME`
and `FORKMESH_PROJECTS_DIR`, and plants canary secrets. Stand-in `claude` and
`codex` executables go through the real launch paths (login shell, jail,
Landlock wrapper, KVM wrapper) and try to read outside the worktree, run a
subprocess, connect over loopback TCP and connect to a Unix socket. Checks
that pin a known weakness fail when the boundary changes in either direction.

## Provider by mode

| Mode (host, no KVM) | Launch | Read | Execute | Reach |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Claude Auto | skips permission prompts | anything the user can read | any command | any destination and socket |
| Claude Edit | edits run, other tools ask in the CLI | same | after the CLI's prompt | same |
| Claude Plan | edits and commands held until the plan is accepted | same | held by the CLI | same |
| Claude Ask | asks before edits and commands | same | after the prompt | same |
| Codex (all modes) | approval `never`, full-access sandbox | same | any command | same |
| Project lock (default rules, Linux) | Landlock helper (`tools/forkmesh_agent_guard.py`) | worktree, project folders, Git metadata, provider login, read-only Git config | as above | as above |
| KVM (Linux, opt-in) | a QEMU/KVM guest via Lima | launch directory and Git metadata only, not the host home | any command in the guest | guest network |

Off Linux there is no folder lock. The external-call gate (a Claude
PreToolUse hook) applies on top of host modes whenever rules need it; it is a
tool-layer classifier, not a kernel policy.

## Secrets

- **Environment.** A host agent inherits the desktop's environment except its
  own provider's credential variables (`desktop/src/AgentCredentialEnvironment.h`).
  Other providers' keys, forge tokens, cloud credentials and `SSH_AUTH_SOCK`
  are inherited.
- **Files.** Unrestricted, the agent reads whatever the user can. Under the
  project lock, `~/.ssh`, `~/.aws` and the rest of home are refused unless
  granted; the provider login directory stays readable.
- **Sockets.** Landlock does not mediate Unix-socket connects, so a loaded SSH
  agent remains usable.
- **KVM.** The environment bridge is deny-by-default; SSH agent forwarding is
  off and host login files are not mounted.

Recommendation: run high-risk work with only staging credentials and no SSH
agent loaded, or in KVM. `.gitignore` is not a secret boundary.

## Egress

No host-mode configuration limits the network at the OS level. The
external-call gate (`AgentNetworkGate.cpp`, `AgentRunRules.cpp`) classifies
shell commands that name a non-local destination and web fetch/search tools,
and asks, blocks or allows per the project rule (default Ask). Commands that
hide their destination (encoded payloads, self-written programs, binaries with
their own HTTP client) are not seen. Server runners have their own egress
rules ([runners](../operations/runners.md)).

## Prompt injection

Teammate prompts instruct models to treat repository, issue, pull request and
external content as untrusted data; that is an instruction, not isolation.
`conformance/agent-adversarial/v1/fixtures.json` holds malicious text per
vector with the tool call it requests. For each fixture the test runs the
rules decision, sends the call through the real hook to a gate that declines,
and runs secret reads with and without the lock. Outcomes are `ask`, `deny`,
`folder-lock` or `known-gap`; to add a fixture, append it with its `expect`.

Known gaps share one cause: anything that looks local to the classifier runs
without a prompt, such as printing an inherited token or decoding and running
a hidden network command. Defences for high-risk work: a narrower environment,
Ask or Plan mode, KVM, and human review of the branch.

## Spend

- Per-session token and cost estimates (display only).
- A concurrency limit (`agents/maxRunning`, default 5).
- Continual teammates wait for a person's decision between cycles.
- A CLI that exits without a result is relaunched at most twice.

There is no hard dollar cap; the only hard ceilings are the provider
account's own limits. Set them at the provider for unattended use.

pages.title: Node link grants: both parties consent
pages.description: Part of Security; key and signature basics are in Encryption and signatures.
pages.markdown:
# Node link grants: both parties consent

Part of [Security](README.md); key and signature basics are in
[Encryption and signatures](../encryption.md).

`POST /api/accounts/link-grant` (`_account_link_grant` in `app/src/entry.py`)
moves a node account to a new owner. A node changes owner only when both
sides prove themselves in one request:

1. **The node** signs a grant with its account key.
2. **The new owner** accepts with its own credentials: an authenticated
   session (cookie, `sessionToken` or `Authorization: Bearer`) or a signature
   from one of its signing keys (account `pubkey` or an enabled `owner_sign`
   device key).

The owner is always the accepting account; a body `user` is only a claim
checked against it. App tokens (`fmat_…`) are not accepted as a session.

## Grant forms

| Form | Canonical string (`\n`-joined) | Names the owner | Who may accept |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| v1 | `forkmesh-link-grant-v1`, node, ts | no | the session account; a body `user` must equal it |
| v2 | `forkmesh-link-grant-v2`, node, user, ts, nonce | yes | only `user`, by session or signed accept |

Signed accept (body fields `user`, `acceptTs`, `acceptSig`); it includes the
grant signature, so it cannot be moved to another grant:

```
forkmesh-link-accept-v1
<node>
<user>
<grant sig>
<acceptTs>
```

`nonce` is 16–64 characters of `[A-Za-z0-9_-]`.

## Freshness and replay

- A grant is valid from 1 minute before its `ts` to 5 minutes after
  (`LINK_GRANT_MAX_FUTURE_MS`, `LINK_GRANT_MAX_AGE_MS`); a signed accept uses
  the ±5-minute login window.
- Each redeemed grant is burned in `link_codes` (`grant:<node>:<ts>:<sig>`
  for v1, `grant2:<node>:<nonce>` for v2). A second redemption answers
  `409 grant_used`, unless the node is already owned by the acceptor
  (`alreadyLinked`, nothing written).

## Errors

| Error | Status | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `bad_signature` | 401 | node signature does not verify (v2: includes a different `user`) |
| `grant_expired` | 401 | `ts` outside the window |
| `session_required` | 401 | no session and no signed accept |
| `accept_expired` | 401 | `acceptTs` outside the window |
| `bad_accept_signature` | 401 | accept does not verify with the account's keys |
| `grant_user_mismatch` | 403 | the grant or body names another account |
| `no_such_user`, `not_a_user` | 404, 403 | acceptor missing, inactive or a node account |
| `grant_used` | 409 | already redeemed |

## Audit

Every decision after a valid node signature writes `node.link_grant` to the
sensitive audit log (success with `{grant, via, from, to}`, or denied with
`{reason, grant, named, from}`). Requests with an invalid node signature are
not audited, so unauthenticated callers cannot fill the log.

## Clients

| Client | Flow |
| --- | --- |
| Desktop (`openLinkNodeInBrowser`) | signs a v1 grant and opens `/dashboard?link_node=…`; the browser session accepts |
| Web dashboard (`redeemLinkGrant`) | redeems with the signed-in session |
| `tools/next_node_owner.py` | signs a v2 grant on the node; the target accepts with its key or session |
| Go daemon, native apps | do not call link-grant |
