pages.markdown:
# Host intrusion detection (IDS)

Part of [Operations](README.md).

Every core node and runner runs `fmnext-ids`, a small root service
(`deploy/core/ids.py`, installed as `/opt/forkmesh-next/bin/fmnext-ids`,
config `/etc/forkmesh-next/ids.json`, state in `/var/lib/fmnext-ids`). It uses
the Python standard library (plus `python3-cryptography` for signing), runs
with a CPU quota and idle I/O priority, stats files instead of re-reading
them, and re-hashes everything every 6 hours.

On an intrusion it **locks the node down**: the vault key leaves memory, the
node is quarantined in rqlite, the firewall closes and services stop. It also
pages the admins, and mails them itself (see *Direct mail*). Only the
operator can end a lockdown (`tools/next_ids.py release`). Fleet runbook:
[runbook](runbook.md); public threat model:
[threat model](../protocol/threat-model.md).

## Threat model

Detects within seconds: a shell as a service user, logins with unknown keys or
passwords, new privileged accounts, tampering with code, units or security
configuration, ptrace of protected processes, runner jobs escaping their
scope, persistence through cron, listeners, unusual egress or kernel modules,
and an IDS that stops reporting while its node keeps serving.

Does not stop:

- **Root acting faster than the IDS.** Mitigated by fast detection (journald
  lines as they arrive, process scans every 5 s), sealing the key first, and
  peers that vote a node into quarantine when its app runs while its IDS has
  been silent for 3 minutes.
- **A node compromised while unsealed**: its memory held `DATA_KEY`. Rotate
  `DATA_KEY` and vault secrets after any real lockdown ([re-keying](rekey.md)).
- **A compromised operator box**, which holds `DATA_KEY`, the fleet SSH key,
  the IDS master key and the operator release key.
- **HTTPS exfiltration by the app user**: only non-HTTP(S) egress is logged.
- **Non-interactive use of a stolen fleet key** raises only `info` unless
  `ssh_allow` is set.

## Detectors

Override any severity with `[ids] severity = { detector = "lockdown" }` in
`deploy/fleet.toml`.

| Detector | Trigger | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `ssh_unknown_key` | key not in `ssh_fleet_fingerprints` | lockdown |
| `ssh_non_key_login` | password or keyboard-interactive login | lockdown |
| `ssh_foreign_ip` | login from outside `ssh_allow` (when set) | alert |
| `ssh_interactive_login`, `ssh_login_user` | a pty shell; a non-root login | alert |
| `ssh_tool_session` | a command without a pty, sftp or tunnel (the fleet tools) | info |
| `integrity_*` | a change outside a signed expected-change window | lockdown for binaries, the release tree, units, sshd, sudoers, PAM, firewall; else alert |
| `account_uid0`, `account_login_shell`, `group_privileged`, `root_password_set` | account database diffs | lockdown |
| other `account_*`, `group_changed`, `shadow_changed` | account changes | alert |
| `service_user_outside_unit` | a service user's process outside its own unit (outermost unit in the cgroup path) | lockdown |
| `service_user_shell` | a shell or interpreter under a service user | lockdown |
| `service_user_exe` | an executable outside the user's allowlist | alert |
| `exe_suspicious_path` | an executable in `/tmp`, `/dev/shm`, `/var/tmp` or a memfd | lockdown |
| `ptrace` | a traced protected process | lockdown |
| `job_user_outside_scope` | runner job-user process outside a job scope | lockdown |
| `listener_unexpected` | a listener on an unexpected port | alert |
| `egress_unexpected` | a new outbound connection (SYN only) from a service user to a non-web port | alert |
| `kernel_module_loaded`, `kernel_module_taint` | a module loaded after start or a tainting module | alert |
| `privilege_tool` | sudo/su by a non-root account | alert |
| `peer_ids_silent` | a peer's IDS heartbeat is stale while its app runs | alert |
| `quarantined_by_peers` | a majority voted this node into quarantine | lockdown |
| `expectation_rejected` | a forged, replayed or stale expected-change manifest | alert |
| `baseline_tampered`, `baseline_missing` | the baseline failed its HMAC check or vanished | lockdown |
| `reboot` | boot id changed outside a window | info |

A process that exits mid-scan is marked `vanished` and skipped by the unit
checks; a live process with no unit still alerts.

`service_user_exe` skips systemd's `systemd-executor` (systemd 255+) while it
starts a service: between dropping to the service user and `execve`, the
process runs `/usr/lib/systemd/systemd-executor` under the unit's cgroup with
a name like `(caddy)`. Only that path, a parenthesised name and the user's own
unit are skipped (a Caddy restart tripped it); the executor anywhere else, or
under another name, still alerts.

### Process context and verdict

Every process incident (`ptrace`, `exe_suspicious_path`,
`job_user_outside_scope`, `service_user_outside_unit`, `service_user_shell`,
`service_user_exe`) records, as soon as it is detected:

| Key | What |
|---|---|
| `cmdline`, `cwd`, `ppid`, `started` | the process's own command line, working directory, parent and start time |
| `parents` | up to six ancestors, nearest first: pid, exe, user, command line |
| `children` | up to five child processes |
| `environment` | only `SSH_CONNECTION`, `SSH_CLIENT`, `SSH_ORIGINAL_COMMAND`, `REMOTE_ADDR`, `REMOTE_PORT`, `HTTP_X_FORWARDED_FOR`, `HTTP_X_REAL_IP`, `HTTP_USER_AGENT`, `GIT_PROTOCOL`, `GIT_DIR`, `GIT_QUARANTINE_PATH`, `SUDO_USER`, `LOGNAME`, from the process or its nearest ancestor; never any other variable, so no secret leaves the node |
| `connections` | inet sockets held by the process and its ancestors (read in each one's own network namespace), public peers first: this is where a remote IP shows |
| `verdict` | what the IDS concluded, also appended to the summary (and so to the Ping title) |

Command lines and environment values pass through `redact`: a URL's password, an `Authorization:` value, `token=`/`password=`/`secret=`/`key=` values and `--token`/`--password`/`--secret`/`--api-key` arguments become `***`.

Verdicts:

- **likely benign: ForkMesh's own `<hook>` hook during a git push**: the
  shell runs a git receive hook, an ancestor is `git receive-pack`, and the
  hook file carries `# Managed-By: ForkMesh` (the mirror-node `post-receive`
  hook, `server/pushhook.go`; the operator-policy hook) or is the gateway's
  push-rewrite `pre-receive` hook (`tools/mirror_gateway.py`).
- **needs a look: a `<hook>` hook ForkMesh did not write**: the same, but the
  file has no marker or is not a small regular file (never opened then, so a
  FIFO cannot stall the IDS).
- **likely benign: the Actions sandbox self-test**: `/bin/sh -c 'exit 0'` under
  `bwrap` (`server/actions.go`, `probeBubblewrap`).
- **probably an Actions job step**: any other process under `bwrap`.
- **needs a look: git ran a shell command**: `sh -c` directly under git (an
  ssh command, credential helper, alias or hook from config).
- **unexplained**: the process exited before it could be read, or nothing
  above matches.

The verdict never changes the severity: a process can fake its command line,
so benign verdicts say what matched and still ask for a cross-check in the
unit's journal. The added context is trimmed (children, connections,
environment, then the farthest parents) so the stored detail stays valid JSON
under the 4000-character column cap. The Ping and email show the verdict
under the summary and list each parent, child and connection on its own line.

Why: an alert that records only pid, exe, name, unit and user cannot be
explained once the process has exited, which happened with a dash under
`forkmesh-mirror-node.service` on n5.

## Lockdown on a core

1. **Seal**: the app drops `DATA_KEY` and every vault value and exits.
2. **Marker** `/var/lib/fmnext-ids/LOCKDOWN`; drop-ins keep the app, daemon,
   Caddy and certsync from starting, also after reboot.
3. **Quarantine**: a signed `self` row in `cluster_quarantine` and the
   incident in `security_incidents`.
4. **rqlite**: stopped only if the other reachable voters are a majority (at
   least two) with a leader and no other node is quarantined; otherwise it
   keeps running behind the firewall. One healthy peer later removes the node
   as a voter when that is quorum-safe, never below two voters.
5. **Firewall** (`inet fmnext_ids`): inbound only replies, loopback, SSH (on
   `ssh.port`, the fleet's `ssh_port`; [SSH port](ssh-port.md))
   and mesh; outbound only root.
6. **Stop** services.
7. **Alerts.**

Peers then exclude the node from the live set, refuse it unseal and mesh
traffic, and drop its WireGuard packets. The operator-box DNS loop removes it
from DNS after failed probes.

On a runner: marker, kill all job scopes, report to
`/api/runners/security-incident` (the app revokes the runner), firewall, stop
the daemon.

## Alerts

Every incident is logged to the journal and recorded in `security_incidents`
(cores) or through the signed runner API. Unsealed core apps
(`app/host/forkmesh_host/ids_alerts.py`, leaderless, compare-and-set claim)
deliver them, so delivery works while the reporting node is down. When no
app is unsealed (every core sealed, locked down or stopped), the IDS's own
direct mail still reaches the admins for lockdown, `test` and unrecorded
incidents (*Direct mail* below); `alert` and `info` rows wait for an app:

| Severity | Record | Ping (inbox, live clients, push) | Email |
|---|---|---|---|
| `info` | yes | no | no |
| `alert` | yes | every admin | no |
| `lockdown`, `test` | yes | every admin | yes, within limits |

The `security_alert` Ping cannot be muted and carries the full incident and
lockdown step outcomes. A lockdown row waits up to 15 s for its step results
before delivery.

Email limits (counters in the rqlite `mail_budget` table): one email per node
and detector per hour, five IDS emails per day in total; suppressed alerts
are summarised in the next allowed email. Service accounts, unverified
addresses and domains that receive no mail are skipped.

All platform mail shares one daily budget (`app/src/mail_budget.py`):
`MAIL_DAILY_LIMIT` per day with `MAIL_ACCOUNT_RESERVE_PERCENT` reserved for
verification, password and account mail. Set the limit to the provider's real
daily limit.

From the IDS process itself, so an alert gets out when every app is sealed
or down: direct mail (`[ids] direct_mail`, on in the ForkMesh fleet, off in `fleet.example.toml`) and an
optional signed webhook (`[ids] webhook_url`, header
`x-fmnext-ids-signature: v1:<ms>:<hex>`).

### Direct mail

Lockdown and `test` incidents, and any incident the IDS could not record
(rqlite down), are mailed by the IDS to `[ids] mail_to`
(`security@forkmesh.com`) from `mail_from` (empty: `founders@forkmesh.com`,
`smtp_mail.SENDER`), envelope sender `no-reply@forkmesh.com`, as the app's
mail. Without it, a lockdown that sealed every app leaves only the journal
and the `security_incidents` row, and nobody is told.

- **Normally** it submits over SMTP to the node's own Postfix on
  `127.0.0.1:25`, so the same route as every other server mail applies:
  OpenDKIM signing, the n4 relay for n3 and n5, and the Mailtrap fallback
  relay when that route fails ([mail log](mail-log.md#sending-from-the-cores)).
  Only a loopback address is accepted.
- **In a lockdown** the IDS firewall lets only root send off the node, so
  Postfix (user `postfix`) could queue the alert but not deliver it, and the
  peers drop the node's WireGuard packets, so the n4 relay is gone too. The
  IDS (root) then posts to the Mailtrap send API first, with the fallback
  relay's own token read from `/etc/postfix/sasl_passwd` (root-only,
  written by `next_mail.py install`). If that fails the mail goes into the
  Postfix queue and leaves after the release. Opening the lockdown firewall
  to Postfix was rejected: a service-user shell could then send mail out
  through loopback while the node is locked down.
- If Postfix does not answer outside a lockdown, the IDS tries the API the
  same way.
- No secret is pushed for it: the recipient is plain config and the token
  is the one Postfix already holds. A core without the Mailtrap fallback
  (no `MAILTRAP_API_TOKEN` at `next_mail.py install`) still mails normally,
  but its lockdown mail waits for the release.
- Each attempt leaves a masked note in #email-log (`kind: ids_direct`,
  `via: postfix|mailtrap`, the routes tried).
- Check it with `python3 tools/next_ids.py test-fire nN --execute`: the
  `test` incident is mailed directly and through the app.

## Retention

The app's `sensitive-cleanup` cron (`prune_security_incidents` in
`app/src/entry.py`) deletes from `security_incidents`:

- `info` incidents older than 90 days;
- every other severity older than 365 days;
- never a `lockdown` incident, and never an incident whose id a
  `cluster_quarantine` row names (the `incident` field of a signed `self`
  body), so the evidence behind a quarantine or lockdown stays.

Each run deletes at most 2000 rows, oldest first, so one cron tick stays
cheap; a backlog clears over several ticks. A failure is logged and does not
stop the rest of the cleanup.

Why: without retention the table grew to 6.5 MiB and 21k rows on 1 GB
nodes. Ids are random, so `INSERT OR IGNORE` never dedupes, and the IDS
dedupe (`DEDUPE_SECONDS`) is per process only.

## Admin console

Security, Intrusion detection (`?view=ids`, `app/src/ids_console.py`): KPIs,
node states (Normal, Lockdown, Silent, No heartbeat), filters, an incident
chart, groups by detector or node, and the incident log. Read-only.

## Quarantine records

Verified by `app/host/forkmesh_host/ids_records.py` (shared by the app, the
IDS and the desktop); rows are trusted only by Ed25519 signature:

| Kind | Signed by | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `self` | the node's own IDS key | the node is quarantined |
| `vote` | a peer's IDS key | counts once a strict majority of other cores voted |
| `release` | the operator key (operator box only) | clears the records it names or predates |

One compromised node cannot quarantine a peer or release itself. Verifiers
remember what they have seen, so deleting rows does not lift a quarantine.
After a release, peers refuse peer unseal until the operator unseals the node
once.

## Expected changes

Fleet tools push an **expected-change manifest** before each step, signed
with the node's own key `HMAC(FMNEXT_IDS_MASTER, "fmnext-ids-node-key-v1:<node>")`
(pushed as `FMNEXT_IDS_KEY`). Manifests are single-use, valid at most 60
minutes, and list exact file hashes (`files`), accepted paths (`rescan`) and
relaxed detectors (`allow`). The `files` step also expects new unit drop-in
directories. A fresh node starts its IDS last, so its first baseline already
contains everything the start step wrote.

For a manual change, open a window first:

```sh
python3 tools/next_ids.py expect n3 --path /etc/ssh --allow modules --execute
python3 tools/next_ids.py expect n3 --allow ptrace --minutes 10 --execute
python3 tools/next_ids.py baseline n3 --execute
```

## Operator commands

```sh
python3 tools/next_ids.py status [nN|rN ...]
python3 tools/next_ids.py test-fire n3 --execute
python3 tools/next_ids.py baseline nN --execute
python3 tools/next_ids.py release nN --note "why" --execute
python3 tools/next_vault.py seal nN --restart --execute
```

Setup: `next_fleet.py init-secrets` adds `FMNEXT_IDS_MASTER`;
`next_ids.py keygen` creates the operator key (its public half goes into
`deploy/fleet.toml [ids]` with `enabled = true`); `install --steps ids`, then
`base,secrets,files,start` one node at a time; `baseline`; `test-fire`. The
unit passes `--config` before the subcommand.

## Release

1. Investigate: `next_ids.py status`, `journalctl -u fmnext-ids`, the state
   file. SSH still works.
2. Real compromise: do not release. Rebuild the node and rotate `DATA_KEY`,
   vault secrets, `RQLITE_PASSWORD`, `FORKMESH_MESH_SECRET` and the fleet SSH
   key.
3. False positive: `release` signs a release, stores it through a healthy peer
   (rqlite `/nodes` queries use a short timeout), tells the IDS to lift the
   lockdown, and unseals the node. A released runner must be registered again.

## Rules

- Never run anything as a service user over SSH (`systemd-run -p User=`,
  `sudo -u`, `runuser`, `su`): that is a lockdown. Probe as root, or read the
  app's journal and `/proc/<MainPID>`.
- Change nodes only through the fleet tools or inside an `expect` window.

## Residual risks

- Root can disable the IDS before it reacts; the peer vote takes about four
  minutes. Runners have no peer watching their heartbeat.
- A false lockdown takes a node out until released.
- Expected-change windows accept any change under `rescan` paths while open.
- A forged quarantine needs two nodes' IDS keys; a forged release needs the
  operator key. Keep the operator key and IDS master offline-backed.

pages.title: Legacy Solana custody migration
pages.description: Part of Operations.
pages.markdown:
# Legacy Solana custody migration

Part of [Operations](README.md).

The live server is non-custodial: it never creates, accepts, signs with, or
broadcasts a Solana private key. Older deployments may still hold encrypted
wallet seeds in compatibility rows from retired signup-deposit, issue-bounty,
bounty-wallet, federated-signup, or central-fund flows. Until every such key is
migrated and scrubbed, the server refuses to start its database-backed API and
reports `legacy_custody_migration_required`.

`tools/legacy_solana_custody.py` performs the migration offline against an
exported SQLite snapshot. It never signs or submits a transaction, never moves
funds, never prints a seed, and never contacts the live database.

## Safety invariants

- Work on a trusted, tightly controlled machine with `umask 077`; quiesce
  server writes for the final snapshot; keep an encrypted database backup.
- Pass `DATA_KEY`, the artifact passphrase, and any RPC URL through hidden
  prompts or environment variables (`FORKMESH_LEGACY_DATA_KEY`,
  `FORKMESH_CUSTODY_ARTIFACT_PASSPHRASE`, `FORKMESH_SOLANA_RPC_URL`), never
  arguments. The passphrase must be new, at least 16 characters, and differ
  from `DATA_KEY`.
- Move funds manually with trusted wallet tooling.
- Never scrub while any inventoried address has a nonzero or unknown balance,
  and never send new funds to a historical address.

## Procedure

1. **Inventory.** Export the database to SQLite, then run `inventory --database
   <snapshot> --network mainnet-beta --output audit.json`. Every row is
   decrypted, each seed must derive its stored address, and finalized balances
   are fetched; any error aborts the whole run.
2. **Export.** `export ... --artifact legacy.fmcustody` writes an AES-256-GCM
   artifact keyed by scrypt from the new passphrase. Seeds exist only inside the
   ciphertext; the file is owner-only and never overwritten. Verify the owner
   can open it before continuing. The tool intentionally has no “sweep” command.
3. **Move funds externally** and rerun `inventory` on fresh snapshots until
   every address reports exactly zero.
4. **Confirm.** Create an owner-only confirmation file:

   ```json
   {
     "format": "forkmesh-legacy-solana-scrub-confirmation-v1",
     "artifactSha256": "64-lowercase-hex-characters",
     "auditSha256": "64-lowercase-hex-characters",
     "confirmedAt": 1784815200000,
     "confirmation": "I HAVE IMPORTED EVERY LEGACY KEY AND RECONCILED EVERY ADDRESS AT ZERO"
   }
   ```

5. **Prepare the scrub.** `prepare-scrub --database <final snapshot> --artifact
   ... --confirmation ... --output-sql scrub.sql` re-verifies the artifact,
   digests, phrase, exact record set, and zero balances, then writes (but does
   not apply) a SQL patch. The patch removes key fields and key-bearing rows
   using the original ciphertext in every predicate, aborts unless each change
   hits exactly one audited row, records key-free evidence in
   `legacy_custody_reconciliation` and a receipt in
   `legacy_custody_migration_audit`, sets the readiness marker last, and is
   idempotent. Do not add `BEGIN`/`COMMIT`; the database's file ingestion
   supplies the transaction.
6. **Apply and verify** through the normal database change process, then export
   again: `inventory` must find zero key-bearing records, the audit table must
   hold one `scrubbed` receipt, and the readiness marker must be `clean-v2:`.

If the guarded update fails, never remove the guard: take a fresh snapshot,
determine what changed, and repeat the audit.

## Retained data

After the scrub, account rows keep only historical public donation fields, and
the retired compatibility tables are empty. The only evidence kept is the public
address, finalized zero balance, RPC slot, timestamp, source-table label, and
digests.

pages.title: Linux release baseline (Debian 12 container build)
pages.description: Part of Releases.
pages.markdown:
# Linux release baseline (Debian 12 container build)

Part of [Releases](README.md).

The Linux release assets (`forkmesh-linux-x86_64`,
`forkmesh-linux-x86_64.AppImage` and its `.zsync`, and
`forkmesh-linux-x86_64.deb` for the [apt repository](apt.md)) are built inside a pinned
Debian 12 (glibc 2.36) image so they run on Ubuntu 22.04+ and Debian 12+. The
Go mirror daemon is fully static (`CGO_ENABLED=0`) and is built by the Actions
job. Development builds are unaffected.

## Code map

| Path | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| `tools/package/linux-baseline.sh` | driver: `engine`, `prepare`, `build`, `check`, `smoke` |
| `tools/package/linux-baseline/image.env` | every pin: base image digest, apt snapshot, toolchain versions and SHA-256s, the glibc ceiling |
| `tools/package/linux-baseline/Containerfile` | the same stages as image layers for podman or docker |
| `tools/package/linux-baseline/stage-*.sh` | image stages: packages, OpenSSL, Qt, nghttp3, AppImage tools |
| `tools/package/linux-baseline/build-forkmesh.sh` | configure, build, install, provenance checks, AppImage, `.deb` (`--build N` sets the package's `+N`) |
| `tools/package/linux-baseline/check_glibc.py` | fails when any ELF needs `GLIBC_` above the ceiling or `GLIBCXX_` above 3.4.30 |
| `tools/package/linux-baseline/smoke-test.sh` | launch test inside Ubuntu 22.04, Ubuntu 24.04 and Debian 12; the `.deb`'s dependencies and binary |
| `tools/package/linux-baseline/oci_rootfs.py` | pulls an image by digest into a directory (bubblewrap engine), refusing unsafe layer members |
| `tools/forkmesh-release-host.py` (`build_linux_assets`) | builds, checks, smoke-tests and publishes into the candidate |
| `app/tests/test_linux_release_baseline.py` | checker, pins and recipe contracts |

## Image contents

- A Debian 12 base image pinned by digest, with apt pinned to a
  `snapshot.debian.org` date, so rebuilds install identical packages.
- Static OpenSSL 3.5 (CA and config in the distribution's standard
  locations), linked with `-DOPENSSL_USE_STATIC_LIBS=ON`.
- Static Qt 6 (`qtbase`, `qtsvg`) with only the modules the app links, xcb,
  offscreen and minimal platform plugins, bundled third-party copies, and
  ICU, glib, GTK and SQL off.
- Static nghttp3 (HTTP/3), libwebp and xcb utility libraries.
- linuxdeploy and appimagetool pinned by SHA-256.

The binary needs only common desktop system libraries (X11/xcb, xkbcommon,
fontconfig, freetype, EGL/GLX, zlib, libstdc++ from GCC 12, glibc); it never
loads Qt, OpenSSL, nghttp3, libwebp or ICU from the system
(`build-forkmesh.sh` checks `NEEDED`). Wayland sessions run it through
XWayland.

## Engines

`linux-baseline.sh` uses podman, then docker, when available to the current
user, else bubblewrap (`FORKMESH_LINUX_BASELINE_ENGINE` overrides). The
bubblewrap engine runs the same pinned image (pulled by digest, every blob
hash-checked) in a single-uid user namespace. Stages are cached and rerun only
when their script, an earlier stage or `image.env` changes. Cache:
`~/projects/forkmesh/toolchain-linux` (`FORKMESH_LINUX_BASELINE_CACHE`).

## Commands

```sh
tools/package/linux-baseline.sh prepare
tools/package/linux-baseline.sh build --source <clean tree> --out <dir> \
    --version X.Y.Z --commit <build commit> [--channel candidate-X.Y.Z]
tools/package/linux-baseline.sh check <dir>/forkmesh-linux-x86_64 <dir>/forkmesh-linux-x86_64.AppImage
tools/package/linux-baseline.sh smoke --out <dir> --version X.Y.Z
python3 -m pytest app/tests/test_linux_release_baseline.py
```

`build` runs `check` itself. The smoke test requires, for both assets on each
target distribution, that every shared library resolves, `--version` prints
the release, and the app started with `QT_QPA_PLATFORM=offscreen` is still
running after 25 s. It runs with a temporary `HOME` and `XDG_*_HOME` and a
cleared environment.

## Release flow

The Linux assets are listed in the release host's `HOST_ASSETS` and required
by the gate, so every new candidate is built by the host timer in a pristine
worktree at the build commit, checked, smoke-tested and published into the
candidate.

The release build passes `-DFORKMESH_PACKAGE_MODULES=OFF`, so Market packages
are compiled into the one `forkmesh-linux-x86_64` binary as they are on macOS
and Windows. Modules are the Linux development default, but a module is a
shared object, and the static `libxcb-*.a` archives in the image are not built
with `-fPIC` (the link fails with "relocation R_X86_64_PC32 against symbol
`xcb_render_id` can not be used when making a shared object"). The release
asset is a single file anyway.
The recipe comes from the release host's checkout, not the tag, so a fix here
applies to the candidate being built.

pages.title: Mail: the #email-log channel, tracking and core delivery
pages.description: Part of Operations.
pages.markdown: # Mail: the #email-log channel, tracking and core delivery Part of [Operations](README.md). Every email the platform sends leaves a note in a private chat channel, **#email-log**, visible only to the account named in `MAIL_LOG_OWNER`. The operator sees all outgoing mail and its outcome in one place. Fleet runbook: [runbook](runbook.md). ## Code map | Piece | Where | |---|---| | Notes, scrubbing, batching, outbox drain, channel provisioning | `app/src/mail_log.py` | | Send-path hook | `entry._mail_log_note`, called from `_send_email` and package mail (`send_mailtrap`) | | Delivery follow-ups | `process_mail_event` / `mailtrap_webhook_handler` → `mail_log.webhook_note` | | Per-send tracking, opens, clicks, views, tracked footers | `app/src/mail_activity.py`, tables `email_sends`, `email_footers` | | Daily budget | `app/src/mail_budget.py` | | Posting into the room | `entry._chat_channel_deliver` (the channel incoming-webhook path) | | Cron phase | `mail-log`, every minute | | Outbox table | `app/migrations/0209_mail_log_outbox.sql` | | Core mail tooling | `tools/next_mail.py`, `deploy/core/mail_events_agent.py` | | Tests | `app/tests/test_mail_log.py`, `app/tests/host/test_mail_log_e2e.py`, `app/tests/test_mail_activity.py` | ## The notices channel #email-log is an ordinary private `chat_channels` row with `kind: "notices"` in its sealed record. The server must write into it, so it is not end-to-end encrypted; it uses the room cipher only. Compared with a normal private channel it is stricter: - Only its creator can see it; admins get the same answer as for a channel that does not exist. - It is read-only: no rename, members, webhooks, visibility change or delete (`403 notices_channel_read_only`). Payloads carry `readOnly: true`, `serverVisible: true`, `kind: "notices"`. - Every client labels it **server-visible** and disables the composer. - Its name index is per owner, so creating it reveals nothing to others. A bot app was rejected for this: app posting is limited to public channels. The server writes the notes itself through the channel delivery path, which marks each envelope `srv` (server-injected) so clients accept these unsealed frames in this private room; ordinary private channels take webhooks the same way ([chat private rooms](../app/chat-private-rooms.md)). ## The note One card per event, sent as block-kit `blocks` plus the same layout as plain text. Headline: kind, result and UTC time. Fields: To, From, Subject, Body (first 200 characters, scrubbed), Reason, Detail (opens, clicks, views), Budget (on suppressed Mailtrap sends), Route (transport and node), Source (mail sent outside the app), Message ID. Each kind, result and field label has its own emoji (`KIND_EMOJI`, `RESULT_EMOJI`, `FIELD_EMOJI`). Results: `accepted`, `REJECTED`, `FAILED`, `suppressed` (budget, provider hold, a domain that receives no mail, or a suppressed recipient), and later `delivered`, `BOUNCED`, `soft-bounced`, `COMPLAINED`, `BLOCKED`, `opened`, `clicked`, `viewed`. Scrubbing: URLs become `[link]`, token-like runs of 24+ characters become `[redacted]`, 6+ digit runs become `[code]`. Notes never contain links, tokens or more than 200 body characters. The queued note is sealed with `encrypt_row`. The send's scrubbed excerpt is stored with the send so later notes repeat it. ## Delivery 1. **Send path.** Each outcome of `_send_email` and package mail inserts one row into `mail_log_outbox`. The hook swallows every exception, so a broken log never changes the send result. 2. **Follow-ups** from the Postfix log or the provider webhook are queued the same way. 3. **Cron `mail-log`** posts up to 40 due notes per run in messages of at most 20 notes, deletes each message's notes once posted, trims the backlog to 1,000 notes, and retries failures with backoff (dropped after 6 attempts). The channel is created on the first drain. **Mail sent outside the app** also lands here: Postfix events with no app send record are labelled "Not sent by the ForkMesh app"; tools that send through a core's Postfix and the IDS direct mailer write `mail_log_node_notes` rows (cores through rqlite, runners through a signed `POST /api/runners/mail-log-note`), which the cron moves into the sealed outbox. A new sender must call `_send_email`, write a node note, or send through core Postfix. ## Configuration - `MAIL_LOG_OWNER`: the owning account; empty or unknown means notes wait. - `MAIL_TRANSPORT = "smtp"` sends through Postfix on the cores; otherwise the configured mail API. - Changing `MAIL_LOG_OWNER` provisions a new channel; never edit a notices channel's members or visibility in SQL. ## Daily mail budget On a metered mail API, `mail_budget.py` caps sends per UTC day (`MAIL_DAILY_LIMIT`) and reserves `MAIL_ACCOUNT_RESERVE_PERCENT` for verification, password and account mail. A provider "daily limit" rejection sets a provider hold until the retry time. With core SMTP the budget does not apply; Postfix's per-client rate limit, the IDS email cap and the marketing limit still do. Package mail over core SMTP (`_PluginApiRuntime._send_package_smtp`) has its own cap: `PACKAGE_SMTP_ORG_DAILY_LIMIT` sends per package, per organization, per UTC day, counted in the `mail_budget` bucket `mail-package-smtp:::`. A package names the organization with an `organization` field in the payload it hands to `send_mailtrap` (the CRM passes its `org_bi`); a send without one shares the package's `-` bucket. Each sending account also gets `PACKAGE_SMTP_ACCOUNT_DAILY_LIMIT` sends per UTC day across every package and organization (bucket `mail-package-smtp-account::`), because one account can hold several organizations. The account is the request's session account; only a send without a request (none today) falls back to the `account` field the package passes. Why: Postfix sees one client (the app), so without these caps one account could create organizations, install a package and use the shared sender as a relay, starving verification and reset mail. Package mail on the shared sender (core SMTP, or the host's Mailtrap key when the package supplies none) always goes out from the platform sender (`MAIL_SENDER`, else `founders@forkmesh.com`) with the display name ` via ForkMesh` (the organization's name with quotes, angle brackets, address punctuation and control characters removed, capped at `PACKAGE_SHARED_SENDER_NAME_MAX` characters; plain `ForkMesh` without an organization). The package's chosen From address becomes `Reply-To` only when it is a valid address. Why: a package caller could otherwise put any display name, such as a bank or "ForkMesh Security", on DKIM-signed mail from our domain. A package that sends with its own Mailtrap key keeps its own From. ## Admin test email Settings, Admin access, **Send test email** (`POST /api/accounts/test-email`) sends kind `admin_test` to the signed-in admin's own address through the normal path, at most once a minute. ## Tracking - Every accepted send gets an `email_sends` row: send id, kind, recipient blind index, `ref`, sealed details and excerpt, and first-time and count for opens, clicks and views. Mail records expire after 90 days. - Opens and clicks are tracked only on notification kinds that carry an unsubscribe header; account and security mail is never tracked. A view token (`mail_activity.view_token`) lets a page opened from an email record a view. - `mail_activity.FOLLOWERS` lets a feature (such as tasks) hear its own sends' events. - Package mail on the cores carries one send id for both mail tables, its package variables, and a tracked logo footer that records opens. A package that tracks its own opens and clicks sends `"tracked": true` in the `send_mailtrap` payload; the host drops the key and skips its footer, so the email carries one logo, not two (the CRM's automated outreach does this). - `GET /api/mail/footer` gives each account a tracked signature footer for mail written in other mail apps; it counts opens per account, not per message. - Bounces, rejects and unsubscribes add the recipient to `mail_suppressions`. - `www/public/privacy.html` ("Email we send") discloses tracking. ## Sending from the cores - Postfix is send-only on loopback, with rate limits and opportunistic TLS. OpenDKIM signs with selector `fmnext`, signing and oversigning the identity and one-click unsubscribe headers, `relaxed/relaxed` canonicalization. - Each core's hostname, HELO, forward DNS and PTR (IPv4 and IPv6) match; Postfix prefers IPv4. `next_mail.py check nN` verifies forward-confirmed reverse DNS. - `fmnext-mail-events` follows the Postfix journal (no network) and turns results into delivery, soft-bounce and bounce events; `mail_sends` maps send ids to Message-IDs and the latest DSN code. - Every send carries `Auto-Submitted` and `Feedback-ID: :forkmesh`. - `/status` checks that Postfix answers on loopback and that recent sends are not stuck. - Postfix's own non-delivery notices are DKIM-signed too (`internal_mail_filter_classes = bounce`, OpenDKIM `SubDomains yes`, so `MAILER-DAEMON@nN.next.forkmesh.com` signs as `forkmesh.com`); unsigned ones fail DMARC (`554 5.7.7 Email policy violation`). Rolling this out needs `next_mail.py install nN --execute` on each core. - A bounce whose reply says the address does not exist sets `mail_sends.cause = 'recipient'` (`mail_tracking.bounce_cause`, migration `0278_mail_sends_cause`), whatever DSN the server used (Tutanota answers `550 5.7.1 Recipient address rejected: Recipient not available`). A reply that also mentions spam, blocking, reputation, policy, SPF, DKIM, DMARC or authentication stays a policy refusal and keeps `/status` red. Either way the address goes into `mail_suppressions`, so it is never mailed again. - A bounce that blames our own sending setup does not suppress the recipient: RFC 7372's sender-authentication codes `5.7.20`–`5.7.27` (no passing DKIM, SPF failed, reverse DNS failed, unauthenticated) and Microsoft's `5.7.515` set `mail_sends.cause = 'sender'` and keep `/status` red, but leave `mail_suppressions` alone, so the address gets mail again once the setup is fixed (a suppressed address would otherwise silently lose its later password-reset mail). - n3 and n5 sit in legacy Vultr blocks (66.135.17.0/24, 66.135.22.0/24) whose public reverse zone keeps answering `*.constant.com`, so the PTRs `next_mail.py rdns --execute` sets never publish (`550 5.7.25 Forward-confirmed reverse DNS failed` at Yahoo); fixing it needs a Vultr support ticket. Until then n3 and n5 relay through n4 (`mail_relay = "n4"` on their `[[nodes]]` blocks in `deploy/fleet.toml`; `render.load_fleet` refuses a relay that is not another core sending mail itself): their Postfix has `relayhost = [10.77.0.4]:25` and still DKIM-signs, and n4 listens on its WireGuard address as well as loopback, accepts only n3's and n5's `/32`s in `mynetworks` and exempts them from its client rate limit (each sender already rate-limits its own app). n4 sends from the one IPv4 address with forward-confirmed reverse DNS. Port 25 is in the core-only `wg0` ports of the firewall (`render.py`), and Postfix starts after `wg-quick@wg0`. On a relaying core `fmnext-mail-events` ignores the `status=sent` hand-off to a `10.77.*` relay; n4's agent reports the real delivery or bounce for the same Message-ID. `next_mail.py check n3` probes the relay. To undo it once `check` shows `PTR : ok` everywhere, remove the `mail_relay` lines, let autodeploy roll, and run `install nN --execute` on every core. - Every core falls back to Mailtrap so mail does not depend on one server (the operator's requirement). Postfix has `smtp_fallback_relay = [live.smtp.mailtrap.io]:587`, used whenever the normal route fails with a temporary error: n4 unreachable from n3/n5, or a provider deferring n4. It logs in as `api` with `MAILTRAP_API_TOKEN` (already a server credential, `optional_secrets`), which `next_mail.py install` sends on SSH stdin into root-only `/etc/postfix/sasl_passwd` (0600, with its `.db`); `/etc/postfix/tls_policy` makes that hop `secure` (verified TLS), so the password never crosses an unverified connection. No other destination gets credentials. `forkmesh.com` already carries Mailtrap's DKIM (`rwmt1`/`rwmt2._domainkey`), so relayed mail still passes DMARC. If a core's own Postfix does not answer, `_send_email` sends that message through the Mailtrap API instead (`mail_providers.fallback`), within the same provider hold and daily budget as any API send; a suppressed recipient never falls back. Without the token in `secrets.env`, install leaves the fallback off and says so. A hand-off to Mailtrap is recorded as delivery: its own webhook carries the later lifecycle. - Adding a core checks reverse DNS. On Vultr with core mail on, the `vm` step of `next_add_core.py` sets the new address's PTR and waits up to 10 minutes for it to publish; if it does not, it deletes the empty VM (nothing is on it yet) and creates another, three addresses at most, then stops and keeps the last one. The `health` step then needs `PTR : ok` (forward-confirmed, as in `check`) before the core joins DNS, unless the core has `mail_relay`. - `/status` checks the same thing all the time: `render.py` writes the cores that send mail themselves (no `mail_relay`) into `FORKMESH_MAIL_SENDERS=nN.next.forkmesh.com=,...`, and the email row turns red with "Reverse DNS does not match for ..." when one of them does not forward-confirm. Results are cached for 10 minutes per process. - The IDS mails its lockdown and test alerts through the same loopback Postfix, and in a lockdown (when its firewall stops Postfix sending) posts to the Mailtrap API as root with the token in `/etc/postfix/sasl_passwd` ([intrusion detection](intrusion-detection.md), "Direct mail"). - Setup with `tools/next_mail.py`: `dkim`, `dns`, `rdns` once; per core `install` then `restart`; `check`. ## The sender Every email the servers send comes from one verified mailbox, `founders@forkmesh.com`, so a recipient who replies reaches a person (the operator's choice over the unread `no-reply@forkmesh.com`). - `smtp_mail.SENDER` is the app's default when `MAIL_SENDER` and `MAILTRAP_SENDER` are unset; package mail always uses it. The IDS direct mailer (`mail_from` empty) and `tools/mac_adhoc_publish.py` use it too. - The envelope sender (Return-Path) stays `no-reply@` (`smtp_mail.envelope_sender`, `sendmail -f` in the build notice), so bounces and delivery reports go to the old address rather than the founders inbox. SPF and DMARC still align: both are `forkmesh.com`. - Mail Postfix makes itself (cron and other system mail as `root@forkmesh.com`, non-delivery notices from `MAILER-DAEMON@nN.next.forkmesh.com`) is rewritten to the same sender by `sender_canonical_maps = regexp:/etc/postfix/sender_canonical` (`next_mail.SENDER_CANONICAL`). The table leaves `founders@` and `no-reply@` untouched, so the app's mail, which OpenDKIM signs as it is received over SMTP, is never rewritten after signing; locally made mail is rewritten by cleanup before its milter signs it. Bounces keep their empty envelope sender. Rolling the table out needs `next_mail.py install nN --execute` on each core. - White-label instances keep their own `MAIL_SENDER` ([self-hosted instances](instances.md)); one that sends through SMTP gets the envelope sender `no-reply@` its own domain. ## Branding Every card from `_forkmesh_email_card_html` starts with `assets/logo-96.png` (see Layout below). Inbox avatars use BIMI: `www/public/assets/forkmesh-bimi.svg` (SVG Tiny PS), TXT `default._bimi.forkmesh.com`, and DMARC at `p=quarantine`. Gmail and Apple Mail additionally need a mark certificate. Every sender for the domain must sign with DKIM before it sends. ### Layout The "Letter" layout (the operator's pick of three): a centred 480px column on `#fafafa` with no bordered card, the logo on its own, a 22px heading, a grey intro, the body, a near-black (`#171717`) button, the action URL written out under it ("Or open this link"), and a hairline footer with "Email settings". The logo is `assets/logo-96.png` (the dark cube, readable without a backing tile) at 32px wide with `height:auto`, never squeezed into a fixed box. The palette stays light-only so a client that half-applies dark mode cannot make it unreadable. The wrapper keeps its two `div`s, so code that inserts before `` (status logs, the manage link, the instance "Powered by" line) still lands inside the column. `_instance_brand_email` rewrites the logo's `alt`, the footer name and the settings link for white-label instances.

pages.title: Mirror Actions control and summary v2
pages.description: Part of Operations.
pages.markdown:
# Mirror Actions control and summary v2

Part of [Operations](README.md).

The website's repository **Actions** tab reads run state from, and sends
control requests to, a mirror node running the Actions executor. This page is
the wire contract (the gateway side is in
[direct-HTTPS mirror gateway](direct-https-mirror-gateway.md#operations), the
daemon in [mirror node](mirror-node.md)) between:

| Component | File |
| --- | --- |
| Website | `app/public/dashboard/js/06-repo-actions.js` |
| Relay server | `app/src/repository_actions.py` |
| Mirror gateway | `tools/mirror_gateway.py` |
| Executor (Go mirror daemon) | `server/actions.go`, `server/actions_control.go`, `server/actions_workflow.go` |

The Go daemon (`forkmesh-mirror-node`) is the executor: it runs workflows,
writes the summary, and consumes control requests. Desktops that publish their
own runs still write a read-only version 1 summary. Nothing here can enable an
executor its operator turned off.

## Enabling Actions on a mirror

Actions run repository-supplied shell, so they are opt-in and fail closed:

1. Deploy a matching gateway and daemon (the daemon names Actions keys only
   when its gateway understands them).
2. Install `server/packaging/systemd/forkmesh-mirror-node-actions.conf` as a
   drop-in for `forkmesh-mirror-node.service`; it allows the namespaces
   `bubblewrap` needs.
3. Set `"enableActions": true` in `mirror-node.json` and restart.

At start the daemon probes a sandbox. On failure it logs `mirror actions are
unavailable: …`, runs nothing, and advertises neither `actions-status` nor
`actions-control`; it never runs a step unsandboxed.

Each step runs under `bwrap --unshare-all --clearenv` with no outbound network,
read-only system directories, a `git archive` export of the commit at
`/workspace`, a scratch home and `/tmp`, and only `PATH`, `HOME`, `LANG`, `CI`,
`FORKMESH_*` run variables, and the workflow's own `env:`. Steps cannot see node
state, identity keys, or other repositories. **A mirror holds no Actions
variables**, so workflows needing secrets or network belong on the owner's own
node (`runs-on:`).

Triggers: `on: push` when a branch head moves (default branch only unless
`on.push.branches` is set; `paths` honoured; ledger branches ignored) and
`on: workflow_dispatch`. `runs-on:` matches the node name, `linux`, and
`mirror`; `needs:` waits for another workflow's success on the same commit.
`pull_request` and `release` runs do not start on mirrors. Limits: one run at a
time, one hour per run, 8 MiB of log, twenty queued, fifty kept; newer pushes
supersede queued runs of the same workflow and branch.

## Trust model

The internet-facing gateway is less trusted than the executor. The executor
writes `actions-summary.json`; the gateway only reads it. For control, the
gateway is a **courier, not an authority**: it stores the router capability
beside the exact request body, and the executor verifies the Ed25519 signature
itself. A compromised gateway can drop or delay a request but cannot author,
alter, or replay one. Authorization requires a session that is the repository
owner, an owner of the node, or an organization writer (checked and audited by
the server) **and** the router key.

## Operation `actions-control`

`POST /v1/repositories/{owner}/{repository}/actions-control`

- Listed in `PUBLIC_OPERATIONS` only; always requires the signed router
  capability; no query parameters.
- Requires `actions-status` and an `actionsControlPath` that is an absolute,
  owner-only (`0700`), non-symlink directory named `actions-control`.
- Body: at most 4 KiB of JSON with exact keys.

| Key | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `schemaVersion` | `1` |
| `type` | `"forkmesh.actions-control-v1"` |
| `requestId` | `^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{16,64}$`, idempotency key |
| `action` | see below |
| `actor` | `^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9._-]{0,63}$` |
| `issuedAt` | integer ms, within ±60 s of the gateway clock |

| `action` | Extra keys |
| --- | --- |
| `dispatch` | `workflow`, `ref` |
| `rerun`, `cancel`, `approve`, `reject` | `runId` |
| `set-workflow-enabled` | `workflow`, `enabled` |
| `set-repository-enabled` | `enabled` |

`workflow` matches `^\.forkmesh/[A-Za-z0-9._-]{1,96}\.ya?ml$`; `ref` matches
`^refs/heads/[A-Za-z0-9._/-]{1,200}$` without `..`, `//`, or a trailing `/` or
`.lock`; `runId` is an integer `1 … 2^53-1`.

### Gateway behaviour

1. Validate the body exactly.
2. Refuse when the summary cannot be loaded or is still version 1.
3. Atomically write `{actionsControlPath}/{requestId}.json` (`O_EXCL|O_NOFOLLOW`,
   `0640`, fsync, rename) as an envelope of type
   `forkmesh.mirror-actions-control` holding `node`, `owner`, `repository`,
   `receivedAt`, the `capability` (method, path, request id, issued-at, body
   SHA-256, signature), and the exact `body` string.
4. A repeated `requestId` with an identical body is accepted again; a different
   body fails.
5. Keep at most 32 pending files; files older than 10 minutes are removed.
6. Success is `202 {"ok":true,"status":"accepted","requestId":"…","node":"…"}`
   with `Cache-Control: no-store`; every refusal is the uniform
   `404 {"ok":false,"error":"not_found"}`.

### Executor behaviour

A 4-second loop reads each regular, single-link `*.json` file (≤ 16 KiB) and:

1. checks exact keys, its own `node`, and the owner/repository path;
2. recomputes `sha256(body)` against `capability.bodySha256`;
3. verifies the signature over
   `forkmesh-masked-proxy-v1\n<node>\nPOST\n<path>\n<bodySha256>\n<requestId>\n<issuedAt>`
   with the configured `routerPublicKey`;
4. rejects capabilities older than 10 minutes and any `requestId` in its saved
   ring of the last 256 (persisted before applying, so a request never runs
   twice);
5. parses the body, deletes the file, applies the action, and records the
   outcome.

| Action | Effect | Rejection reasons |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `dispatch` | Run a workflow with `workflow_dispatch` at `ref` | `repository_not_found`, `actions_disabled`, `ref_not_found`, `workflow_not_found`, `workflow_invalid`, `not_manual`, `workflow_disabled`, `wrong_node` |
| `rerun` | New run of the same workflow and commit | `run_not_found`, `actions_disabled`, `wrong_node` |
| `cancel` | Stop or dequeue a run | `run_not_found`, `not_cancellable` |
| `approve` / `reject` | Nothing on a mirror awaits approval | `run_not_found`, `not_awaiting_approval` |
| `set-workflow-enabled` | Toggle the path in `disabledWorkflows` | `repository_not_found`, `workflow_not_found` |
| `set-repository-enabled` | Toggle `webDisabled` (can only narrow `enableActions`) | `repository_not_found` |

A `runId` from another repository is `run_not_found`.

## Summary v2 (`actions-summary.json`)

Readers accept `schemaVersion` 1 and 2; the Go runner writes 2. Version 2 adds:

- per run: `workflowPath`, `pullNumber` (0 if none), and up to 64 `steps` of
  `{"name","status"}` with status `pending | running | success | failed |
  skipped | cancelled`;
- `repositories` (≤ 64): `{"owner","repository","actionsEnabled","workflows"}`,
  each workflow (≤ 32) `{"path","name","events","manual","enabled","runsOn","valid"}`;
- `controls` (≤ 32, newest first): `{"owner","repository","requestId","action",
  "status","reason","runId","finishedAt"}` with status `applied | rejected`.

No workflow content, commands, variables, or local paths appear. The 256 KiB
bound applies, trimming log tails first. The gateway filters the response to
the requested repository; a repository without an entry reports
`actionsEnabled: false` and empty `workflows`.

## Server routes

| Route | Method | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `/api/repo/{owner}/{repo}/actions/runs` | GET | Revalidates and passes through v2 fields; adds `controlAvailable`. |
| `/api/repo/{owner}/{repo}/actions/control` | POST | Session required; audited as `repository.actions_control`. Browser sends `node`, `requestId`, `action`, action keys; the server adds `schemaVersion`, `type`, `actor`, `issuedAt`. |

The request goes only to the node named by `node` (run ids are per executor);
`node` is not forwarded in the gateway body. Responses: `202` accepted; `400`,
`401`, `403`, `404`, `405`, `413`; or `503 {"error":"actions_node_unavailable"}`
with the expected-degraded header. The browser learns the outcome from the next
`actions/runs` poll.

pages.title: Mirror node service
pages.description: Part of Operations.
pages.markdown:
# Mirror node service

Part of [Operations](README.md).

`forkmesh-mirror-node` is the headless Go runtime for a public mirror host. It
synchronizes repositories, supervises the loopback Git gateway (and optionally a
Cloudflare Tunnel), publishes the node's signed catalog record and endpoint
lease, runs collaboration intake, and can execute owner-authorized merges and
website agent jobs. No desktop app or GUI process is involved. It is the
running part of the [mirroring](../mirroring.md) and
[self-hosting](../self-hosting.md) pillars; roles and profiles are in
[service roles](service-roles.md).

## Architecture

- **Operator API, loopback only.** `GET /healthz` (event loop alive),
  `GET /readyz` (gateway running and a recent successful sync), `GET /v1/status`
  (bounded, secret-free process, sync and ref state) and `POST /v1/control/sync`
  (sync doorbell).
- **Gateway.** Listens on `127.0.0.1:8790` behind an operator-managed HTTPS
  reverse proxy. Set `disableCloudflared` when that origin is directly
  reachable; otherwise the daemon supervises Cloudflare Tunnel as a fallback.
  `mirrorUrl` advertises a separate direct Git origin while `publicOrigin`
  stays the Tunnel control endpoint.
- **Identity.** The owner-only Ed25519 node key (and the connector token, when
  enabled) is never accepted in argv, JSON, an HTTP request or a catalog record.
- **Event socket.** One WebSocket to the relay's per-owner node event channel
  (`wss://…/api/nodes/events`), authenticated with the node key. The relay
  pushes payload-free `{"type":"event","topic","repo"}` frames
  ([polling elimination](polling-elimination.md)).

## Data flow

- **Collaboration intake.** An issue, pull or discussion frame makes the daemon
  lease only the changed inbox, write the repository-native record in a
  temporary worktree, commit it, and acknowledge the exact rows with a signed
  refs attestation. There is no poll; every reconnect fires one catch-up drain.
- **Repository sync.** A `commits` frame triggers a fetch. It carries the
  source's signed refs digest, so a fetch from a stale peer is retried on a
  2s→15s backoff until that generation lands. Direct pushes to a managed host
  ring the doorbell from a service-owned `post-receive` hook. Peers listed in
  `eventDrivenUpstreams` are push-notified; upstreams that cannot push use
  `syncInterval`. A reconciliation every 5 minutes (`relaySafetySyncInterval`) covers a lost event.
- **Catalog and lease.** A four-minute heartbeat republishes the catalog record
  and renews the endpoint lease from local refs reads, over the event socket
  when the relay advertises that frame and over HTTPS otherwise.
- **First clone.** Until a repository has a readable clone the daemon retries it
  on 15s→5m backoff; the gateway refuses to serve refs it cannot pin
  (`integrity.expectedRefsSha256`). `journalctl -u forkmesh-mirror-node` shows
  the chain.

## Owner-authorized web merges

Every served repository advertises `merge-preview`, `merge-pull` and
`update-pull-branch`. The gateway's `mergeExecutorCommand` points at this binary
(`forkmesh-mirror-node --config … --execute-mirror-merge`). The relay
authenticates the account (an owner to merge; for `update-pull-branch`, anyone
who may push the pull's head branch), signs the exact-OID request and hands it
to one healthy mirror. The executor verifies the pinned pull record on the `forkmesh/pulls`
ledger, the base and head tips, the peer-review gate (an owner may waive it with
`overrideReview`) and any `.forkmesh/required-checks.json` policy ([required checks](required-checks.md)), then moves the
base branch, the ledger and `forkmesh/pull/<n>` in one atomic `update-ref`.
Patch-backed pulls are replayed onto the exact base in a temporary worktree,
preserving authorship. The result carries a node-signed refs attestation that
the relay admits as the repository's current generation and announces with a
`commits` event. Nothing rewinds a ref: a stale pin fails closed. Job state lives
under `mirror-gateway/pull-jobs/` (owner-only). `"disableMergeExecutor": true`
keeps a node strictly read-only.

## Running website agent jobs

A node that finds `claude` or `codex` on its PATH (or Ollama beside Codex, for
`local-llama`) advertises those providers and runs sessions the website queues
for it. The relay rings the socket with an `org-agents` push; the daemon claims
the job over the signed `org-agent-jobs` lease. For each job it validates the
envelope (provider, model allowlist, prompt of at most 8,000 characters, kind
`start`/`continue`/`steer`, target node and repository), fetches up to five
verified image attachments, clones into `mirror-gateway/agent-jobs/work/`, runs
the provider on a new `agent/web-<job>-<title>` branch (never `main`), pushes
the branch, optionally opens a node-signed pull, and reports status, transcript,
token counts and cost. A run is capped at two hours; a failed run reports one
bounded `lastError`. The browser can sign a provider CLI in through a relayed
pseudo-terminal that runs only the provider's own login command.
`"disableAgentJobs": true` and `"disableAgentLogin": true` turn these off.

## Policy, hardening and logs

- Storage limits, takedowns and protected branches: see the
  [node operator policy guide](node-operator-policy.md).
- Key-only SSH (`server/packaging/ssh/10-forkmesh-hardening.conf`) and a
  fail2ban `sshd` jail (`server/packaging/fail2ban/forkmesh-sshd.local`).
- The gateway streams the host journal at `GET /v1/node/logs` to Ed25519 viewer
  keys in `/etc/forkmesh/log-viewer-keys` (signed, single-use requests).

## Setup

Start from `server/packaging/systemd/mirror-node.json.example`. Upstream lists
may hold several URLs, tried in order. For a tunnel-free bootstrap pass
`--disable-cloudflared` with the public HTTPS origin; the node then advertises
`https://<origin>/<owner>/<repository>.git` behind a signed direct-origin
manifest. Independent dashboard, SSH writes and forks are covered in
[direct-HTTPS mirror gateway](direct-https-mirror-gateway.md); backups,
`--preflight` and key moves in
[node backup, recovery, and key moves](node-backup-and-recovery.md).

## Build and test

```sh
cd server
go test -race -cover ./...
CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -trimpath -ldflags='-s -w' \
  -o forkmesh-mirror-node ./cmd/forkmesh-mirror-node
```

## Rolling migration

1. Install the binary, configuration and unit without stopping the old node.
2. Run `forkmesh-mirror-node --config ... --check` and `--preflight` as
   `forkmesh-node`.
3. Start `forkmesh-mirror-node` and confirm `/readyz`.
4. Remove any retired compatibility unit.
5. Confirm signed external health, one pushed collaboration submission and one
   clone before moving to the next host.

Keep the prior unit and binary as rollback artifacts until the whole fleet has
passed reachability checks.

pages.title: Mobile push notifications (APNs)
pages.description: Part of Operations.
pages.markdown:
# Mobile push notifications (APNs)

Part of [Operations](README.md).

Apple Push Notification service wakes the iOS app when iOS has suspended or
killed it, the one case the account event socket cannot cover (see
[polling elimination](polling-elimination.md)). A write that changes an unread
count calls `notify_account_event`, which sends a payload-free socket frame
and, for the topics below, one alert to every phone registered to the account.

There is no third-party push provider: the server signs its own APNs provider
token and posts to Apple directly (`app/src/apns.py`). On the phone,
`native/ios/ForkMesh/Platform/ApplePushBridge.swift` registers the device and
the `native/ios/NotificationService` extension enriches each banner.

## Payloads

Every alert names its event; nothing generic is sent. Device tokens are stored
encrypted under a blind-index row key.

| Line | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| Title | Record and headline, e.g. `#42 Issue submitted` |
| Subtitle | `owner/repo · by actor` |
| Body | The notification body, up to 900 characters |
| Image, badge | Actor avatar and unread count, added on the phone |

Alerts set `mutable-content` and `thread-id` (per repository or conversation).
The extension reads `GET /api/push/alert` (unread rows, own account only) with
the session shared through the app's keychain group, stored
`AfterFirstUnlock`; Keychain Sharing must be enabled on both App IDs. If the
read fails, the banner keeps the server text.

Chat and direct-message text is end-to-end encrypted: the alert carries only
the relay `ref`, `keyVersion`, and `channelId`, and the extension fetches and
decrypts the ciphertext on the phone, falling back to "End-to-end encrypted".
Every payload includes `origin`, `alertId`, and `href` so a phone signed in to
several deployments routes taps correctly.

## Topics

`APNS_PUSH_TOPICS`: `pings`, `code-push`, `direct-messages`, and `chat`.
`catalog` and `issues` are freshness hints and never alert.

- Each ping and each direct message is its own banner (no collapse id).
- `code-push` (kind `code_push`) fires on observed pushes for readers of the
  repository, at most one banner per recipient per branch per 60 seconds, and
  can be turned off in ping settings.
- Chat alerts require the sender to set plaintext `notify: true` on a `chat` or
  `thread-reply` envelope. Audience: the other participant of a direct message,
  members of a private channel, or every registered phone for public channels
  and rooms, minus the sender where known; at most 32 phones per message and
  one push per room every two seconds.

## Configuration

`push_account_apns` is a no-op unless all three secrets are set; deploy refuses
to run without them.

| Secret | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `APNS_AUTH_KEY` | The `.p8` APNs key with its PEM armour (literal `\n` accepted). |
| `APNS_KEY_ID` | The ten-character Key ID. |
| `APNS_TEAM_ID` | The ten-character developer Team ID. |

The App ID needs the Push Notifications capability and the key must belong to
the same team. Debug builds and the Simulator register sandbox tokens; release
builds register production tokens. The app sends `environment` with its token
and the server routes each token to the matching gateway.

## Verification

Settings → Notifications on the phone shows each link of the chain and offers
**Send test notification**, which calls `POST /api/accounts/push-test` (one call
per ten seconds). It returns `configured`, `devices`, `delivered`, and Apple's
status per device:

| Answer | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| `configProblem: missing_secrets` | Set the three secrets and redeploy. |
| `key_id_malformed` / `team_id_malformed` | Copy the ten-character IDs exactly. |
| `devices: 0` | Allow notifications or sign in again on the phone. |
| `400 BadDeviceToken` | Token from the other gateway; reopen the app to re-register. |
| `DeviceTokenNotForTopic` / `TopicDisallowed` | Key team or App ID mismatch. |
| `403 InvalidProviderToken` | Key ID or Team ID does not match the key. |
| `410 Unregistered` | App uninstalled; the token is pruned. |
| HTTP `502 apns_provider_key` | The key does not import; re-paste it. |

## Limits

Delivery is best effort and inline with the triggering request: at most eight
devices per event within three seconds, twenty tokens per account, and tokens
idle for 180 days are dropped. Android has no push transport; the native
Android app reports push as unsupported.

pages.description: Part of Operations.
pages.markdown:
# Node backup, recovery, and key moves

Part of [Operations](README.md).

[`forkmesh-mirror-node`](mirror-node.md) backs up, restores, and checks the node
it runs ([self-hosting](../self-hosting.md); community-wide recovery is the
[disaster recovery guide](../disaster-recovery/README.md)):

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--preflight` | Read-only checks of configuration, identity, Git version, disk space, and backup/drill freshness |
| `--backup PATH` | Writes one encrypted archive of everything the node needs |
| `--restore-drill PATH` | Restores into scratch space, verifies, times it against the RTO, then deletes it |
| `--restore PATH` | Restores onto a host, verifies, and removes what it created if a check fails |
| `--export-identity PATH` / `--import-identity PATH` | Moves only the Ed25519 identity key |

Every command takes `--config` and prints JSON. Run them as the service
account:

```sh
node() {
  runuser -u forkmesh-node -- /usr/local/bin/forkmesh-mirror-node \
    --config /var/lib/forkmesh/mirror-node.json "$@"
}
```

## Passphrases

Archives and identity exports contain the private key and connector token, so
they are encrypted with AES-256-GCM in 1 MiB authenticated chunks, keyed by
PBKDF2-SHA256. Any tampering or truncation fails to open. The passphrase is read
only from `--passphrase-file`, which must be owner-only and at least 12 bytes;
it is never accepted as an argument or environment variable. Keep a copy off
the node.

## Preflight

`node --preflight [--json]` reports `ok`, `warn`, or `error` per check and
exits `2` on any error: configuration does not load, a required binary or the
identity key is missing, `git` is older than 2.27, the key does not match the
advertised public key, the connector token is not owner-only, or a state volume
has under 512 MiB free. Warnings cover low free space or inodes, uncloned
repositories, a backup older than 24 hours (RPO), and a restore drill older
than 92 days, over its objective, or never run. Run preflight before and after
every install or update; if it fails after an update, reinstall the previous
release (see [rolling migration](mirror-node.md#rolling-migration)).

## Backups

```sh
node --passphrase-file /var/lib/forkmesh/backup.passphrase \
  --backup /var/backups/forkmesh/node-$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ).fmbackup
```

The service can keep running. An archive contains the service and gateway
configurations, identity key, connector token, the gateway state directory
(`mirror-gateway/`), and every path the gateway configuration names
(repositories, release stores, private replica store, fork registry, writable
root, operator policy state). Each bare repository is stored as a
`git bundle --all` snapshot plus its `HEAD`, `config`, hooks, and releases.

Excluded: `tmp/`, `.cache/`, agent and merge worktrees, partial files, and
agent CLI sign-ins (sign in again after a restore). Archives are written under
a temporary name and never replace an existing file; symlinks in state are
refused. Each run is recorded, without secrets, in
`mirror-gateway/node-ops/last-backup.json`.

Schedule backups daily (for example a systemd timer running the command above
as `forkmesh-node`, pruning old archives) and copy archives off the host.

## Restore drills

```sh
node --passphrase-file /var/lib/forkmesh/backup.passphrase \
  --restore-drill /var/backups/forkmesh/node-<timestamp>.fmbackup --rto 30m
```

A drill decrypts into `--work-dir`, checks every file's size, mode, and
SHA-256, each repository's refs digest and `git fsck --connectivity-only`, and
that the key and configurations load and agree. It then deletes the scratch
copy, records `last-restore-drill.json`, and exits `3` if it exceeded `--rto`.
Run one at least quarterly. `/v1/status` reports both objectives under
`recovery`.

## Restoring a node

1. Install ForkMesh on the new host without bootstrapping an identity or
   starting the service.
2. Copy the archive and passphrase file over, owned by `forkmesh-node`, mode
   `0600`.
3. Optionally rehearse: `node --passphrase-file ... --restore <archive> --dry-run`.
4. Restore: `node --passphrase-file ... --restore <archive>`.
5. Run `node --preflight`, enable the service, and confirm `/readyz`.

Files return to their original absolute paths (or under `--restore-root DIR`).
A restore never overwrites existing files, refuses existing repository
directories, refuses to run as root, and on failure removes only what it
created. `--config` must match the path stored in the backup. The restored node
keeps its name and key, so it takes over the old node's catalog entry and
lease; never run the old and restored hosts at once.

## Moving or replacing an identity key

```sh
node --passphrase-file ... --export-identity /var/lib/forkmesh/node.fmkey          # old host
node --passphrase-file ... --import-identity /var/lib/forkmesh/node.fmkey --dry-run  # new host
node --passphrase-file ... --import-identity /var/lib/forkmesh/node.fmkey --replace-identity
```

An export is bound to its node name. Import reports `install` (no key yet),
`unchanged` (same key), or `replace` (different key; requires
`--replace-identity` and keeps the old key as `ed25519.pem.replaced-<unix time>`).
A changed key also updates the gateway's advertised public key and, on a
tunnel-free node, re-signs the direct-origin manifest. Restart the service
afterwards.

pages.title: Node logs on the operator desktop
pages.description: Part of Operations.
pages.markdown:
# Node logs on the operator desktop

Part of [Operations](README.md).

The desktop's Log page follows every fleet node's systemd journal live (cores,
runners, autoscaled replicas and burst runners), every Caddy request, and the
operator box's own deploy output. Nothing is stored in the database: live
logs stay on the desktop. Fleet runbook: [runbook](runbook.md).

## Transport: the desktop pulls over SSH

The desktop opens one SSH session per node with a dedicated reader key
(`next_logread_ed25519`, created by `tools/next_fleet.py logread-key`), not the
fleet key. It connects on the fleet's `ssh_port`, read from
`~/projects/forkmesh/src/deploy/fleet.toml`. Every other retry after a failure
uses 22, for a node that has not moved yet ([SSH port](ssh-port.md)).
On each node it is a forced command:

```
restrict,command="/usr/bin/python3 -I /opt/forkmesh-next/bin/fmnext-logread" ssh-ed25519 ... fmnext-logread
```

`fmnext-logread` (`deploy/core/logread.py`) accepts only `follow`,
`follow lines N`, `follow after <cursor>` or `hello`, drops privileges to
`nobody` plus the journal group with `no_new_privs`, and runs
`journalctl --follow --output=json`. Messages are redacted on the node
(the `tools/secret_gate.py` rules, credentials in headers, assignments, JSON
and URLs, long tokens).

Stream format: a header line (`{"logread":1,"node":…,"role":…}`), one line per
journal entry with its `__CURSOR`, an idle heartbeat after 60 s, and a
resource sample (`logread_vitals`) every 15 s from world-readable kernel
counters (memory, load, file handles, disk, uptime, CPU busy share) for the
Visualizer. Missing counters are omitted, never sent as zero.

The desktop resumes from the last cursor it saved, so lines written while it
was off are read later (bounded by journald rotation). Each stream is
authenticated by its node's host key, so a compromised node can only lie
about its own logs. Pushing logs into the app database was rejected: it would
write every line through rqlite and let any compromised core write every
node's stream.

## IDS

The reader key's fingerprint is part of the IDS fleet fingerprints, so a
reader login is an `info` `ssh_tool_session`. `restrict` refuses a pty. The
authorized-keys line is written only after the IDS has restarted with the new
config, and a fresh node starts its IDS after the line is written
([intrusion detection](intrusion-detection.md)).

## Caddy access log

`[logs] access_log = true` adds JSON access logging to the journal: request and
response headers dropped, client address and `user_agent` kept, Cloudflare and
edge visitor fields (`cf_*`, `edge_*`) only when the TCP peer is in
Cloudflare's published ranges (requests relayed by the `forkmesh-www` Worker,
[edge client](../www/edge-client.md)), the `expected_degraded` response header,
credential query parameters redacted, `/readyz` and `/health` skipped. The app
never sees the `Cf-*` headers.

The redacted query keys are `ACCESS_LOG_QUERY_KEYS` in `deploy/core/render.py`.
They include `ticket` (chat room, call and event-socket tickets on socket
URLs; a short-lived socket credential) and `node` (ties each signed read to
an account).

Bearer tokens never travel in a path. Chat invite tokens go in the
request body (`POST /api/chat/invites/preview|accept`) and webhook tokens in
the `token` query key or the `x-forkmesh-webhook-token` header
(`/api/chat/webhooks?token=<token>`); the old `/api/chat/invites/<token>` and
`/api/chat/webhooks/<token>` paths answer `410`
([chat private rooms](../app/chat-private-rooms.md#invite-links)). Caddy
applies one filter per log field and `request>uri` already uses the `query`
filter, so redacting a path would need hand-written regular expressions over
the whole URI that nothing here can validate before it ships; moving the
tokens is safer. A client on an old path is logged once, gets the `410`, and
the owner rotates the token. The app's own error and Sentry logs replace both old paths
with `[token]` (`_privacy_safe_log_path` in `app/src/entry.py`). Tests:
`deploy/tests/test_render.py`, `app/tests/test_sentry_worker.py`,
`app/tests/test_chat_relay_hardening.py`.

## Rolling it out

1. `tools/next_fleet.py logread-key --execute`; copy the printed `[logs]`
   block into `deploy/fleet.toml`.
2. Per core, drained from DNS: `install nN --steps logread --execute`, undrain,
   `next_ids.py status nN`. For a runner, only the install and status check.

The `logread` step pushes an expected-change window for exactly its files and
refuses a node with another pending change; if Caddy rejects the reload, the
previous Caddyfile is restored.

## New and autoscaled nodes

A node's logs register on the desktop when it is:

- **Discoverable:** labelled `fmnext-core-N`, `fmnext-auto-N`, `fmnext-run-N`
  or `fmnext-burst-N` and tagged `forkmesh-next`. The desktop reads
  `fleet-instances.json`, `autoscaled-instances.json` and a cached provider
  listing (refreshed hourly or shortly after a scaler create/destroy line, with
  backoff on failure).
- **Carrying the reader:** installed by the `files`/`start` or `logread`
  steps. Burst-runner snapshots must be taken after that.

Autoscaler rules: app replicas are `fmnext-auto-N`, burst runners
`fmnext-burst-N`, never `fmnext-run-N` (reserved for always-on runners); keep
the tag; report scaled nodes in `next_autoscale.py status --json`; rebuild the
snapshot when the reader or its key changes.

## What reaches the Log page

`desktop/src/CoreNodeLogs.cpp` forwards every journal line with a message,
sorted into a source (mail, app, rqlite, web, job, mirror, ids, ops, ssh,
kernel, system) and a fleet category; error lines go under **Error**.
Identical lines from one node and source fold to one per 10 minutes. Streams
pause past 20,000 queued lines and resume from the cursor.

- JSON journal messages are shown as one readable line (level, logger,
  message, fields; IDS incidents as `severity detector: summary`).
- Each Caddy access record is one line with method, host, path, status,
  duration, size, client flag and address, and User-Agent. A 5xx is an error,
  except an expected-degraded 503, which is a warning.
- Client details: country from a cached DB-IP Lite table
  (`desktop/src/IpCountry.cpp`), labels for fleet nodes, loopback, the mesh
  and Cloudflare egress, the relayed visitor from the signed edge header, and
  an optional `whois` owner per network (`desktop/src/IpWhois.cpp`, rate
  limited, never for private ranges). The same enrichment applies to any line
  with an `IP <addr>` field.
- A host-side 500 is reported by `app/host/forkmesh_host/error_log.py` as an
  `ERROR <context> -> 500: <repr>` line plus a traceback, which the desktop
  joins into one error. The client response is unchanged.

## Deploy output

`desktop/src/DeployLogs.cpp` follows `<fleet logs>/autodeploy/*.log`,
`<fleet logs>/ops/*.log` and the user journal of the publisher, fan-out and
node-deploy units (`<fleet logs>` is `~/projects/forkmesh/logs/fleet` or
`FMNEXT_LOGS_DIR`). Each line reads `Deploy <kind>: <line>`; duplicates
between file and journal are dropped. Only real failures (journal err,
`result: FAILED`, tracebacks) are errors; per-test failure lines are not.

`next_common.Runner` tees every `--execute` run's output to
`<fleet logs>/ops/<stamp>-<tool>-<command>.log` (0600). Dry runs and
children of the deploy agent write nothing. Deploy tests point
`FMNEXT_LOGS_DIR` at a temp folder.

## Planned restarts are quiet

`desktop/src/PlannedRestarts.cpp` keeps one planned-restart window per node,
opened by the node's IDS "expectation accepted" line for a deploy or roll (or
the desktop's own deploy line) and closed by "back in DNS" or the deploy's
version check, at most 15 minutes. Inside a window, restart symptoms
(connection refused to the app or gateway, Caddy 502/503, local 500s, sealed
vault) raise one info Ping instead of error Pings; they still count as errors
in the Log. A window that expires logs "did not come back" as an error. IDS
lines and other errors always ping. Roll nodes with `roll` or undrain through
`next_dns.py` so the window closes.

## Turning all logging off

**Stop logging** in the Log page header (`logs/allOff`) drops every line before
it is recorded, stops every network log feed (Worker tail, node SSH streams,
host feeds, provider inventory polls) and the deploy-log follower, and flushes
the queue with a final `Logs: all logging is off.` line. Turning it back on
restarts each feed whose own setting is on.

## Recording only some log types

Each category chip on the Log page has a record checkbox under it, a shortcut
for the Log types dialog's switches (`logs/mutedCategories`), so the choice
survives a restart. A ticked box means the category is recorded right now:
logging is on and the category is not muted.

- Ticking a box while all logging is off turns logging on for that category
  alone (every other category is muted), so picking a few types from the off
  state is a matter of ticking each one.
- Ticking a box while logging is on adds that category back; unticking mutes it.
- The **All** box is checked when every category is recorded, partly checked
  when some are muted, and empty while logging is off. Unticking it turns all
  logging off; ticking it unmutes everything and turns logging on.

Muted categories still let their network feeds run; only **Stop logging**
stops those.
