pages.description: Part of Operations.
pages.markdown:
# Node operator policy and legal response

Part of [Operations](README.md).

An operator decides, for their own node only, what it stores and serves, how
much disk it may use, and how it answers abuse reports and legal requests. None
of this is a network-wide rule: a repository this node refuses or quarantines is
reported unavailable here and the router sends readers to another mirror. The
policy is opt-in; a gateway without `operatorPolicy` is unaffected. It applies to
the [mirror gateway](direct-https-mirror-gateway.md) and
[SSH gateway](git-ssh-gateway.md); background is in [self-hosting](../self-hosting.md),
[mirroring](../mirroring.md) and [censorship resilience](../censorship-resilience.md).

## Enabling it

Create an owner-only (`0600`) policy file and a `0700` state directory for the
gateway's service user, then add to `mirror-gateway.json`:

```json
"operatorPolicy": {
  "policyPath": "/var/lib/forkmesh-mirror/operator-policy.json",
  "stateDirectory": "/var/lib/forkmesh-mirror/operator-policy"
}
```

`mirror_gateway.py --check` validates it; `node_operator_policy.py` must sit
beside the gateway or validation fails. Commands below are
`python3 -I tools/node_operator_policy.py <command>` and print JSON.

## Policy reference

`profile` (`home`, `community`, `commercial`) sets finite defaults for
`limits.maxRepositoryBytes`, `maxBlobBytes`, `maxPushBytes`, `maxRepositories`
and `storageBudgetBytes`, `seeding.privateReplicas` (off except commercial),
`violationAction` and `retention.evidenceDays`. Any field can be overridden.

- `repositories.allow` / `.block` take an owner or `owner/repository`; a
  non-empty allow list restricts the node to those repositories.
- `content.blockedExtensions`, `blockedPathPatterns` and `blockedObjectIds`
  refuse matching names, paths or exact objects in every new tree.
- `violationAction`: `quarantine` lets `enforce --apply` stop serving stored
  violators; `report` only lists them. Violating pushes are always refused.
- `jurisdiction` (`us`, `eu`, `uk`, `other`) selects the case runbook.
- `secrets` enables the [secret scanning](../security/secret-scanning.md) gate.
- Unknown fields, duplicate keys and group- or world-writable files are refused.

## Protected branches

```json
"branches": {
  "rules": [
    {"pattern": "main", "requireSignedCommits": true},
    {"pattern": "refs/tags/v*", "blockForcePush": false}
  ],
  "allowedSignersPath": "/var/lib/forkmesh-mirror/allowed_signers"
}
```

The same pre-receive hook enforces these on the HTTPS gateway and the
[SSH gateway](git-ssh-gateway.md). A bare `pattern` means `refs/heads/<name>`;
`repositories` scopes a rule. `blockDeletion` and `blockForcePush` default to
`true`. `requireSignedCommits` accepts only SSH signatures from the OpenSSH
allowed-signers file and checks every commit the update adds. A stale expected
old value is refused as `stale-ref`. A refused push changes no ref, stores no
object and prints recovery steps; admitted and refused protected pushes are
audited. Tightening a rule requires `apply --confirm`.

## Enforcement

- **Pushes.** The gateway sets `core.hooksPath` to `<stateDirectory>/hooks`,
  holding only its own `pre-receive`. Staged objects are checked for allow/block
  lists, quarantine, push and storage size, blob names and ids, and secrets. Any
  failure discards the staged objects. An unreadable policy refuses every push.
- **Stored data.** Upstream fetches bypass the hook, so run `enforce` (preview)
  and `enforce --apply` after tightening a policy or on a timer.
- **Quarantine** writes `<state>/quarantine/<owner>/<repo>.json`: the repository
  answers as not found and its signed health says `available: false`. Bytes stay
  on disk until `release` or `remove`.

## Changing a policy

Never edit the active file in place. `preview` reports capacity and which
repositories would become unavailable; `apply` archives the previous file under
`<state>/policy-history/` and requires `--confirm` for any change that reduces
availability; `history` and `rollback` restore through the same checks.

## Reports, appeals and removal

`report`, `action`, `appeal`, `resolve --decision reverse|uphold|dismiss` and
`remove` (quarantined repositories only, `--confirm`, irreversible on this node)
manage cases. Evidence holds metadata only, never refused content;
`prune-evidence` honours `retention.evidenceDays` and never prunes open,
appealed or legal-hold cases. `runbook` prints a jurisdiction checklist
(process reminders, not legal advice).

## Audit and status

Every policy, case, quarantine and push decision is appended to the hash-chained
`<state>/audit.jsonl`; `verify-audit` exits 4 at the first broken record.
`status` returns secret-free counters for dashboards. Bandwidth caps, a desktop
policy editor and per-pusher branch rules are not provided.

pages.title: Non-custodial organization succession
pages.description: Part of Operations.
pages.markdown:
# Non-custodial organization succession

Part of [Operations](README.md).

Organization succession is a governance mechanism for one organization
roster. It is not inheritance, account recovery, custody, or asset transfer.

## Transfer boundary

A completed succession performs exactly two scoped changes: the configured
owner becomes an organization administrator, and the named successor becomes
the owner. Only those two `org_members.role` values change; repository records,
links, teams, memberships, private-repository shares, and encryption recipients
are untouched.

Never transferred:

- wallets, wallet addresses, funds, rewards, or signing ability;
- private keys, account credentials, agent credentials, or private agent data;
- user accounts, personal data, devices, or device ownership;
- repository ownership, content, or ACLs.

Every succession response states this boundary.

## Configuration and lifecycle

Only the sole current owner configures a policy with
`PUT /api/orgs/{org}/succession`. The successor must be an active existing
administrator or member. Unknown or transfer-shaped fields are rejected.

| Setting | Range | Default |
|---|---|---|
| Inactivity threshold | 30–730 days | 180 |
| Grace period | 7–90 days | 30 |
| Independent approvals | 2–20 | 2 |

Approvals cannot exceed the eligible roster; owner and successor cannot approve.

1. `POST .../check-in` (or enabled-device and owned-node activity) refreshes the
   owner's activity and cancels an open grace case.
2. An hourly job sends one warning before the deadline; it never opens a case.
3. After the threshold, a current member calls `POST .../activate` to open grace.
4. During grace the owner may `cancel` or `check-in`; other current members
   `approve` (idempotent; removed members' approvals stop counting). Only
   members who already held an approving role when grace opened may approve:
   opening the case records that roster in `org_succession_case_approvers`
   (a trigger on the case insert, migration 0295), and both the approval
   insert and the completion check require the approver to be in it. An
   account added or promoted during grace gets
   `approver_joined_after_grace_opened`, so an administrator cannot reach the
   threshold with accounts made for the purpose.
5. After grace, a member calls `POST .../finalize`. One transaction rechecks
   deadline, owner, successor, and current approvers before changing the roles;
   any change fails closed.

`DELETE /api/orgs/{org}/succession` disables the policy and cancels any case.

## Authorization and audit

The API uses organization session and roster checks only; it has no
platform-administrator authorization path, and the tables are hidden from the
generic admin editor. Cases and approvals are immutable snapshots, and every
action appends a metadata-only event; triggers keep history append-only.
`GET /api/orgs/{org}/succession` (`no-store`) returns status, counts, and
dates, never device data.

pages.markdown:
# Operator files

Part of [Operations](README.md).

Where the fleet's code lives in this repository and where the operator box
keeps the fleet's secrets, keys, state and logs. No secret is in the
repository: `deploy/fleet.toml` names every secret by credential name only.
How the stack fits together: [served stack](served-stack.md); what to run:
[runbook](runbook.md).

## Code

The stack's code is part of this repository: `app/host/`, `deploy/`,
`tools/next_*.py` and `tools/cutover_*.py`. It was built in its own
repository and is now production. `tools/next_import.py` can replay the old
separate repository's history onto a branch here; it is deterministic,
refuses to rewind a diverged branch without `--force`, and is tested by
`deploy/tests/test_next_import.py`.

## Folders

Operator state lives under the never-erase project folders (`AGENTS.md`).
The real folders are `~/projects/forkmesh/data/core/{config,ssh,logs}/fleet`
and `data/core/fleet`; the `~/projects/forkmesh/<root>` links below reach
them ([projects layout](../tools/projects-layout.md)):

| Folder | Holds |
|---|---|
| `~/projects/forkmesh/config/fleet/` | the files in the next table, `ids-operator.key`, `known_hosts`, deploy and autodeploy locks and manifests, `add-core/` and `remove-core/` run state |
| `~/projects/forkmesh/ssh/fleet/` | the fleet SSH key and its `known_hosts` |
| `~/projects/forkmesh/data/fleet/` | `backups/`, `dist/` (release tarballs and the mirror-node binary), `dl/` (the pinned rqlite and Caddy tarballs; sha256 in `deploy/fleet.toml`, checked on both ends), `bin/` (rqlite and Caddy for tests) |
| `~/projects/forkmesh/logs/fleet/` | tool and run logs |

`config/fleet/` is mode 0700 and its files 0600. There is no object storage:
backups are pulled to the operator box and certificates are shared over
WireGuard.

## Files in `config/fleet/`

| File | Contents |
|---|---|
| `vultr.env` | `VULTR_API_KEY`. Tools touch only instances labelled `fmnext-*` and tagged `forkmesh-next`. Prefer a sub-user limited to instances. |
| `aws.env` | optional AWS credentials for an IAM user with only the fleet policy ([fleet tooling](fleet-tooling.md#iam-policy)) |
| `cloudflare-dns.env` | `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN`, `CLOUDFLARE_ZONE_ID`: the DNS token file `next_dns.py` reads; scope it to DNS edit on the zone |
| `cloudflare.env` | account token for the `forkmesh-www` Worker deploy and the cutover tools |
| `secrets.env` | `DATA_KEY`, `ADMIN_PASS`, router seed and public key, `FORKMESH_MESH_SECRET`, `FORKMESH_CERTSYNC_SECRET`, `WWW_EDGE_SECRET`, `RQLITE_PASSWORD`, integration values. Generated by `next_fleet.py init-secrets`. |
| `DATA_KEY` (0400) | the vault key alone; keep an offline copy |
| `fleet-instances.json` | label → instance id, plan, region, IPv4, IPv6: the only place node addresses are kept ([node addresses](fleet-tooling.md#node-addresses)) |
| `fleet-state.json` | WireGuard and IDS public keys |
| `dns-health.json` | per-node health counters, `in_dns`, `held` |

## Paths in the tools

`tools/forkmesh_paths.py` is the one source for these paths; `next_common`
derives `config_dir()`, `ssh_key_path()`, `data_dir()` and `logs_dir()` from it.
The overrides `FMNEXT_CONFIG_DIR`, `FMNEXT_SSH_KEY`,
`FMNEXT_DATA_DIR`, `FMNEXT_LOGS_DIR`, `FMNEXT_BACKUPS_DIR` and
`FMNEXT_DIST_DIR` let an operator point the tools elsewhere without moving
anything.

## Rules

- Copy, never move, operator state. Delete a copy only by explicit file name.
- The hourly minimal backup must not archive `config/fleet` or `ssh/fleet` in
  plaintext; those folders are backed up encrypted.
- The private backup decryption key belongs offline, not next to the backups.
- The operator units (`fmnext-backup`, `fmnext-unseal`, `fmnext-dns-health`)
  run the repository venv from `~/projects/forkmesh/src`; that venv needs
  `cryptography`.
- `~/projects/forkmesh-backup` is the retired folder of the old repository,
  kept as a backup. Never erase it.
- Remote node paths (`/etc/forkmesh-next`, `/opt/forkmesh-next`,
  `/var/lib/forkmesh-next`) and the `forkmesh-next` instance tag are identity
  names, not operator paths, and do not change.

pages.title: Organization agent offline queue
pages.description: Part of Operations.
pages.markdown:
# Organization agent offline queue

Part of [Operations](README.md).

Organization owners can queue Claude Code and Codex work for the desktop linked
to an organization repository while that desktop is offline. The queue is
durable and has no admission-count limit; list responses are bounded. Online
nodes take website jobs as described in
[mirror node](mirror-node.md#running-website-agent-jobs).

## Admission

Offline admission requires that the requester holds the organization `owner`
role, the repository has an exact `org_repos` link, the requester owns the
linked source node, the signed catalog record places the repository on a
`desktop` runtime, and that record advertises the requested provider. Other
members use the online, provider-capable mirror route.

Admission does not authorize execution. The reconnecting desktop proves node
ownership when it claims a job, validates the lease envelope, and rechecks the
provider binary and login before dispatch. Job and session rows are encrypted
at rest.

## Drain and recovery

The server leases one job per repository at a time, oldest first, using a
conditional queued-to-leased update. The desktop requests the next job only
after its result is acknowledged. A lease abandoned for two minutes
(`ORG_AGENT_JOB_LEASE_MS`) returns to `queued`; queued and running rows are
never deleted by this flow. The desktop starts a drain after each sync,
persists the running job's lease with the local session, and retries the
terminal report after a restart.

## Diagnostics

Rejections carry a stable `error`, a user-facing `message`, `retryable`, and
where relevant `requiredAction`, `provider`, and `targetNode`. Actions include
`link_repository`, `publish_repository`, `link_owned_desktop`,
`link_desktop_target`, `publish_provider_capability`, `select_linked_desktop`,
`select_eligible_target`, `bring_agent_mirror_online`, and `relink_desktop`.
Clients show the server message verbatim.

## Verification

Run `python3 tools/quality_gate.py run --profile core` (and `--profile release`
before a release). Rolling back the server needs no data migration; do not
reintroduce a per-organization task-count trigger.

pages.markdown:
# Owner pushes to the core nodes

Part of [Operations](README.md).

The cores hold the flagship repository and every repository whose namespace is
a core node's account. Owners push with plain `git push` over HTTPS:

```
git push https://app.forkmesh.com/<owner>/<repo>.git <branch>
```

The per-core names serve the same app and take the same pushes. Hosted
repositories follow the same rules ([hosted repositories](core-hosted-repositories.md));
how the cores fit together is in [architecture](../architecture.md).

Code: `app/src/entry.py` (`_https_mirror_push_proxy`, `_core_push_permitted`,
`_admit_core_push_state`, `_ref_updates_from`), `app/src/core_push.py` (tag
moves, branch deletes and trash listing, audit, hooks),
`tools/mirror_gateway.py` (`enforce_push_ref_policy`, `X-ForkMesh-Ref-Updates`),
`server/gateway.go` (`adoptAdmittedTagMoves`), migration `0205_git_tag_moves`.
Each accepted branch push is also recorded for the pusher's "recent pushes"
bar ([recent push banner](../app/recent-push-banner.md)).

## Who can push

| Repository | May push |
|---|---|
| Linked to an organization (`org_repos`) | an organization **owner** |
| Personal (a core node's namespace without an organization) | the account that owns the node |

Anyone else gets `403 push_forbidden` before any core is contacted, audited
as `git.push_authorize`. Anonymous requests get a `401` Basic challenge.

The same rule covers every commit the App makes on a user's behalf: web file
edits, renames and deletes (`/file-edit`), release notes, assets and tags
(`/release-edit`), project boards and security advisory ledgers all push
through `repository_file_edits._push`, which calls `_core_push_permitted`
for a core-held repository and answers `403 push_forbidden` otherwise.
Write permission alone is not enough because the operator's source checkout
deploys the cores' `main`, so a maintainer's commit or release tag there
would ship (`test_core_held_save_needs_an_organization_owner`,
`test_a_maintainer_cannot_tag_a_core_held_repository`). Writers propose
changes as pull requests. Repositories that are not core-held use ordinary
write permission.

## Who serves the flagship

When `HOSTED_GIT_CORE_NODES` is set, only those cores serve, pin and merge
the flagship. The flagship is `forkmesh/forkmesh` and the node it is linked
to, found by `_flagship_core_nodes` in `app/src/entry.py`.

- `_https_mirror_public_context` sets the routing set (`nodes`) to the
  cores, so read candidates, the direct-mirror 307 target, release blobs and
  owner-merge executors are always cores.
- The flagship quorum (`_https_mirror_flagship_quorum`, also in
  `_https_mirror_accepted_forkmesh_refs`) counts only core endpoints.
- The catalog peer-quorum recovery is skipped for the flagship.

Mirrors run by anyone else may publish a catalog record in the flagship's
group and appear in `groupNodes`, but never serve it and their agreement
never admits a state: a mirror's proof is only its own signature over the
digest it claims, and the app never sees the bytes behind a 307, so any two
accounts could otherwise be routed flagship clones. Without
`HOSTED_GIT_CORE_NODES` (development, self-hosted instances) group-based
routing applies (`test_flagship_serving_nodes_are_the_fleet_cores_only`,
`test_flagship_context_and_quorum_never_count_outside_mirrors`).

Credentials:

- Basic with the account name or email as the username and either the
  session-bound push credential (`fmp1.…`, from
  `POST /api/hosted-repositories/push-credential`) or, for an account without
  two-factor authentication, the account password.
- Signed requests (`forkmesh-git-push-v1`, `X-ForkMesh-Pubkey/-Ts/-Sig`) with
  the account's primary or an enabled device key.

Admins may also commit one edited `docs/**/*.md` file through the developer
docs page, under the same ref rules. There are no SSH pushes and no personal
access tokens.

**Account password over git** (`hosted_git._password_git_account`). The
username may be the account name or sign-in email, and the password the
account password. The password path checks exactly what the website login checks
(`_account_password_record`: active user account, PBKDF2 password) and spends
the same `login_attempts` budgets (`_login_attempt_keys`, `_login_record_fail`,
`_login_clear`), so git cannot be used to guess passwords faster than the
sign-in page. It refuses a password for an account with two-factor
authentication because Git cannot supply the second factor; sign in through
the website and use a session-bound push credential instead. Push
permission is re-checked the same way for both credentials, and the audit row's
`credential` says `password` or `session-mac`. An instance turns the password
path off with `GIT_PASSWORD_AUTH=0`. Private hosted clones accept the same
credentials. Tests: `test_account_name_or_email_and_password_push` and the
tests after it in `app/tests/test_hosted_repositories.py`.

**Retired cores.** A core removed from the fleet is listed in
`[hosted] retired_cores`; `deploy/core/render.py` writes
`FORKMESH_VAR_HOSTED_GIT_CORE_OWNERS` (live plus retired cores), and
`hosted_repos.core_owners` backs `_core_push_nodes`, so repositories owned by a
retired core's account stay core-held while pushes go only to live cores.

**"Open a pull request" after a push to a fork** (`_fork_push_notice`,
`git_http.with_sideband_message`). After an accepted receive-pack
(`POST`, 200) whose `X-ForkMesh-Ref-Updates` name a new or moved branch other
than the default, on a repository whose catalog record has `forkedFrom` (or
a contributor's `pr/<account>/` branch on the repository itself, see
[hosted repositories](core-hosted-repositories.md)), the proxy reads the result and adds one
side-band 2 packet before the final flush:

```
remote: Open a pull request for 'fix' by visiting:
remote:      https://app.forkmesh.com/<you>/<repo>/compare/main...fix
```

On a fork that page targets the parent (`pullRequestParent`); for a `pr/`
branch it opens a pull request on the repository itself. Results without side-band
(`docs_book.py`'s report-status push) and non-fork pushes are passed through
untouched, and the body is only read when the line applies. Up to five
branches are listed. `_https_mirror_push_send` is unchanged. Tests:
`app/tests/test_fork_push_notice.py`, including a stock `git push` against
`git http-backend` that prints the lines.

## Ref rules

| Ref | Rule |
|---|---|
| default branch, protected branches, `forkmesh/*` | fast-forward only, for everyone |
| other branches | force-push allowed for accounts that may write them ([force pushes](#force-pushes)) |
| any branch | never deleted by a push (use the Branches page) |
| new tag | allowed |
| existing tag | moves only to the exact object of a pending owner tag move; never deleted |
| outside `refs/heads/` and `refs/tags/` | refused |

## Force pushes

Updating a pull request after `git commit --amend`, `git rebase main` or a
squash needs a non-fast-forward update. It is allowed GitHub-style: on any
branch except the default branch, protected branches and the `forkmesh/`
ledger branches, by an account that may write that branch.

**Who may rewrite what.** The decision needs the pusher, so it is not a static
`receive.denyNonFastForwards`:

- `_https_mirror_push_send` adds `rewrite=<patterns>` to the router-signed
  receive-pack capability, only on the user push route
  (`_https_mirror_push_proxy`, which the SSH relay also reaches), and only
  for a repository the core nodes hold or host (`core_held`, or
  `hosted_push_candidates` answers; `_push_target_on_cores`). A mirror of a
  repository published from someone's own node never gets the grant: the
  owner's node and the other mirrors would not take the rewrite, and the
  copies would split against the node's signed refs pin. A writer
  (owner, organization writer, signed key) gets `rewrite=refs/heads/`; a
  contributor gets `rewrite=refs/heads/pr/<account>/`, the same prefix as
  `pushPrefix`. Web edits (`repository_file_edits.py`, `docs_book.py`) never
  send it.
- The gateway (`tools/mirror_gateway.py`, `parse_rewrite_refs`,
  `rewritable_refs`) refuses a contributor grant naming refs outside its
  prefix, then narrows the grant to the refs this push updates that are
  under `refs/heads/`, not `HEAD`'s branch on that core, not under
  `refs/heads/forkmesh/` and not protected (`protect=`, which already refuses
  any update to those refs).
- With a grant, receive-pack runs with `receive.denyNonFastForwards=false` and
  `core.hooksPath` pointing at a gateway-owned directory (inside its private
  runtime directory) whose `pre-receive` (`push_rewrite_hook_script`) reads
  the `old new ref` lines and refuses any non-fast-forward branch update whose
  ref is not in `FORKMESH_PUSH_REWRITE`, the exact list the gateway passed in
  the environment. It then hands the same input to the operator-policy hook,
  when one is configured, so `blockForcePush` rules still apply.
- Fail closed: no `rewrite=` field (an older app, a web edit, a runner grant)
  or a missing hook file keeps `receive.denyNonFastForwards=true`; an empty
  `FORKMESH_PUSH_REWRITE` makes the hook refuse every rewrite.
  `receive.denyDeletes=true` always stays, and `enforce_branch_deletes`
  answers a branch delete with a pointer to the Branches page: a pushed delete
  would be fetched back from the other cores.

**Messages.** A forced push to the default branch prints "`<b>` is the default
branch: it only moves forward" and suggests `git pull --rebase origin <b>`. A
plain `git push` of a branch the server moved (after **Update branch** or a
web edit) is refused by git itself with "fetch first"; the docs and the
accepted-push notice recommend `git pull --rebase`, then
`git push --force-with-lease`. An accepted forced update adds `remote:` lines
(`_fork_push_notice`) naming the old and new tips and a compare link.

**Nothing is lost.** Pushes with a grant to the same repository run one at a
time (`rewrite_push_lock`). Before receive-pack runs, the gateway stores the
current tip of every granted ref at
`refs/forkmesh/history/<branch>/<10-digit sequence>` (create-only; on a name
clash it tries the next sequence numbers). If a tip cannot be stored the push
is refused before anything moves, so a forced update never lands without its
backup. After the push, a backup whose branch did not move, or moved forward
(`merge-base --is-ancestor old new`), is removed again (that commit is still
reachable from the branch); a forced one is reported as `kept`. History refs
are never pruned, since a cap would let anyone allowed to force-push evict
older tips by pushing repeatedly. Replicas keep their own copy the same way before adopting a forced
tip (`keepSupersededTip`, also never pruned). `refs/forkmesh/` is hidden from upload-pack and
receive-pack, so old commits stay resolvable for reviews and comments without
being advertised. To restore, an operator runs
`git update-ref refs/heads/<b> <oid>` on a core (or pushes the commit from a
clone that has it).

**Reporting.** The `X-ForkMesh-Ref-Updates` entry of a forced update carries
`forced: true` and `kept` (the history ref), and `record_accepted_push` audits
`git.force_push`. The open pull requests of the branch are reported for every
branch push, forced or not (see [pull requests follow their
branch](#pull-requests-follow-their-branch)). Older ledgers keep `force-push`
events from before that change; the timeline still renders them.

### Pull requests follow their branch

A pull request opened from a branch of the same repository (a writer's
`feature` or a contributor's `pr/<account>/<topic>`) follows that branch the
way GitHub does: a push to the branch updates the pull request.

**Why not re-sign the pull.** The author's signature (`verify_pull_event`)
covers title, base, head name, `changes.patch` and `commits.mbox`, never a
commit id. `headOid` and `headBaseOid` are the node's own record of the commit
the signed series replays to (`recordPullHead`), unsigned like `status`. So a
push leaves the signed creation diff alone and records the new head next to
it, which keeps every old signature valid.

**Detection.** For every accepted push that moves an existing branch (not the
default branch, not `forkmesh/`, not a new branch), the gateway lists the open
pull requests whose `pull.md` names that branch as `head`
(`open_pulls_for_head`, at most 8 branches per push and 10 pulls per branch)
and puts them in the update's `pulls`. `head` values of the form
`<copy>:<branch>` (patch-backed pulls from another copy) never match, so those
still update only by resubmitting.

**Who may move a pull.** Only a push the platform accepted (HTTPS gateway,
contributor push, core push): the gateway already checked that the pusher may
write that ref (owner, organization writer, or a contributor inside
`pr/<account>/`). `may_synchronize` checks again that a contributor push only
moves `pr/<pusher>/` branches, and an anonymous push moves nothing.

**The event.** `record_accepted_push` queues one `synchronize` event per pull
in `pull_inbox` (`type, id, author, authorName, ts, ref, before, after,
commits, forced, body`, `sig: ""` like force-push and ForkBot events), with
`source: "synchronize"`. The id is `synchronize-<n>-<after[:16]>`, so the same
(pull, head) is recorded once however often it is queued.

**Applying it (node).** `materializePullInbox` checks the event before it
writes anything (`pullSynchronizeTarget`): the pull is open, `head` is a plain
branch of this repository that equals the event's `ref`, `after` is a commit
the repository has and the branch still contains (an older event for a commit
a later force push dropped is skipped), and the pull is not already at
`after`. It then writes the event file and, for a patch-backed record, sets
`headOid: <after>`, `headBaseOid: <merge-base of after and the base branch>`
and `syncedHeadOid: <after>` in `pull.md` (`applyPullSynchronize`) and moves
`refs/pr/<n>/head`. `derive: branch` records already follow their branch, so
only the timeline event is written. `ensurePullHeadRefs` publishes `headOid`,
so the sweep keeps the synced head instead of reverting it.

**Readers.** `syncedHeadOid` equal to `headOid` means "the head is a real
branch commit, not a replay of the signed series":

- the web reads Files changed and Commits from `compare(headBaseOid, head)`
  (`loadRepoPullSyncedPatch`, `loadRepoPullCommits`); the host's first paint
  (`repo_views.plan_pull`) does the same;
- the merge trial, checks and merge box use `headOid` as before;
- the merge executor merges that commit instead of replaying the series
  (`syncedPullHead`; an unresolvable synced head fails with `stale_head`);
- anything else that reads `headOid` or `refs/pr/<n>/head` follows too.

**Re-queued work.** When the node acknowledges the inbox rows, the relay looks
at the acknowledged `synchronize` rows (`_pull_inbox_synchronized`) and calls
`core_push.pulls_synchronized`, which hands the moved branches to the pull
hooks a build has (`pull_attention_moved`, `ai_review_note_push`,
`pull_actions_sync_repo`, each optional). Waiting for the acknowledgement
matters: before it, `pull.md` still names the old head.

**Timeline.** "`<pusher>` pushed N commits to `<branch>` `<after7>`" or
"force-pushed `<branch>` from `<before7>` to `<after7>`", each with a compare
link; reviews submitted before the newest push show "on an older commit".
There is no "dismiss stale reviews" rule, so approvals still count.

**Repair.** Pulls whose branch moved before this existed (or while the node was
old) are moved with the host CLI, dry run first:

```sh
cd /opt/forkmesh-instance/src/app/host && /opt/forkmesh-instance/venv/bin/python \
  -m forkmesh_host pull-resync --owner <storage-owner> --name <repo> \
  [--number <n>] --dry-run --env-file /etc/forkmesh-instance/app.env \
  --db sqlite:/var/lib/forkmesh-instance/app.db \
  --data-dir /var/lib/forkmesh-instance/data
```

It reads the hosted repository as `forkmesh-node`, lists every open pull with
an action (`sync` or `skip` and why) and, without `--dry-run`, queues the same
`synchronize` events as a push (author `--actor`, default `--owner`), then
asks the local node to drain its inboxes now (`POST /v1/control/sync` on the
loopback `listen` address from `--node-config`). The wake is needed because
`notify_repo_host` reaches the node through the Durable Object emulation
(`durable.py`) of the calling process, which lives inside the serving app; a
doorbell rung from a CLI process reaches no socket, and the row would wait
for the node's next reconnect or push. A pull is
moved only when its head branch exists, contains the pull's base, and holds a
commit whose subject matches one in the signed `commits.mbox`; `--number`
names a pull explicitly and skips the subject match. The node applies the
events with the checks above, so a dry run is safe and a real run is
idempotent.

**Replicas.** Cores converge by fetching (`reconcileUpstreamRefs`), which never
rewinds a branch and lets the newer commit win a divergence. So the app
records each forced tip in the hosted repository record (`forced`, newest 32,
kept 7 days, `hosted_repos.note_forced`) before it moves `pushed_at`, and the
replica desired set carries `forced: {ref: oid}`. A replica that fetches
exactly that tip for that ref keeps its own old tip under
`refs/forkmesh/history/` and moves the branch (`adoptForcedBranches`, never
`HEAD`'s branch or `forkmesh/`). Every core also refuses to move a branch to a
tip recorded in its history (`supersededBranchTips`), so a stale peer cannot
bring a replaced commit back.

**SSH gateway.** The relay mode forwards to the HTTPS route and inherits all of
this. The local mode (`ssh_gateway.py` without `httpGit`) sets no deny rules
and relies on the operator-policy hook, as before.

### Moving a tag

1. `POST /api/git/tag-moves` `{"owner", "repo", "ref", "target"}`, by session
   or signed `forkmesh-tag-move-v1\n{owner}\n{repo}\n{ref}\n{target}\n{ts}`.
   Only core-held repositories and permitted pushers; the row lives 15
   minutes in `git_tag_moves`.
2. `git push --force origin refs/tags/<tag>` within 15 minutes; the app puts
   the pending moves into the router-signed capability and the gateway allows
   exactly those.
3. The move is audited as `git.tag_move`.

## Consistency

1. The app streams the push to one core.
2. `_admit_core_push_state` records that core's freshly signed routing digest
   and sends the `commits` wake to every core, including the canonical owner
   when it is a core. The wake goes out even when the digest could not be
   admitted (then without state, as a plain sync request).
3. Other cores fetch from the pushed core and converge fast-forward only
   (a recorded force push excepted, see [force pushes](#force-pushes)); a
   moved tag is adopted only when it yields exactly the admitted digest.
4. The source publisher ([source publisher](../tools/source-publisher.md))
   pushes the source checkout the same way and absorbs commits owners pushed
   directly (fast-forward, or a clean merge; conflicts are logged and left
   alone).

Robustness: before every fetch the daemon drops broken or dangling loose refs
and stale lock files (`dropBrokenRefs`); failed fetches retry while avoiding
the failing peer; a node serving broken refs fails its integrity check and is
routed around.

## Deleting branches

A push never deletes (the gateway answers with a pointer to the Branches page). Branch deletion goes through the merge executor, which
first saves the tip under `refs/forkmesh/trash/branch/<b>/<token>` (or
`agent-branch/`) so peers do not fetch it back.

- `POST /api/git/branch-deletes` `{"owner", "repo", "branch", "expect"}`
  (signed `forkmesh-branch-delete-v1\n…` or session; same owners as tag
  moves). Refuses `main`, `master`, `HEAD` and `forkmesh/*`; deletes only if
  the branch is still at `expect`, then fans out to every core. The source
  publisher uses it for branches deleted in the source checkout.
- `POST /api/git/branch-trash` `{"owner", "repo"}` (signed
  `forkmesh-branch-trash-v1\n{owner}\n{repo}\n{ts}`) returns the union of the
  cores' trash entries `{branch, oid}`, with unanswered cores named. The
  gateway serves its list only behind a router capability; deleted tips are
  never exposed to ordinary readers. Results are cached 30 s per repository.
  The desktop uses it to delete local branches the cores deleted.
- A delete still running answers 202 with `requestId`, `node` and `pinBase`;
  the caller re-posts them until it settles, and a re-post can answer 503
  `merge_status_pending` or `merge_node_unavailable` (`retryable: true`).
  Those 503s, and the `cores_unavailable` 503 from both routes, carry
  `x-forkmesh-expected-degraded`, so a publisher's polling does not turn the
  API row on /status red; a core that is really down shows on its own row.
- Operator: `python3 tools/next_fleet.py delete-ref nN --repo <owner>/<repo> --ref refs/heads/<b> --expect <sha> --execute`
  (only branches merged into `main`, trash first, run on every core) and
  `delete-refs --from FILE` for many at once.

## Hooks

An accepted core push that moved refs raises the same events a node
publication raises: the `repository.push` webhook and Apps event (with
`pusher` and every ref transition), `branch.push` when the default branch
moved, and the code-push Ping to the owner and organization readers.

## Audit

Every accepted push writes one `git.push` row per updated ref in
`sensitive_audit_log` (actor, target, ref, old, new, node, credential kind,
commit count). The gateway lists at most 40 ref updates per push; larger
pushes add a `refsNotListed` row.

## Rollout and tests

Roll the gateway and daemon one core at a time (drained), then the app. Tests:
`app/tests/test_core_push_ref_policy.py`, `test_git_push_route.py`,
`test_core_push.py`, `test_node_event_push.py`, `server/core_push_test.go`.

pages.markdown:
# Paid microjobs

Part of [Operations](README.md).

A useful issue report or a focused pull request can receive a small,
discretionary SOL reward after a repository owner reviews it. There is no
separate claim form, no fixed amount, and no payout schedule.
ForkMesh never holds a key: the owner pays directly from the owner's ForkMesh
desktop wallet.
Page: [`/microjobs`](https://app.forkmesh.com/microjobs).

A reward is a thank-you for useful work, not employment, an investment, a
balance, or a promise of future payment.

## Contribute

Submit the work once, through the repository's normal form:

- **Issues:** the [New issue form](https://app.forkmesh.com/forkmesh/forkmesh/issues/new).
  Check for duplicates first, then include reproduction steps, what happened,
  what you expected, and the version you tested.
- **Pull requests:** the [New pull request form](https://app.forkmesh.com/forkmesh/forkmesh/pulls/new).
  Keep the change focused, explain what it fixes, and include verification
  evidence.

Nothing else needs to be filed. Duplicates and spam are closed without a
reward.

## Estimate, pending, paid

| Stage | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| No estimate | The owner has not attached a reward. Most work, including accepted work, may stay here. |
| Estimate | The owner recorded an amount on the issue or pull request. Issue estimates are typically 0.001–0.005 SOL. An estimate is not an approved or earned payment. |
| `pending_merge` | A pull request estimate. It stays conditional until the pull is merged; a pull that is closed unmerged is not paid. |
| `pending_wallet` | The work qualifies, but no payment has been sent yet. It stays blocked while the contributor has no payout address. |
| `paid` | The owner sent the transfer. The ledger row carries the finalized Solana transaction signature. |

Estimates and their status appear on the issue or pull request and in the
public [Ledger → Pending payments](https://app.forkmesh.com/ledger). Only a
`paid` row with a transaction signature is a completed payment.

## Getting paid

Save a public Solana address under
[Settings → Verification and payout](https://app.forkmesh.com/dashboard/settings).
Never give anyone a wallet key or recovery phrase. The owner's desktop unlocks
the owner's wallet locally and broadcasts the exact direct transfer; the server
never signs or broadcasts. Timing is up to the owner.

## Legacy claim API

An earlier fixed-amount claim system. The web app no longer offers it, but its
server code (`app/src/microjobs.py`, `/api/microjobs/claims`, the hourly
`microjob-payouts` cron phase) still answers direct API calls. Nothing here
applies to work submitted through the forms above, and none of it promises a
fixed amount or an hourly payout.

### Jobs

| Job | Amount | Paid when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `issue_report` | 0.005 SOL | An AI reviewer finds no existing issue or code already covering it |
| `merged_pull` | 0.05 SOL | The pull is merged **and** carries the MCP agent tool's signed marker |
| `referral_post` | 0.01 SOL | The public page still links the referral **and** its hostname has sent counted visitors |

Amounts are fixed in `microjobs.JOBS`. Claims reuse the
[community reward pool](community-reward-pool.md) custody boundary: an approved
claim becomes a public, unsigned `chain_intents` plan that the repository
owner's desktop re-validates, signs in its encrypted vault, and broadcasts.

### Claim lifecycle

```
submitted -> pending_review | approved | rejected
             pending_review -> approved
             approved -> queued -> paid
```

`pending_review` waits for referral counters; `queued` is batched into an
unsigned plan; `paid` records the matching finalized transaction signature;
`rejected` returns the reason. A UNIQUE blind index
(`microjob_claims.subject_bi`) over the exact work item makes each issue, pull,
or page claimable once.

- A merged pull's key is its signed MCP marker (number, base, head, author,
  ts), not the repository: forks copy the pull ledger branch, so a
  repository-based key would pay one pull again from every fork.
- A referral page's key (`referral_subject` in `app/src/microjobs.py`) names
  the post, not the spelling of its URL:
  - A same-site `<link rel="canonical">` becomes the key; every key then goes
    through the steps below.
  - The host is lowercased and `www.`, `old.`, `m.`, `mobile.` dropped; the path
    loses repeated and trailing slashes, percent-encoding is normalised, and the
    fragment is dropped.
  - Hosts that identify a post by query keep only that key
    (`news.ycombinator.com`: `id`; `youtube.com/watch`: `v`; `/playlist`:
    `list`). Elsewhere the query is kept, sorted, minus tracking keys (`utm_*`,
    `ref`, `fbclid`, `gclid`, `si`, `s`, `t` and similar); dropping the whole
    query would merge every Hacker News item into one claim.
  - `youtu.be/<id>`, `/shorts/<id>`, `/embed/<id>` and `/live/<id>` become
    `youtube.com/watch?v=<id>`. Reddit (`*.reddit.com`, `redd.it`) paths are
    lowercased and reduced to `reddit.com/comments/<post>[/<comment>]`.
  - On other hosts without a same-site canonical link, a second key
    `microjob:referral_post:account:<account_bi>:<scheme://host/path>` (no
    query) allows one claim per account per page path. It is stored as a
    companion row in `microjob_claims` (same account, `status='rejected'`,
    `amount_lamports=0`, `data` naming its claim), written in the same batch
    only if the claim row was written. A companion row is never paid, counted
    or batched; listings show only rows with `amount_lamports>0`.
- Keys written before these rules (repository plus pull number, the full
  normalized URL, a URL's own key when a canonical link gave another) still
  count as claimed.
- The claim insert is one conditional `INSERT ... SELECT` that re-checks the
  subject (including companion keys) and the open, daily-count and daily-amount
  caps, so concurrent requests on different cores cannot pass the caps together;
  the UNIQUE `subject_bi` index settles any race.

### Verification

- **Issue reports.** Existing issues are read over the public mirror gateway, a
  fixed-string `git grep` finds related code, and an AI model classifies the
  report as `new`, `duplicate`, `already_addressed`, or `unclear`. Only `new`
  files the issue and approves the claim. `unclear`, an unparseable answer, or a
  missing `AI` binding fails closed with a retryable response. The ordinary
  issue endpoint is unaffected.
- **Merged pulls.** `tools/forkmesh_mcp_server.py` writes `client:
  forkmesh-mcp-v1` and `clientSig`, an Ed25519 signature over
  `forkmesh-mcp-pull-v1\n<number>\n<base>\n<head>\n<author>\n<ts>`. The server
  checks the signature and that the signing node belongs to the claimant. Pull
  stores must carry both fields through rewrites.
- **Referral posts.** The URL is normalized to an ordinary public HTTPS page
  (no credentials, IP literals, non-443 ports, or internal names) and fetched
  once to find the claimant's `/r/<name>` link. `site_referrers` must show
  `MIN_REFERRAL_SITE_VISITS` visits from that hostname and `referral_stats`
  `MIN_REFERRAL_CLICKS` clicks. Until then the claim is `pending_review` and is
  rechecked hourly.

### Payout batching

The hourly `microjob-payouts` phase is `microjobs.queue_payouts`: it reads
approved claims oldest first, looks up each claimant's public payout address
(claims without one stay approved), merges claims per recipient, and writes one
`chain_intents` row of policy `microjob-payout-v1` with at most 8 transfers,
expiring in 4 hours. The owner's desktop picks it up from
`GET /api/rewards/signing-jobs`. A finalized matching transfer marks the claims
`paid`; a rejected or expired plan returns them to `approved`. The phase only
moves claims made through the API; it never touches issue or pull request
estimates.

### Limits

At most 12 open claims, 8 claims per day, and 0.12 SOL per day per account,
and one claim per work item globally. These bounds raise the cost of farming;
they are not proof of personhood.

Payouts need the reward pool configuration (`COMMUNITY_REWARD_POOL_ADDRESS` or
`TREASURY_SOLANA_ADDRESS`, `COMMUNITY_REWARD_NETWORK`,
`REWARD_SIGNER_ACCOUNT`); otherwise `queue_payouts` returns
`pool_not_configured`. `microjob_claims` cannot be edited from the admin
console.

pages.title: Patreon membership operations
pages.description: Part of Operations.
pages.markdown:
# Patreon membership operations

Part of [Operations](README.md).

Patreon is the membership payment rail for the Supporter, Pro, Builder, and
Studio tiers. The server never sees card data. Member OAuth tokens are
discarded right after identity lookup and are never stored or logged.

## Application setup

1. Create a Patreon creator application for the campaign with OAuth scopes
   `identity`, `identity[email]`, and `identity.memberships`.
2. Register the callback `https://<your-origin>/api/integrations/patreon/callback`.
3. Point a webhook at `https://<your-origin>/api/integrations/patreon/webhook`
   for `members:pledge:create`, `members:pledge:update`, and
   `members:pledge:delete`.
4. Record the numeric campaign ID and a creator-scoped access token that can
   read `GET /api/oauth2/v2/members/{id}`.

## Configuration

Non-secret variable: `PATREON_OAUTH_REDIRECT_URI`. Secrets, set together in the
core fleet's `secrets.env` and secret list (`deploy/fleet.example.toml`,
[operator files](operator-files.md)); on a
Workers self-host, `app/deploy.sh secrets` publishes them and
`app/deploy.sh validate-secrets` checks them:

```text
PATREON_CLIENT_ID
PATREON_CLIENT_SECRET
PATREON_WEBHOOK_SECRET
PATREON_CAMPAIGN_ID
PATREON_CREATOR_ACCESS_TOKEN
```

## Runtime behavior

- OAuth state is random, account-bound, single-use, and valid ten minutes.
- Callbacks redirect to `/dashboard/settings/account?patreon=<outcome>`.
- Webhooks verify `X-Patreon-Signature` (hex HMAC-MD5 of the raw body).
- Members are matched by linked Patreon user, then by email blind index.
  The email match counts only when the account has confirmed that email;
  signup accepts an unconfirmed address, so otherwise anyone who registered a
  patron's email first would receive their tier. An unconfirmed match stays
  unmatched until the patron links through OAuth.
- Entitled cents map to roles: 1–999 `supporting_member`; 1000–4999 adds
  `pro_member`; 5000–9999 adds `builder_member`; 10000+ adds `studio_member`.
  Higher tiers inherit every lower role.
- Deletion or zero entitlement revokes the membership roles after grace.
- Membership roles also fund [ForkMesh Ads](ad-network.md) slots, read from the
  same `role_grants` at serve time.

## Secret rotation

Generate the new secret in Patreon, update and deploy the secrets, confirm
OAuth start and a test webhook succeed, then revoke the old secret. Until a rotated creator token is published, webhook
reconciliation cannot fetch member snapshots.

## Failure recovery

| Symptom | Likely cause | Recovery |
| --- | --- | --- |
| OAuth start returns 503 | Missing client, campaign, or redirect config | Publish the secrets and variable |
| Callback `expired` / `replayed` | State TTL or retry | Start Connect again |
| Callback `wrong_campaign` | Membership on another campaign | Check `PATREON_CAMPAIGN_ID` |
| Callback `duplicate_identity` | Patreon user linked to another account | Unlink the prior account |
| Webhook 503 `patreon_webhook_not_configured` | Missing webhook secret | Publish `PATREON_WEBHOOK_SECRET` |
| Webhook 503 `patreon_reconciliation_not_configured` | Missing campaign or creator token | Publish `PATREON_CAMPAIGN_ID` and `PATREON_CREATOR_ACCESS_TOKEN` |
| Webhook 503 `patreon_reconciliation_failed` | Patreon member fetch failed or token revoked | Check the token; Patreon retries the delivery |
| Webhook accepted, roles unchanged | Creator token or campaign mismatch | Rotate the token; check the campaign |

The two `*_not_configured` answers, like OAuth start's, carry
`x-forkmesh-expected-degraded: 1`: a deployment without Patreon is a choice,
not an API failure, so they never reach the error log or the `/status` API
alert. A failed member fetch or membership write is still logged. The core fleet's
`secrets.env` has no `PATREON_*` secrets yet, while Patreon still posts webhooks
to forkmesh.com, so those deliveries get the `*_not_configured` answers.

Git, collaboration, mobile, and self-hosted paths never depend on Patreon;
only Connect, webhook sync, and membership-gated hosted features do.
Authorization always comes from active `role_grants`; the account `membership`
projection is display metadata.

pages.title: Plan trials and self-serve usage meters
pages.description: Part of Operations.
pages.markdown:
# Plan trials and self-serve usage meters

Part of [Operations](README.md).

Users can start a trial, see usage, pay, change plan, and cancel without
support intervention. The pricing contract is the
[business model](../business-model.md); the rollout runbook is
[business-model rollout](business-model-rollout.md).

## Endpoints

- `GET /api/plans/usage`: per-account usage meters (published repositories,
  owned organizations, SSH keys, stored notifications) against the operational
  caps their routes already enforce. Limits are plan-independent; a numeric plan
  allowance may be added only once it is published in `business-model.json`
  with metering tests.
- `GET /api/plans/trial`: `eligible`, `used`, `active`, `endsAt`. One trial per
  account, never while a paid membership is active.
- `POST /api/plans/trial`: starts the single 14-day Supporter trial. One batch
  writes the `plan_trials` register row (the primary key arbitrates races) and a
  `role_grants` upsert under `scope_type='promotion'`.

The dashboard's **Plan usage** card on `/dashboard/settings/account` renders
the meters and the trial button. Membership payment is described in
[Patreon](patreon.md).

## Grant scope

Membership sync revokes only platform-scope grants, so a trial in the
`promotion` scope expires by its own `expires_at`: a billing-provider outage
cannot revoke, extend, or resurrect it. The upsert only lengthens an unrevoked
expiry, so replays are safe. Trial expiry withholds member perks only; portable
identity, public read/clone, and protocol access are never affected.

## Register and metrics

`plan_trials` is the trial register that the `trialsCompleted` and
trial-to-paid metrics in `docs/outcome-metrics.json` reconcile to:

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM plan_trials WHERE ends_at > :start AND ends_at <= :end;
```

Account deletion purges the row; rename moves it with the account.

## Failure and rollback

- A failed trial batch writes nothing; the API returns `trial_already_used` or
  `already_subscribed`.
- The usage endpoint reads only local state; provider outages cannot affect it.
- The down migration drops only the register; live grants lapse on their own.

Managed services stay unavailable for purchase
(`launchGates.managedCheckoutEnabled: false`); managed plans must reuse this
register before checkout can open.

pages.title: Polling inventory and elimination plan
pages.description: Part of Operations.
pages.markdown:
# Polling inventory and elimination plan

Part of [Operations](README.md).

Goal: no ForkMesh client polls the relay for data. Every "did anything change?"
question becomes a payload-free push over a WebSocket, answered by the one
signed HTTPS read the client would have made anyway. The transport is the
per-owner `ForkMeshNodes` object behind `GET /api/nodes/events` (desktops,
headless nodes and, via tickets, browsers) plus the chat, world, office and note
room sockets. These objects run on the core nodes
([architecture](../architecture.md)); the mobile wake-up path is
[mobile push notifications](mobile-push-notifications.md).

## Rules

- **Read on a reason, never on a display timer.** A client reads when a page
  opens, when the reader presses Refresh, when the app or window comes back, or
  when a socket frame says something changed.
- **No fallback polls.** A safety-net poll silently becomes the load. The socket
  owns liveness: reconnect is unconditional with bounded backoff, and every
  (re)connect fires one catch-up read.
- **Heartbeats are not polls.** Liveness proofs (presence, endpoint lease) keep
  their cadence but ride an already-open socket; HTTPS is only the recovery path.
- **The socket is transport, never authority.** A frame carries the same signed
  proof as the HTTPS route and is handed to the same handler.
- **Count requests per event, not timers per minute.** One request per row or
  several callers reading the same resource is a poll in disguise; coalesce and
  revalidate with ETags.
- **Server phases read one indexed row to learn nothing changed**, never the
  table itself (for example the `catalog_rev` counter before a catalog scan).
- **Clients go direct.** The desktop reads saved hosts' signed `/health` and
  `/v1/public/repositories/...` itself and pulls over the host's SSH remote; the
  relay is the last fallback ([mirroring](../mirroring.md)).
- **Bounded failover.** At most four mirror candidates, tried in turn with
  bounded timeouts; errors become bounded 404/503 responses.
- **Measure before tightening.** Add rate-limit rules only after sampled logs
  name the abusive paths, and exclude Git clients and crawlers.

## Account event channel

`notify_account_event(env, owner, topic)` fans a payload-free frame to the
account's `ForkMeshNodes` object from the writes that move a count: pings
(`pings`), direct messages (`direct-messages`), private channels, issues,
catalog changes and cloud agent runs (`cloud-agents`). Browsers join with a
60-second ticket from `GET /api/accounts/event-ticket` (a WebSocket upgrade
carries no `Authorization` header) through the shared `public/account-events.js`.
The chat header badge advances locally from the room socket
(`noteSeenChatActivity`) and is re-read once on `visibilitychange`/`pagehide`.

## Eliminated

| Former poller | Replacement |
| --- | --- |
| Mirror collaboration intake `GET /api/repo/*/pending` | Node event socket; push leases the changed inbox, catch-up on reconnect |
| Desktop inbox sync and `/pending` badge fetch | Socket-driven sync; badge fetched once and invalidated by push, drain or open |
| Unread counts: `refreshWebAlerts`, `startNotificationPolling`, `refreshDirectMessages`, `markChatActivitySeen` | One read on open, then account event pushes |
| Mirror git sync loop | `commits` push carrying the signed refs digest; 5-minute reconciliation backstop |
| Account heartbeat and endpoint lease over HTTP | Frames on the node socket, HTTPS fallback |
| Session validity, dashboard and World (`validateActiveWorldSession`) | Event-ticket handshake refusal; focus/visibility check behind a 5-minute floor (`WORLD_SESSION_REVALIDATE_MIN_MS`) |
| Signed-out session restore on every page | 401 remembered per tab (`forkmesh.sessionRestoreMiss`) |
| Portable grant re-signing on each session read | Reused while younger than `PORTABLE_SESSION_REISSUE_MS` |
| Desktop status/page probes on a minute tick | Launch, recheck and window activation (`refreshFooterStatusOnActivation`) |
| Desktop user directory (`m_chatDirectoryTimer`), notes, pull requests, agent sessions, host probes | Read on open, Refresh, or a socket frame |
| Mobile agents, actions and inbox timers | Tab open, pull to refresh, push and resume catch-up |
| World admin error badge (`ADMIN_ERROR_POLL_MS`) and Office agent bots (`WORLD_AGENT_BOT_POLL_MS`) | Slowed to 60s and 30s, visible tabs only |
| Catalog republish from several publishers | Single publisher (the Go mirror daemon), fingerprinted records |

## Still polling

- Desktop: admin pending-user verification (5m, admins only), mirror
  registration renewal (5m), agent limits (60s).
- Dashboard: pending badge while a repository shows pending items (10m).
- World: community events, mirror catalogs, action runs, QA/build/status boards,
  imports and deploy status; all visible-tab only.
- Chat pages: the visible-tab `USERS_DIRECTORY_REFRESH_MS` directory tick (a new
  account has no frame to announce itself) and the room presence proof.
- Server: the App minute cron, which runs every due phase on one coordinator
  object (`/api/accounts/admin-cron-report` shows the cost per tick).

## Remaining plan

1. Fold per-topic tallies into event frames so the desktop `/pending` read
   disappears, and move admin, notes and agent-limit reads onto socket topics.
2. Add a read-only per-repository event channel for the website and move the
   dashboard badge and World repository pollers onto it.
3. For each minute-cron phase, trigger the work from the write that made it
   necessary; keep cron only for time-based work such as expiries.

Acceptance for each step: the eliminated endpoint's request group in the API
traffic chart drops to about zero, not merely lower.

pages.title: Pull request rules
pages.description: Part of Operations.
pages.markdown:
# Pull request rules

Part of [Operations](README.md).

Repositories and organizations can set rules every pull request must meet:
tests, documentation, size, commit message format, secrets, protected paths,
and a required AI model. The pull request page lists each rule, whether it
passes, and how to fix it. Signed status checks are a separate gate:
[required checks](required-checks.md). Each rule either **blocks** the merge (no waiver
reaches it) or only **flags** the pull request (`warn`).

| Scope | Where the rules live | Who changes them |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Repository | `.forkmesh/pull-rules.json` on the base branch | Anyone who can push to that branch (or **Settings → Pull request rules**) |
| Organization | Stored by the hosted service, applied to every linked repository | Organization owners and admins |

Both sets apply. A pull request is judged by the rules on its **base** commit,
never its head, so it cannot loosen its own rules.

## The rules file

```json
{
  "schema": "forkmesh-pull-rules-v1",
  "rules": [
    { "id": "tests", "kind": "tests", "branches": ["main"] },
    { "id": "docs", "kind": "docs", "paths": ["api/**"], "enforcement": "warn" },
    { "id": "small", "kind": "size", "maxFiles": 40, "maxLines": 800 },
    { "id": "commits", "kind": "commits", "subjectPattern": "^(feat|fix|docs|chore)(\\(.+\\))?: ", "maxSubjectLength": 72 },
    { "id": "secrets", "kind": "secrets" },
    { "id": "workflows", "kind": "paths", "paths": [".github/workflows/**", "deploy/**"] },
    { "id": "model", "kind": "model", "models": ["claude-opus-5-5"] }
  ]
}
```

Every rule takes `id` (lowercase, digits, dashes, up to 48 characters, unique),
`kind`, and optional `title`, `branches` (up to 16 base-branch patterns; `*`
matches within a segment, `**` across segments; empty means all),
`enforcement` (`block` default, or `warn`), and `suggestion` (fix text).

| Kind | Checks | Fields |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `tests` | A change to `paths` includes a change to `testPaths`. | `paths`, `testPaths` (sensible defaults) |
| `docs` | A change to `paths` includes a change to `docsPaths`. | `paths`, `docsPaths` |
| `size` | At most `maxFiles` files and `maxLines` changed lines. | `maxFiles`, `maxLines` |
| `commits` | Every non-merge subject matches `subjectPattern` and fits `maxSubjectLength`. | RE2 pattern, length |
| `secrets` | No added line looks like a private key or common cloud/API credential, or matches `patterns`. | `patterns`, `paths` |
| `paths` | No changed file matches `paths`. | `paths` |
| `model` | Every commit carries a verified model attestation for one of `models`. | `models` (1–16) |

Patterns without `/` match a file name at any depth; patterns with `/` match
from the root. Regular expressions use RE2. A rules file that does not parse
locks every merge it covers.

## Model attestation

Commit trailers such as `Co-Authored-By` are ignored. The `model` rule accepts
a commit only with a verified `ForkMesh-Attestation` trailer:

1. When a hosted pool runner claims an agent job, the router signs a **model
   grant** naming the runner key, repository, branch, provider, model, and
   lease. Personal runners, mirrors, and desktops never receive one.
2. The runner daemon rewrites each new commit with `ForkMesh-Agent:
   <provider>/<model>` and `ForkMesh-Attestation: <grant>.<signature>`, signed
   with its node key over tree, parents, message, and grant. The sandboxed agent
   process never holds that key.
3. At merge, the host verifies the grant under the trusted router key, the
   commit signature under the granted key, and the model against the rule.

Editing, amending, or rebasing an attested commit breaks the signature. A merge
commit that only brings in the base passes if its tree equals the automatic
merge of its parents. The proof covers which model the runner ran, not the
provider's internals.

## Enforcement points

| Step | Behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| Pull request page | The host evaluates both rule sets on current base and head; a failing blocking rule locks the merge button. |
| Hosted merge request | Organization rules are evaluated on the pinned commits; refusal is `rules_required`. |
| Repository host merge | The Go merge executor evaluates the base's rules file and refuses with `rules_required`. A headless Python mirror cannot verify signatures and refuses every merge into a base with a rules file. |

Rules gate merges made through ForkMesh; a direct push to the base branch is
not stopped, the same limit as [signed required checks](required-checks.md).
Organization rule management needs `organization.pull_rules.manage`
([Organization roles](../security/organization-roles.md)).

## Auditing open pull requests

An audit of open pull requests evaluates each signed record whose status is
`open` against the current `main`:

- whether the exact head still exists on the authoritative remote;
- whether the stored patch applies to the current index, and whether the
  reverse patch applies (the change is already represented);
- for a live head, `git diff --check` and a `git merge-tree` conflict check;
- a conservative content/path scan (credential paths, dynamic code, HTML
  sinks, shell downloads) that marks the change for security review. A trigger
  is not itself a vulnerability finding.

Each record gets one disposition:

| Disposition | When |
|---|---|
| Merge | The head is live, merges cleanly, and focused tests pass. |
| Hold | The head is gone but the patch still applies: recreate a signed branch and review it before any merge. |
| Close | The patch conflicts, is empty, is already in `main`, or is superseded. |

The audit never edits signed pull metadata by hand: merged pulls close through
normal pull synchronization, and other closures go through the authenticated
pull-request workflow.

pages.title: Re-keying the database (DATA_KEY rotation)
pages.description: Part of Operations.
pages.markdown:
# Re-keying the database (`DATA_KEY` rotation)

Part of [Operations](README.md).

`DATA_KEY` encrypts stored rows, keys every blind index, and seeds several
HMAC secrets. Rotating it means decrypting everything under the old key and
re-creating it under the new one, offline, with the apps stopped. The tool is
`tools/next_rekey.py`; its tests are `app/tests/host/test_next_rekey.py`. It
runs only on the operator box, against a local SQLite file, never on a node.
Users keep their passwords: password hashes are salted PBKDF2 inside the
encrypted account record and do not depend on `DATA_KEY`. See
[vault](vault.md), [runbook](runbook.md) and the
[encryption overview](../encryption.md).

## What depends on `DATA_KEY`

| Kind | Examples | Handling |
|---|---|---|
| Stored ciphertext | `encrypt_row` rows (AES-256-GCM, key `SHA-256(DATA_KEY)`), `ad_network_ads.owner_sealed`, chat history envelopes | re-encrypted with fresh nonces |
| Vault rows | `host_secrets` (HKDF of `DATA_KEY`, [vault](vault.md)) | emptied; `next_vault.py sync` re-seals them |
| Stored blind indexes | `blind_index(v) = HMAC-SHA256(SHA-256(DATA_KEY + ":blind-index"), lower(strip(v)))` in `*_bi` columns, token columns, `_bi` JSON keys | recomputed from recovered plaintext, or replaced by one consistent random pseudonym per value |
| Derived on the fly | password-reset and email-verify links, session token digests, admin sessions, signed tickets, push passwords, room chat passphrases | nothing stored; outstanding tokens stop verifying, sessions end |
| Not affected | client-side end-to-end keys, password hashes, router key, mesh and edge secrets, node-local caches | untouched |

Identity indexes (`STRICT_BI`: `users.user_bi`, `nodes.node_bi`,
`orgs.org_bi`, `repositories.key_bi`) must be recomputed; if any value cannot
be recovered the tool aborts unless `--allow-orphans` is given. A strict row
whose data the old key cannot open is pseudonymised and reported.

## What the tool does

`tools/next_rekey.py run --in <backup> --out <file>`:

1. Reads both keys from 0400/0600 files only (or `--old-key-env FILE:NAME`),
   never argv or environment. Refuses to run on a node.
2. Works in a fresh 0700 directory; plaintext never touches disk.
3. Pass 1 decrypts every row in memory, harvests identifiers (with every
   blind-index family prefix in `BI_PREFIXES`) and builds the old-to-new map.
4. Pass 2 writes a fresh SQLite file with the same schema, re-encrypting,
   rewriting indexes, re-sealing chat and emptying the dropped tables.
5. Pass 3 verifies: integrity, every ciphertext opens under the new key and
   none under the old, no old index remains, dropped tables are empty, counts
   match. Only then is the output written (0600).
6. Prints per-table counts and both key ids, never a value.

`verify --in <file>` repeats pass 3. `find-key --key <file> [paths]` names
files containing a key or its derived keys (raw, hex or base64). An
unregistered `*_bi` or ciphertext column is still processed and listed as a
warning (`--strict-registry` aborts instead).

## Runbook

1. Stop the operator timers and the app on every core (rqlite keeps running).
2. `next_backup.py run --execute`, then `restore` the newest backup into the
   re-key directory.
3. `next_rekey.py run` from the old key to the new key; read the summary.
4. Load the output through the rqlite leader (`/db/load`) and compare row
   counts on every voter.
5. Switch the operator `DATA_KEY` file to the new key.
6. `next_vault.py sync --execute` to re-seal the vault.
7. Start the apps and unseal; re-enable timers.
8. Confirm no old-key material remains: `find-key` reports `0 file(s)`,
   `next_vault.py status` shows the new key id on every row, and `verify`
   passes on a fresh backup. Then destroy the old key copies by name.

## Residual risk

- Pseudonymised indexes start fresh on the next lookup (rate counters,
  notification dedupe, unstored bot and webhook tokens must be re-issued).
- An unrecoverable 64-hex value in an unregistered column is left as is; it
  reveals nothing about either key.
- Old ciphertext remains in earlier backups and in rqlite's Raft log until
  compaction; delete those copies by name when no longer needed.

## Table coverage

The test `test_inventory_doc_names_every_registered_table` requires every
table the tool registers to be named here.

The `repo_bi` column in `pull_review_ledger` is re-keyed with the `pull-review-ledger:`
repository prefix so recorded approvals and change requests remain available
after rotation.

`account_store_keys.wrapped` holds each account's store key under `DATA_KEY`
and is re-encrypted; `account_store.data` is sealed with that per-account key,
not `DATA_KEY`, so it is copied unchanged and still opens after rotation
([account data](../app/account-data.md)).

`pull_batch_sent` keys `repo_bi` on the lowercased `owner/repo` and
`target_bi` on `pull-batch-target:` plus the lowercased target fork URL, so a
re-key keeps the record of which commits were already sent to each fork.

`pull_ai_reviews` (AI review queue, [ai review](../app/ai-review.md))
keys `repo_bi` on the lowercased `owner/repo`, which re-keys. `head_bi`
indexes `owner/repo:branch` of a branch-backed pull's head and has no
plaintext to recompute, so it gets a pseudonym: after a re-key a push to that
branch re-queues the pull only after its next review records a fresh index.
`ai_review_budget` holds daily counters and is emptied.

**Blind-index tables (`BI_COLUMNS`):** `about_inbox`, `account_activity_days`, `account_devices`, `account_presence`, `account_sessions`, `account_signup_intents`, `account_ssh_keys`, `account_store`, `account_store_keys`, `ad_network_ads`, `ad_network_reports`, `ad_network_reviews`, `admin_signup_referral_code`, `affiliate_leads`, `affiliates`, `agent_guestbook_rate`, `agent_prompts`, `ai_ask_rate`, `ap_actors`, `ap_comments`, `ap_digest_queues`, `ap_followers`, `ap_mentions`, `ap_objects`, `ap_org_digest_settings`, `ap_outbox`, `ap_repo_settings`, `apns_device_tokens`,
