  show joins `DEFAULT_ON`, so no update silently removes it.
- **Opt-in (`OPT_IN`).** forkmesh.com (an unbranded core) normally runs every
  plugin. An `OPT_IN` plugin changes pages enough to be a choice everywhere:
  off on instances, and on a core only when `FORKMESH_CORE_PLUGINS` (comma
  list in the core's environment) names it.
- **The changelog on an instance.** The page is the static
  `www/public/changelog.html`, which loads `/changelog.js` and reads
  `/changelog.json`, the `changelog/changelog.json` of the running commit
  ([changelog](../engineering/changelog.md)), so it needs nothing from forkmesh.com.
  `build_site_assets.stage_app` copies page and script into `app/dist`
  (`BACKEND_ASSETS`, like `blog.html`) with the JSON beside them;
  `/changelog.json` is served even with the plugin off (public release
  notes). With `WWW_ORIGIN` set to the instance's origin,
  `external_site_delivery` answers `local` and `_serve_site_document` serves
  the copy. forkmesh.com's app origin still 308s `/changelog` to
  forkmesh.com. The brand pass renames the platform word.
- **The Company group.** The sidebar's `sidebarGroupCompany`
  (`app/public/dashboard/partials/sidebar.html`) and the site header menu's
  Company group (`www/public/site-header.js`) carry
  `data-instance-plugin="website"`, so `chrome_css` hides the whole group,
  title included, from first paint while `website` is off.
- **Not only hidden.** The dashboard asks `instancePluginOff(id)`
  (`02-helpers.js`, from the page's `/api/instance`) and leaves the prompt,
  Fediverse thread and watch menu out of its markup; `loadFederatedReplies`
  never calls `fedi-comments` while `fediverse-ui` is off. The SSR issue page
  and About rail ask `repo_ssr_issue.plugins_off()`
  (`instance_features.switched_off()` for the env remembered by
  `remember_instance`), and the issue render cache is keyed by it. Until the
  dashboard has the instance document, `chrome_css` (`PLUGIN_ELEMENTS`)
  hides the same elements, so nothing flashes in.
- **How it applies.** Every instance request passes
  `Default._instance_plugins_load` before the plugin gate. It reads the row at
  most every 30 seconds (`CACHE_MS`) into a process cache that `enabled_ids`
  uses; a failed read keeps the last value. The saving process updates its
  cache at once; `/api/instance` (cached 60 s) and the brand script follow
  within a minute. forkmesh.com never reads the row: every plugin stays on
  there, and the page says so.
- **The most specific prefix wins.** `feature_for` picks the plugin with the
  longest matching prefix, so `/api/world/store` and `/api/world/wallet`
  belong to `rewards` and `/api/world/community-ads` to `ads` even while
  `world` (owner of `/api/world`) is on.

### The World on an instance

The World client lives in `world/public/world`, and forkmesh.com serves it
from a separate `world/dist`. The instance build runs
`app/tools/build_site_assets.py instance-world` after `forkmesh_host build`
and before `apply_instance_brand.py` (`build_app` in the installer). It
builds `world/dist` as for world.forkmesh.com (bundled scene, minified and
versioned modules, three.js r184 vendored under `/world/vendor/`) and copies
it into `app/dist`: all of `world/`, plus World-only files the app lacks (bot
avatars, marketplace World packages, `security/latest.json`). It never
overwrites an app file, drops the World's `_headers` and removes the canonical
link to forkmesh.com. About 10 MB on disk (6 MB source maps); it needs the
esbuild the Office build installs. A plain `build_site_assets.py` run skips
this target.

The World is always bundled; the plugin decides per request. The installer
sets `WORLD_ORIGIN` to the instance's origin, so `external_site_delivery`
answers `local` and `_serve_world_asset` (`app/src/app_runtime.py`) serves
`/world` and `/world/` from `world/index.html` and other `/world/...` paths
from the exact bundled file (`static_routes.world_asset_path`; dot segments
and unknown files 404). Headers:

- `content-type` from the file (`text/javascript` for modules, `image/webp`
  and so on).
- `cache-control`: `public, max-age=31536000, immutable` for `?v=` URLs and
  `/world/vendor/`; `no-store, max-age=0, must-revalidate` for the document
  and unversioned files, so a rebuild never mixes module graphs.
- The World CSP (`WORLD_DOCUMENT_SECURITY_HEADERS`): `script-src 'self'
  'unsafe-inline' https://static.cloudflareinsights.com`, no CDN since
  three.js is local. The Cloudflare origin is the Web Analytics beacon
  Cloudflare injects when the operator proxies the instance through
  Cloudflare; the site-wide CSP allows it too. `connect-src 'self' https:
  wss:` for the API and the `/api/world/ws` presence socket; frames `'self'`
  for the embedded chat; `frame-ancestors 'none'` (the global HTML layer
  sets `X-Frame-Options: DENY`).

With the plugin off, the gate answers 404 for `/world`, `/world/*`,
`/api/world/*` and `/office` first.

Every World API call is page-relative, and `api-client.js` keeps
`location.origin` on any host but forkmesh.com, so presence, chat, the
Office, plots, notes and preferences reach the instance's own app. The
World's server code calls no forkmesh.com address (satellites read
celestrak.org, social boards x.com and reddit.com), so the egress guard
needs no new allowance.

Branding: the brand tool renames the World's title ("Acme Code World") and
adds the brand script. Canvas text (signs such as "FORKMESH OFFICE") is
renamed by `world/public/world/world-brand.js`, which on a branded page
wraps `fillText`, `strokeText` and `measureText` of 2D contexts so measured
and painted text match. It leaves "ForkMesh World" (the portal home),
"ForkMesh Desktop", `forkmesh.com` addresses, `@forkmesh` handles and
lower-case repository names. The logo is `/assets/logo.svg`, replaced by the
instance logo.

Not on an instance: rewards and ledger parts (World store, wallet, central
fund, pending rewards), community ads, the ForkMesh blog board, the
`forkmesh/forkmesh` mirror and agent-bot boards (an instance has no
repository by that name), Discord, and the relay federation towers. They
are hidden in the instance's hexagon (below).

The World asks `/api/instance` once (`instanceInfo()` in `world.js`) and
skips what the instance switched off, so the console stays clean: with
`rewards` off it skips `/api/accounts/central-fund` and
`/api/rewards/pending`; with `ads` off the community placement and
`/api/ads/serve`; on any instance (`branded: true`) the forkmesh.com
directory `/api/start/instances` (the ForkMesh World next door is drawn from
`/api/instance`). `instancePluginOff` and `instanceKeepsDirectory` in
`world-instance-portals.js` decide. `/api/accounts/central-fund` belongs to
`rewards` on the server too, so it answers 404, not 503. The one error left
for a signed-out visitor is the 401 from `/api/accounts/sessions`: the
session cookie is HttpOnly, so asking is the only way to learn there is
none.

The World never changes the page address by itself: it opens repositories,
issues and other sites with `window.open(..., "_blank")` and travels only on
a portal or site-menu click. An embedded browser that loads `_blank` in the
same tab, or a tool driving a shared browser's active tab, can look like the
World navigating away.

### An instance World is its own hexagon

An instance World is one hexagon of its own, placed where the directory put
it, with the ForkMesh World across the road, so visitors do not take it for
a copy of world.forkmesh.com.

**What is drawn.** `territoryFromInstance()` (`world-territory.js`) turns
`/api/instance` into the hexagon's settings whenever `branded` is true. The
World hides every ForkMesh town element (Office tower, beach, coaster,
districts, boards, bots, mirror-node yard, desert plots: the
`TERRITORY_HIDDEN_ELEMENTS` list, passed with the visitor's own choices as
`initialDisabledElements` to the Elements panel's registry) and keeps what
comes from the instance's data: the Members Circle and the repository portal
ring. `scene/instance-territory.js` builds a starter world: ground, a road
around the hexagon, a plaza with a sign carrying the instance name and logo
(`/instance-logo.*`, else `/assets/logo.svg`), benches, lamps and trees.
Fresh visitors arrive on the plaza (`TERRITORY_FRESH_SPAWN`). The Office
stays at `/office`; its tower walls and door zone are off
(`territoryWalkActive()`).

**Style.** `style` is `meadow` (green ground, stone plaza) or `security`
(dark ground, red accents, padlocks and a shield over the sign, terminal
green lettering). `accent` overrides the accent colour; empty takes the
instance theme's dark `primary`, then the style's own (`TERRITORY_STYLES`).

**Buildings that link out.** `objects` lists up to 12 houses
`{type: "house", label, url, position: [x, z], color}`; `position` is from
the plaza centre, within 300 on each axis, and at most 330 from the hexagon
centre (the plaza sits 85 in front of it), the reach the ForkMesh World draws
a neighbour scene to (`NEIGHBOUR_SCENE_REACH`). Clicking a house leaves for
`url` (https only, no credentials) in the same tab after the "Entering …"
notice (`openTerritoryLink`). Nothing opens by walking.

The neighbour scene (`/api/world/neighbour-scene`) is served from the
instance's own `PUBLIC_BASE_URL` and answers 404 without one, so a request's
`Host` never picks the address the server fetches the bug list from. Until an
operator saves World settings the route falls through to the existing
handler, so `WORLD_NEIGHBOUR_SCENE` and the default scene still apply.
Answers are edge-cached (600 s, or 60 s when the bug list could not be
read), so anonymous requests do not repeat the reads and fetch.

**Bug terrarium.** `bugs: {repo, ref, path, title, limit, position}` draws a
glass enclosure with up to 60 crawling bugs. The list is a JSON file in one
of the instance's repositories, read through
`/api/repo/<owner>/<name>/raw?path=...&ref=...`: an array of
`{domain, name, url, favicon, count}` (`count` optional). `favicon` is a
path next to the list (`favicons/<domain>.png`; png, ico, gif, jpg or webp)
drawn on the bug's back, so the browser loads only same-origin files and no
third-party favicon service sees who looks. A path that leaves the
repository, an absolute address or an SVG favicon is dropped
(`territoryFaviconURL`). Clicking a bug shows its domain, name and count with
a link to `url` (https only).

**Settings.** The `instance_settings` row `world`
(`app/src/instance_world.py`, cleaned on save, defaults when missing or
invalid), reported by `/api/instance` as `world`. Admins edit it as JSON in
Platform → World (`save_world`, CSRF-checked, audited as
`admin.console_save_world`).

**The ForkMesh World next door is live.** The hexagon stands on one of the
ForkMesh town's desert petals: the one the hub publishes for it in
`/api/world/mesh`, else slot n's petal n + 1 (`territoryPetal`). ForkMesh's
town, petals, roads, Office tower, coaster, beach and other scenery
(`TERRITORY_NEIGHBOUR_ELEMENTS`) are moved beside the hexagon, walkable and
solid, with no reload at the border ([federation](../world/federation.md)).
Stepping onto ForkMesh's ground moves the walker's presence to ForkMesh's
relay over a visit socket with a visitor token (`name@<this host>` there);
the Office runs against ForkMesh's API (`setOfficeOwner`). Pieces that would
show the instance's data inside ForkMesh's town stay off
(`TERRITORY_HIDDEN_ELEMENTS`) while the walker stands in the instance.

**Stepping into the ForkMesh World.** Crossing the road's midline onto
ForkMesh's ground (`territoryOwnerAt()`) puts the page in the ForkMesh World
without a reload, as world.forkmesh.com enters an instance: the address
stays, and the walker stays signed in here, visiting ForkMesh with a visa.
`enterMeshWorld()` calls `leaveOwnTerritory()`, which moves ForkMesh's
scenery back, hides the hexagon and its clicks, switches on the hidden
ForkMesh pieces the visitor had not switched off, and restores the town's
walk surface. The walker is recentred by the hub's offset, the mesh is laid
out from the hub (`placeWorldMesh`, the instance as the hub's neighbour),
town reads go to ForkMesh through the federation client (`meshRoot`),
residents arrive over the visit socket, and the notice reads
`Entering ForkMesh · world.forkmesh.com`. Stepping back calls
`placeTerritoryNeighbour()` → `enterOwnTerritory()`, restoring the hexagon,
clicks, hidden list and ForkMesh next door. The saved position stays in the
instance's frame, so a reload on ForkMesh's ground switches again.

**What ForkMesh's World draws.** From a distance forkmesh.com draws the
hexagon from `GET /api/world/neighbour-scene`
(`app/src/instance_world_scene.py`: ground, plaza, sign, lamps, houses with
links, the terrarium with up to 32 bugs). A ForkMesh walker who steps onto
it, without a reload, stands in this World as it draws itself: built with
the same code from this instance's `/api/instance`, ForkMesh's town next
door, and Members Circle, portals and town content read from this instance
([World mesh](../world/mesh.md#standing-in-an-instances-hexagon)). They
open a visit socket to this relay with a visa and appear as
`name@world.forkmesh.com`.

**Crossing the road (address arrivals).** The instance installs no
crossings (`crossings` stays empty), so walking never navigates; the
in-place switch above replaces it. `checkTerritoryCrossing()` would navigate
on entering a listed crossing tile (`crossedInto`) to
`<home>?from=<instance domain>&slot=<n>&pos=<x>,<z>` (`home` is the
directory's `portal.home` or `https://world.forkmesh.com/world/`; `pos`
relative to the hexagon centre, rounded to a tenth, within 400). Walking from
world.forkmesh.com into an instance is the world-mesh flowers' job
([World mesh](../world/mesh.md)); the territory turns off the mesh
neighbours (`placeWorldMesh`) so the layouts never overlap. On arrival
`territoryArrival()` validates the parameters (a domain or `forkmesh`, slot
0-11, two short numbers), places the visitor on the matching road edge 14
units in, facing away (`edgeArrival`), and strips them from the address.
Sign-ins do not cross: cookies are per origin, so the URL carries no token
and the visitor sees "Visiting from <origin> as a guest" unless signed in
there. A crossing waits four seconds before it can fire again.

### Platform name

The instance name replaces "ForkMesh" wherever the platform itself is meant,
in three layers so nothing depends on the browser alone:

- **Server.** `instance_features.display_name(env)` is the name (`ForkMesh`
  without `INSTANCE_NAME`); `instance_features.rename(env, text)` /
  `rename_html` swap it in (no-ops on forkmesh.com). They cover the
  repository page's `og:site_name`, `og:title`, `twitter:title` and default
  description, the profile `<title>`, the repository fediverse page, the
  repository card's default line, every email subject and body
  (`_send_email`; the "Powered by ForkMesh" footer is added after the
  rename), hosted-repository limit messages, "unavailable" pages, and
  plain-text Git errors (`_git_error_as_text` gets the env and drops the
  forkmesh.com help link). The founders' day-one feedback email is not sent
  on an instance.
- **The git node account.** The instance's git node (`INSTANCE_FLAGSHIP_NODE`,
  `forkmesh`) authors merge and metadata commits and owns the platform
  mirror. `/api/instance` reports it as `gitNode`; the dashboard shows it as
  the instance name wherever a commit author is shown (latest-commit line,
  history, commit detail, contributors, Insights) via `shownAccountName()`,
  the Actions snapshot does the same for a run's actor, and repository cards
  drop "published from <node>".
- **Build.** `apply_instance_brand.py` renames `<title>`, the
  application-name and `og:site_name` metas, and the platform word in
  `description`, `og:title`, `og:description`, `twitter:title` and
  `twitter:description`. It writes the name beside the header logo
  (`<span data-instance-name-label>`) so it is there at first paint without a
  layout shift; re-branding replaces the label.
- **Switched-off plugins at first paint.** `/instance-theme.css` ends with
  `instance_features.chrome_css`: one rule per switched-off plugin hiding its
  `[data-instance-plugin~=id]` elements and links to its pages in `header`,
  `nav`, `aside` and `footer` (and `world.forkmesh.com` links when World is
  off), with `li:has(...)` wrappers in a separate rule so a browser without
  `:has` keeps the rest. It starts with `--instance-plugins: ready`; seeing
  that, `instance-brand.js` no longer hides every plugin element until
  `/api/instance` answers.
- **Dashboard.** `platformName()` in `02-helpers.js` reads the brand tag's
  `data-instance-name` (default `ForkMesh`); every platform reference in a
  dashboard string goes through it (Insights "<name> traffic", "Could not
  reach <name>", hosting and import notices, webhook and mirror help, the
  command palette, the profile link title, account-search placeholders).
  Static partial text inside `main` on repository and profile pages (which
  `instance-brand.js` leaves alone so READMEs and user text are never
  rewritten) is wrapped in `<span data-platform-name>`, filled by
  `applyPlatformName()` at boot. `instance-brand.js` renames chrome and other
  pages; it skips identifiers (`X-ForkMesh-Ref`, `ForkMesh-Attestation`) and
  "ForkMesh, Inc.", and drops the word before "desktop". Elements marked
  `data-user-content` keep their own words.

A branded instance also names itself in: the `/docs` and `/desktop` pages
(no "ForkMesh desktop app" or "forkmesh.com/desktop"; no Powered by footer
when `poweredBy` is off), the plugin-off page, email unsubscribe pages, JSON
error messages (`message`, `hint`, `detail`, `title`, `reason` of any 4xx/5xx
JSON answer, via `HostRuntime._instance_error_text`), the queued-agent
notice, nodeinfo `nodeName`, the instance ActivityPub actor's name, default
profile and repository actor summaries, the fediverse daily digest, and the
`User-Agent` other servers see (webhooks, fediverse fetches, workflow HTTP
steps and imports, provider mirrors, repository metadata:
`<name-slug>-<kind>/1.0 (+<origin>)`, from
`instance_features.remember`/`user_agent`). The web manifest takes the name
even without a logo. The build-time brand tool renames the platform word in
all page text and shown attributes outside `<script>`/`<style>`. "ForkMesh
desktop app" reads "desktop app" (`desktopBrand()` in the dashboard,
`data-desktop-brand` spans in partials, both brand passes). The start page
that launches instances is the `instance-launcher` plugin, off on an
instance.

Kept on purpose: the software's identity where it is a fact ("a ForkMesh
node", "runs a ForkMesh version", "other ForkMesh instances", "a checkout of
ForkMesh itself", nodeinfo `software.name` `forkmesh` and its repository);
technical names never shown as prose (`.forkmesh/` like `.github/`,
`forkmesh-actions`, `FORKMESH_*` variables, the `forkmesh` MCP server and its
config path, header and trailer names, the `forkmesh-profile=` DNS record,
service and file names); the `<owner>/forkmesh` mirror, its description and
"Mirror of forkmesh.com/forkmesh/forkmesh" label; the upstream installer
command `curl -fsSL https://forkmesh.com/install.sh | bash` on `/desktop` and
in Settings > Nodes; license and credit text, the optional Powered by badge
and email footer; and strings of ForkMesh-only plugins (ads, hackathon,
links, referrals, rewards, Patreon membership, the Market, developer docs,
the instance launcher). `app/tests/test_instance_platform_name.py` fails on
any other platform literal in dashboard JS (`KEPT` is the allow-list) and on
any "forkmesh", in any case, in the shown text of branded static pages
(`PAGE_KEPT` and `GATED_PAGES`).

### What an instance hides

Besides plugin routes and `data-instance-plugin` UI: the profile Tips card
(`rewards`), the profile "Referred users" panel (`referrals`), the profile
footer's "© ForkMesh, Inc." line and the "Open the dashboard from
forkmesh.com" setting (`website`), and the Patreon connection and membership
cards (`patreon`). The dashboard requests the ads slot (`/api/ads/serve`) or
blog feed (`/rss.xml`) only when `instancePluginEnabled()` says the plugin
is on, so a switched-off plugin costs no 404 per page. The Mirrors tab's
availability-proof links to forkmesh.com docs are left out, and the
repository Watch handle is the instance's own repository actor
(`GET .../about` `fediverse.handle`), not `@forkmesh.forkmesh@forkmesh.com`.

## Dashboard on an instance

The dashboard knows it runs on an instance from the
`<script data-instance-brand>` tag `apply_instance_brand.py` writes into
every page (`dashboardOnInstance()` in `02-helpers.js`); forkmesh.com pages
never carry it.

- **Reconnect node.** On forkmesh.com the header shows "Reconnect node" to a
  signed-in account with no linked node, because nothing else drains its web
  writes. On an instance the git node serves every repository, so a web-only
  account is never told to reconnect and the Settings > Nodes "No node is
  linked" callout stays hidden. The header shows "Desktop offline" only when
  the account linked a node of its own and that node's public profile
  (`GET /api/accounts/<node>`, from its heartbeat) says offline; the title
  names the node. Unknown presence stays quiet.
- **Served by.** On forkmesh.com any of several mirrors can answer, so the
  header pill ("served by <node>", "served by mirror", "mirror
  online/offline"), the card's mirror label, the home list's serving status
  and the About rail's "Direct access" list are real routing information. On
  an instance one node serves everything, so they are not rendered (the pill
  gets `hidden`) and the card reads "online"/"offline" instead of "via
  mirror". The Mirrors tab stays as the diagnostic view; the Powered by
  badge stays.
- **Mirror goal.** The rail's "Mirrors" card counts plain git copies kept
  elsewhere (this instance, the original named by
  `.forkmesh/forge-source.json`, and registered copies) against a goal the
  maintainers set, and shows on instances too
  ([mirror goals](../mirror-quota.md#how-it-is-built)).

## Accounts, sign-up and moderation

An admin chooses under People → **Sign-up & moderation**
(`app/src/instance_console.py`, view `accounts-moderation`); the choice is
the `instance_settings` row `accounts` and applies within 30 seconds without
a restart. Defaults: email required, people pick usernames, no review, no
limits. Details, APIs and storage:
[accounts and moderation](../app/accounts-and-moderation.md).

| Setting | Choices |
| --- | --- |
| Sign-up | open with email required; open with email optional (no address stored, a one-time recovery code instead); invite code only (the Controls code, email optional); closed |
| Usernames | people choose; suggest a random name like `quiet-otter-7f3k`; random names only |
| Only signed-in accounts can post | off / on |
| First-post approval | off / on: a new account's posts wait in the organization's Moderation queue until a moderator approves one |
| New-account period, threads and comments per day | 7 days, 0 (no limit), 0 (no limit) |
| Hide the posts of accounts blocked with "hide their posts" | on |

The page also lists instance moderators (they moderate every repository),
server-wide blocked accounts and the moderation log. Organization owners and
admins name their own moderators and block accounts from the organization
settings.

For a public forum: email optional, suggest random names, only signed-in
accounts can post, first-post approval on, 3 threads and 20 comments a day
for the first 7 days. Sign-up still needs the Turnstile keys
([Limits](#limits)).

## Directory

After a successful launch, `instance_directory.publish_new` writes an
`instance_directory` row keyed by domain (name, URL, logo, choices, World
slot), only when no row exists for that domain and the domain is the
launch's own `sslip.io` name or resolves only to the address the launch
connected to. A launch never updates or removes an entry: the launched
server reports its own success, so anyone with an SSH server could otherwise
overwrite or delete any domain's entry. Later changes go through the
instance's signed announcement. An instance installed directly joins from
its admin console (Platform → ForkMesh directory) or with
`"directory": {"listed": true, "world": true}`: it publishes
`/.well-known/forkmesh-instance.json` and sends a signed announcement that
forkmesh.com checks against that document before writing the row, again
every six hours ([instance federation](../app/instance-federation.md)).
The World has 12 instance slots. Cron phase `instance-health` probes
`https://<domain>/readyz`; two misses in a row hide the entry, a day offline
pings the admins once per outage.

The forkmesh.com homepage's "Federated instances" section
(`www/templates/pages/index.html`) reads `/api/start/instances` without
credentials and shows each listed instance's logo, name, address and status:
"Online" when its last `/readyz` check answered, "Checking" before the first
check or after one miss (entries carry `status` and `checkedAt`; two misses
drop an instance from the list). The list starts with a fixed OWASP BLT card
(logo `www/public/assets/owasp-blt-logo.svg`, from the instance's
`/instance-logo.svg`) linking to `https://git.owaspblt.org/BLT`; a directory
entry on `git.owaspblt.org` (the `data-instances-pinned` value) is skipped so
it does not show twice. It ends with a dashed "Add your instance" card to
`/start` (a card, not a button, because the page's green call to action is
sign-up). The section always shows on forkmesh.com and stays hidden on an
instance. Tests: `app/tests/test_homepage_federated_instances.py`. The admin
console's Instances view can hide, show or delete entries (CSRF-protected,
audited); deleting does not touch the instance.

## Commit identities

Commits the git node and instance runner make themselves (pull merges and
their metadata commits, mirror intake, the issue reconciler, agent
workspaces) are authored as the instance name with `noreply@<domain>`: the
installer sets `FORKMESH_COMMIT_NAME` and `FORKMESH_COMMIT_EMAIL` on
`forkmesh-mirror-node.service` and in a
`forkmesh-runner@<owner>.service.d/identity.conf` drop-in, read by
`server/commit_identity.go` (without them: the node name and
`<node>@users.noreply.forkmesh.com`). Pull-rule and sync-status hints name
the platform the same way. Node and runner run the signed release binary, so
this needs a release that contains it. Web edits and hosted pushes are
authored by the signed-in account with `<account>@users.noreply.<host>`, and
Actions commit-back by `<owner>-actions`.

## Mail (`app/src/mail_providers.py`)

`MAIL_PROVIDER` selects `mailtrap`, `sendgrid`, `mailgun` or `none`;
otherwise SMTP or Mailtrap by configuration. `MAIL_SENDER` and
`MAIL_SENDER_NAME` set the sender. Budgets, suppression and the mail log
([mail log](mail-log.md)) apply to every provider.

## Privacy mode

An admin can make the instance keep no visitor records beyond what it needs
to run: Platform → Privacy mode (`instance_settings` key `privacy`), or the
install setting `privacyMode: true` (`INSTANCE_PRIVACY_MODE=1` in `app.env`).
Only the install setting also reaches Caddy, uvicorn, the git node and the
journal; for an existing instance add `"privacyMode": true` to
`/etc/forkmesh-instance/instance.json` and run `install-instance.sh --update`.
[privacy mode](../app/privacy-mode.md) audits what is recorded normally,
what privacy mode stops, and what remains and why.

## Limits

- Public sign-up needs Turnstile keys in `app.env`; it fails closed without
  them.
- Turnstile tokens must name the instance's own host. The installer writes
  `TURNSTILE_HOSTNAMES=<domain>` (an existing value is kept); without it a
  branded instance accepts the host of `APP_ORIGIN`, never forkmesh.com's
  hostnames (which would fail every check with `hostname_mismatch`).
- Without a fingerprint the first host key is trusted (and shown).
- SSH credentials pass through the app once, in memory only.
- The instance app's egress guard refuses forkmesh.com except
  `app.forkmesh.com` (`FORKMESH_EGRESS_PRODUCTION_ALLOW` in the app unit),
  used only by the directory announcement, and the instance's own domain, so
  an instance on a `*.forkmesh.com` name can still register its own endpoint
  (otherwise: "production host … is off limits for Next").
- Server text not listed under "Platform name" (admin-only operational
  alerts, plugin descriptions on the Plugins page, Solana/ledger notices of
  switched-off plugins, the referral preview page) still says ForkMesh.
- The repository card image keeps the ForkMesh mark in its corner.
- Commit identities, the runner name and the Go node's messages change only
  with a signed release that contains them ([Commit identities](#commit-identities)).

## Tests

`app/tests/test_instance_launch.py`, `test_install_instance_script.py`,
`test_install_instance_staged_build.py` (staged build, rollback, source
switch, git node program), `test_start_instance_page.py`,
`test_instance_white_label.py`, `test_instance_platform_name.py`,
`test_git_error_text.py`, `test_instance_theme.py`, `test_instance_pages.py`,
`test_instance_plugins.py`, `test_instance_registry.py`,
`test_instance_legal_pages.py`, `test_server_update.py`,
`test_instance_directory.py`, `test_instance_git_routing.py`,
`test_accounts_moderation.py`, `test_instance_node_reconnect_frontend.py`,
`test_instance_served_by_frontend.py`, `test_repo_canonical_addresses.py`,
`test_single_org_contributors.py`, and
`app/host/tests_unit/test_ssh_helper.py`, `test_instance_bootstrap.py`,
`test_instance_repo.py`, and `app/tests/host/test_instance_repo_e2e.py` (a
served app with a temporary SQLite database: a repository created from the
web and one from the command list the same way on the dashboard).

pages.title: Self-setup node: DNS in, node running, no desktop
pages.description: Part of Releases.
pages.markdown:
# Self-setup node: DNS in, node running, no desktop

Part of [Releases](README.md).

A signed-in user can bring up a mirror node on their own server without the
desktop: one install command (SSH) or one cloud-init script installs the
native `forkmesh-mirror-node` service, links it to their account, waits for
their DNS record, and serves the node over HTTPS through Caddy with a Let's
Encrypt certificate. Whole white-label instances use a different path
([self-hosted instances](../operations/instances.md)); the options for running your own
infrastructure are in [self-hosting](../self-hosting.md), and what
a mirror node does in [mirroring](../mirroring.md).

## Flow

1. **Command.** `POST /api/accounts/link-install` returns a fresh six-digit
   installer link code parked for the signed-in account. The command is:
   `curl -fsSL https://forkmesh.com/install.sh | FORKMESH_PUBLIC_HOSTNAME=<host> [FORKMESH_NODE_NAME=<node>] FORKMESH_LINK_CODE=<code> FORKMESH_OWNER=<user> bash`
   (as cloud-init user data, prefixed with `#!/bin/bash` and
   `export HOME=/root`). A relay on another origin adds `FORKMESH_HOST=<origin>`.
2. **Link code** (`_account_link_install()` in `app/src/entry.py`). The session
   proves the user half. The server mints the code itself and never reuses a
   parked code, so a browser cannot adopt someone else's node. One code per
   account every 10 s (`LINK_INSTALL_COOLDOWN_MS`); codes live 30 minutes
   (`LINK_CODE_TTL_MS`) and are redeemed through the normal finalize path.
3. **Installer** (`www/public/install.sh`). With `FORKMESH_PUBLIC_HOSTNAME`
   set, `provision_direct_https()`:
   - initialises the mirror config, reusing an existing identity;
   - writes the managed Caddyfile (`direct_https_bootstrap.py`), using the DNS
     provider API when a token is set and manual DNS otherwise;
   - registers the link code, then starts the service;
   - with manual DNS, prints the exact record (`<host> A <ip>`) and polls
     public DNS every 15 s for up to `FORKMESH_DNS_WAIT_SECONDS` (default
     3600);
   - reloads Caddy only once DNS resolves, so the first ACME attempt succeeds
     and does not spend the failed-validation allowance;
   - waits for `https://<host>/health` and the public manifest.
   If DNS never resolves, Caddy stays enabled and obtains the certificate
   later; `FORKMESH_REQUIRE_DIRECT_HTTPS=1` makes that a failure instead.

## Tests

- `app/tests/test_users_nodes_claim_link.py`: minting, session requirement,
  throttling, no reuse of parked codes.
- `app/tests/test_installer_headless_checkout.py`: manual-DNS order (register,
  start, wait for DNS, Caddy) and the record-type helper.
- `world/tests/test_world_instance_launcher.py`.

pages.description: Part of Operations.
pages.markdown:
# Signed required checks

Part of [Operations](README.md).

A repository can require status checks before a pull request merges on a
mirror node. Each result is an Ed25519-signed attestation from a runner the
repository trusts, so the gate does not depend on any runner service or
storage location. Forged, stale, replayed, and unauthorized results cannot
satisfy it. The Go mirror node (`forkmesh-mirror-node`) enforces it for web
merges (`merge-pull`, see [mirror node](mirror-node.md#owner-authorized-web-merges));
blocking rules beside it are [pull rules](pull-rules.md).

## Policy

Commit `.forkmesh/required-checks.json` to the base branch:

```json
{
  "schema": "forkmesh-required-checks-v1",
  "branches": ["main"],
  "maxAgeSeconds": 604800,
  "checks": [
    { "name": "CI tests", "signers": ["<runner public key, 43-character base64url>"] }
  ]
}
```

| Field | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| `schema` | Exactly `forkmesh-required-checks-v1`. |
| `branches` | Base branches covered; empty covers every base. |
| `maxAgeSeconds` | 60 to 31,622,400. Older results do not count. |
| `checks` | 1–32 checks with distinct names (1–128 bytes, no control characters). |
| `signers` | 1–16 canonical, prime-order Ed25519 runner keys per check. |

Unknown keys or any validation failure lock merges into covered branches; a
broken file never disables the gate. The policy is read from the **base
commit**, never the pull request's head. A runner prints its key with
`forkmesh-mirror-node --config <path> --public-key`.

## Reporting a result

```sh
printf '%s' '{"schema":"forkmesh-check-v1","owner":"example","repository":"demo","commit":"<head sha>","check":"CI tests","conclusion":"success","runId":"run-1234"}' \
  | forkmesh-mirror-node --config /etc/forkmesh/mirror-node.json --sign-check-attestation
```

The signer adds `issuedAt`, `signer`, and `signature`; callers cannot supply
them. `conclusion` is `success`, `failure`, `cancelled`, or `skipped`; only
`success` satisfies a check. Publish the JSON on the `forkmesh/pulls` ledger
branch as `.forkmesh/pulls/<N>/checks/<name>.json` (name matching
`[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._-]*\.json`; at most 256 files of 8 KiB each).

The signature covers these fields joined by LF, no trailing LF:

```
forkmesh-check-v1
<owner, lowercase>
<repository>
<commit, lowercase hex>
<hex SHA-256 of the check name>
<conclusion>
<runId>
<issuedAt, decimal milliseconds>
```

## Evaluation

For each required check the mirror discards attestations that fail to parse or
verify, name another owner, repository, or head commit, are signed by a key not
listed for that check, are older than `maxAgeSeconds`, or are dated more than
five minutes ahead. The newest remaining `issuedAt` wins; on a tie a
non-success beats a success. The merge proceeds only when every check's winner
is `success`; otherwise the executor records `checks_required` and moves no
refs. The review waiver (`overrideReview`) never waives required checks.

## Limits

- Patch-backed pulls have no published head to attest and cannot merge on the
  web under a covering policy.
- `tools/headless_mirror_refresh.py` has no Ed25519 verifier and refuses every
  merge whose base carries a policy.
- An attestation is bound to the owner name in the merge request.

Tests: `server/checks_test.go`, `server/merge_test.go`, and
`app/tests/test_pull_merge_executor.py`.

pages.description: Part of Operations.
pages.markdown:
# Stock Git conformance operations

Part of [Operations](README.md).

The public [compatibility matrix](../git-compatibility.md) is generated from
the claims in `conformance/git/v1/matrix.json` and the retained run reports in
`conformance/git/v1/evidence/` (indexed by `conformance/git/v1/results.json`).
Never hand-edit the generated Markdown, HTML, JSON, results index, or evidence;
change the source or a probe, then run:

```sh
python3 tools/git_conformance.py validate
python3 tools/git_conformance.py render
python3 tools/git_conformance.py render --check
```

## Published status

A cell marked `supported`, `local`, or `conditional` keeps that status only
when a retained run covering it passed within `suite.freshnessDays` (30 days).
Otherwise it is published as `failing` (a covering run failed), `stale` (the
newest pass is too old), or `unverified` (no covering run). Only smart-HTTP
runs count for the relay and mirror-failover columns. The hosted page re-checks
run dates against the reader's clock, and
`/docs/git-compatibility/evidence/<run>.json` holds each raw report.

## Attesting evidence

```sh
python3 tools/git_conformance.py attest \
  artifacts/git-conformance-v0.json artifacts/git-conformance-v2.json
```

`attest` validates reports (suite version, operation inventory, summary
consistency, privacy flags, and a scan for unredacted paths, file URLs, or
loopback addresses), stores them by content address, and regenerates outputs.
The newest report per client configuration replaces older ones. Bumping
`suite.version` invalidates existing evidence. `attest --drop <run-id>` retires
a configuration.

## Release gate

```sh
python3 tools/git_conformance.py gate
python3 tools/git_conformance.py gate --operations-only \
  --report artifacts/git-conformance-v2.json
```

`gate` exits non-zero and names every failing, stale, or unverified claim.
`--report` also counts a fresh unattested run; `--operations-only` skips
hand-recorded client rows. The `release` quality-gate profile runs the full
gate.

## Evidence chain

The conformance workflow runs Git protocol v0 and v2 on Linux, macOS, and
Windows. Protocol v2 proves partial clone and lazy fetch; protocol v0 proves the
safe rejection without relaxing hidden-object policy. Each matrix cell maps to a
stable probe ID, and each report records the repository commit, exact
Git/Python/OS versions, per-operation status and time, generalized
origin/proxy counts, the signed fixture commit, and a digest of the final refs.

The offline smart-HTTP fixture exercises direct read/write, a masked relay
proxy, and failover from a failed origin to a matching mirror. Gateway tests
separately prove that HTTPS receive-pack returns an actionable 501, SSH
receive-pack enforces authorization and quotas, upload-pack serves shallow and
partial clones while rejecting hidden-object wants, object bytes survive every
read path, and damaged refs or packs fail strict fsck.

With `--transport auto` the suite selects HTTP only after a completed loopback
round trip (IPv4, then IPv6) and otherwise falls back to a clearly labelled
file-transport run that does not count as relay evidence. The public workflow
requires `--transport http`. CI runs each suite in a private network namespace
(`unshare -rn`) when possible so host firewalls cannot drop loopback traffic.

## Promoting a client row

Run the suite with the exact Git executable a client ships, for both protocol
versions, then attest the reports:

```sh
python3 tools/git_conformance.py run \
  --git /path/to/client/bundled/git \
  --client-label "Client name and version" \
  --transport http --protocol-version 2 \
  --output artifacts/git-conformance-client-v2.json
```

A passing bundled-Git probe proves protocol compatibility only; a desktop UI
stays pending until its own authentication, clone, push, and recovery flows are
exercised.

## Failure and recovery

Probes run entirely in temporary directories and never touch production
repositories. Keep a failed report and log, reproduce with the same Git and
protocol version, and attest the failure before a release so the gate blocks
it; a later passing run supersedes it. For a failed production fetch, retry
rather than delete the clone, run `git fsck --full --strict` after corruption,
and create and verify a bundle before force-updating a ref.

## Telemetry and privacy

Reports are retained for 30 days and contain no repository contents, paths,
URLs, credentials, SSH keys, client addresses, or raw Git stderr: only
generalized request and timing counts.

## Rollout and rollback

Partial-clone filtering and protocol-v2 forwarding are gateway transport
policies requiring no repository migration. Deploy them through the normal
packages, validate the scoped `AcceptEnv GIT_PROTOCOL` SSH drop-in with
`sshd -t`, then run the conformance workflow. Rollback removes
`uploadpack.allowFilter=true`, protocol-v2 forwarding, and the SSH hint;
existing clones are unaffected, and the matrix must change with the contract.

pages.description: Part of Operations.
pages.markdown:
# The served stack

Part of [Operations](README.md).

app.forkmesh.com and world.forkmesh.com run on a small self-hosted fleet:
three equal core nodes that hold data and secrets, reached directly by DNS round
robin, and a runner tier that runs untrusted work. `deploy/fleet.toml`
describes the fleet. This page is the design in detail; the public summary is
[architecture](../architecture.md), the commands are in the
[runbook](runbook.md) and the code map is [fleet tooling](fleet-tooling.md).

## Who serves what

| Host / page family | Served by |
|---|---|
| `forkmesh.com`, `www.forkmesh.com` (homepage, blog, docs, static pages) | the `forkmesh-www` Cloudflare Worker (`www/worker.js`, `www/wrangler.production.toml`); it proxies app paths to `app.forkmesh.com` with a signed edge header. `www/public/_redirects` is read only by that Worker. |
| `app.forkmesh.com` (dashboard, API, WebSockets, Git over HTTPS) | Caddy on each core: precompressed static assets from the release's `app/dist`, dynamic routes to the Python app on `127.0.0.1:8080` |
| `world.forkmesh.com` | Caddy on each core: `world/public` plus the app for the API and sockets |
| `nN.next.forkmesh.com` | one core's Git gateway (the Go daemon) and health |
| DNS | Cloudflare DNS only; unproxied round-robin A records (TTL 60) for the app and world names |

## Architecture

```
          browsers, desktops, phones, mirrors
                       │
     DNS round robin, one A/AAAA per healthy core, TTL 60
                       ▼
  ┌──────── core cell: 3 small VMs (trusted: data + secrets) ────────┐
  │ Caddy · Python app on CPython · rqlite (Raft) · Go daemon/gateway │
  │ WireGuard mesh between cores. No agents, no untrusted code.       │
  └──────────────▲────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                 │ outbound only: claim lease → clone → run → push → report
  ┌──────── runner tier (untrusted, stateless, no core secrets) ──────┐
  │ an always-on runner, burst runners from a snapshot, user runners  │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

- **Trust split.** Agent runs execute arbitrary code, so they never run on a
  node holding `DATA_KEY`, password hashes or the database. A runner gets a
  short-lived, router-signed push capability for exactly
  `refs/heads/agent/<session>` of one repository ([runners](runners.md)).
- **Host shim.** The app's Python code targets a Workers-style runtime (`js`,
  `ffi`, `env` bindings); `app/host/forkmesh_host/` provides it on CPython
  (`js.py`, `ffi.py`, `workers.py`, `env.py`, `asgi.py` under uvicorn).
  `tools/js_surface_inventory.py` fails when the app uses an attribute the shim
  does not implement. Its test requires a binding only for `DB`, `ASSETS`,
  `REPOSITORY_METADATA` and names the app calls through
  (`env.X.idFromName()`); an `env.FORKMESH_*` name read as a plain value (such
  as `FORKMESH_CALLS_NODES`) is an optional var. Any name `ctx` in app, World
  or marketplace worker code is read as the execution context, so a local of
  that name fails the test and blocks the node deploy: call it `context`.
- **Database.** rqlite. `d1_rqlite.py` gives it the D1 shape; plain reads are
  served by the node's own copy (`level=none` over HTTP, the fleet's
  `read_mode = "http"`, or read-only `sqlite3` on the local file with
  `read_mode = "local"`), reads after a write use `weak`, primary-first reads
  use `linearizable`. `tools/rqlite_migrate.py` applies migrations.
- **Room objects.** `durable.py` implements the Durable Object API on the
  cores: rendezvous
  hash of `ns:name` over live members, storage in rqlite, alarms in
  `do_alarms` delivered exactly once, HMAC-authenticated forwarding over
  WireGuard. A node without quorum reports not-ready and serves read-only
  (below).
- **No leader.** Membership, cron, alarms, DNS health votes and certificates
  are leaderless: each node writes only its own membership row, the cron
  coordinator rotates across live nodes every minute, and
  `deploy/core/certsync.py` runs the same on every core.
- **Secrets.** Nodes start sealed and hold `DATA_KEY` only in memory; the
  operator unseals them ([vault](vault.md)). Other secrets come from
  systemd credentials, never from rqlite or backups.
- **Integrations start off.** A service credential is added to
  `optional_secrets` only on purpose. ForkMesh Next starts with Solana rewards
  off mainnet; production enables them only through `[production.vars]`.
- **Backups.** The operator box pulls an rqlite backup nightly over SSH,
  verifies it and keeps 7 daily and 4 weekly copies (`tools/next_backup.py`,
  [runbook](runbook.md#routine-operations)).

## Read-only mode

Three cores are three rqlite voters, and we chose not to add servers
(2026-10-28). With two cores down the survivor has no rqlite leader, so
nothing can be written. It keeps serving everything that only reads, from
its own full copy of the database, and refuses writes with one clear answer.
When a leader returns it goes back to normal by itself.

**When.** `cluster.Membership.read_only`: the node has gone 10 s
(`QUORUM_LOSS_SECONDS`) without seeing an rqlite leader, or 15 s without a
successful heartbeat write, and is not sealed, quarantined or leaving. The
first 10 s after the process starts never count, so a restart during a
normal deploy does not refuse writes while the first heartbeat is in
flight. `HostRuntime.read_only` exposes it; the same 1 s loop that checks it
logs `read-only mode ON` / `read-only mode OFF`.

**Database (`d1_rqlite.py`, `read_only.py`).** While read-only:

- Reads stay local. Every read uses `level=none` (or the local `sqlite3`
  file) without the `freshness` bound, including primary-first sessions and
  reads after a write. An empty result is not re-asked at `weak`, because
  that leader read would fail the whole request.
- A write is never sent to rqlite, so it can neither hang on a missing leader
  nor wait out the 15 s timeout. What happens depends on the request:
  - `GET`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS` and `POST .../git-upload-pack` only read, so
    their side writes (session stamps, counters, `clone_sticky`, download
    counts, rate-limit rows) are skipped: the statement returns no rows and
    `changes = 0`, and the page renders.
  - Every other request, plus the GET links whose point is a write
    (`WRITING_GET_PATHS`: e-mail verification, marketing unsubscribe, the
    Discord and Patreon OAuth callbacks), gets `ReadOnlyError`. Its text is a
    D1 overload error, so the app's existing `database_unavailable` path
    handles it with no app change and no Sentry event.
  - Writes outside a request (cron, queue consumers, background loops) also
    raise.
- A statement that starts like a read but contains a write keyword (a
  `SELECT` matching `'delete'`, a `WITH ... INSERT`) is tried as a read: the
  local `sqlite3` connection is `query_only`, and over HTTP rqlite answers a
  real write with "leader not found". Either way a write is refused and a read
  is served.
- `d1_sqlite.py` follows the same rules (it switches `PRAGMA query_only` on),
  which is how the host tests drive the real app in read-only mode.

**Request layer (`asgi.py`).** While read-only, a response is replaced with
the read-only answer when:

- it is a 5xx; or
- a write was refused; or
- the request is a write request and the app answered 4xx (the signup form,
  for example, answers 403 `signup_page_required` because its GET could not
  store the signup intent).

The answer is HTTP 503 with `Retry-After: 30`, `x-forkmesh-read-only: 1` and
`x-forkmesh-expected-degraded: 1`. The body is
`{"error": MESSAGE, "message": MESSAGE, "code": "read_only", "readOnly": true}`,
or a short HTML page when the client accepts `text/html`. The desktop, the
phones and the dashboard all show `error` or `message`, so they show "ForkMesh
is read-only while servers recover…". Every response the app itself answers
on a read-only node carries `x-forkmesh-read-only: 1`. A WebSocket upgrade
that fails with a 5xx gets the same answer as an HTTP denial.

**Off while read-only.** Durable Objects, which need quorum for storage and
placement, are off; the fetch-only ingress objects run on every node and keep
working. Off with them: alarms, the cron loop (skipped like a sealed node),
queue consumers (paused; messages wait in memory and resume when writes come
back), DNS reconciler votes and peer unseal ([vault](vault.md#peer-unseal)).

**Readiness and DNS.**

- `/readyz` still answers 503 on a read-only node, so deploy gates,
  `next_fleet.roll_healthy`, the release host and add-core see it as degraded.
  Its body adds `"readOnly": true` and the reason `read_only`. A node whose
  local rqlite is unreachable, or that is sealed or quarantined, is not
  flagged: it cannot serve reads.
- `dns_rules.probe_state` reads that flag and reports `ready`, `read_only` or
  `down`. `tools/next_dns.py health-loop` counts a read-only core as healthy
  only while no core is ready (`dns_rules.serving`):
  - In a partition, the isolated read-only core leaves DNS and the two ready
    ones keep the writes.
  - With two cores down, the survivor stays in, or comes back, and the dead
    ones leave.
  - Undrain still needs a fully ready core.
- Caddy on each core proxies only to its own app, so it needs no change. The
  in-node DNS reconciler needs quorum to vote and does nothing while
  read-only.

**What works read-only.** These need no leader:

- the website, static pages and assets;
- dashboard and API reads with an existing session (the session-stamp write
  is skipped);
- public profiles, organizations, notes and chat history reads;
- repository browsing through the fast path and the app;
- release downloads;
- `git clone` and `git fetch`:
  - over `nN.<domain>`, the gateway touches no rqlite at all;
  - over the app name, the app skips its `clone_sticky` and counter writes.

**What does not.** These need a leader and answer the read-only message:

- sign-up, login and logout (a session is a row), password reset, and e-mail
  verification links;
- every create, edit and delete;
- pushes;
- chat sends;
- anything behind a Durable Object: World rooms, live sockets, the status
  WebSocket, cron jobs and alarms.

**Risks.**

- Data is as fresh as the survivor's copy when the leader was lost.
- A GET handler whose write matters later fails on that later step. The
  signup intent is one; the 4xx rule above turns its POST into the read-only
  answer.
- A new GET route that must write has to be added to `WRITING_GET_PATHS`,
  or its write is silently skipped while read-only.

**Tests.**

- `app/tests/host/test_host_read_only.py`: policy, bindings, membership
  transitions, readiness flag, DNS rules.
- `app/tests/host/test_host_read_only_e2e.py`: the real app with the
  `FORKMESH_HOST_DEBUG` toggle `/_host/read-only?on=1|0|auto`.
- `app/host/tests_rqlite/test_read_only_survivor.py`: a real 3-node rqlite
  cluster with two nodes stopped, then restarted.
- `deploy/tests/test_next_dns.py`: the health loop.

## Core node

- systemd units for rqlite, the app, Caddy and the Go daemon (role `core`),
  with memory limits; zram plus swap and `earlyoom`.
- Caddy issues certificates leaderlessly; ACME HTTP-01 challenges are
  forwarded across cores so any A record works.
- The firewall allows 22, 80, 443 and the WireGuard port.

## Runner tier

The Go daemon with role `runner` runs no gateway and keeps no repositories.
Each job runs in its own systemd scope with memory and CPU limits and a
private tmp dir, and its workdir is wiped afterwards. Burst runners
(`server/runnerpool.go`) are created from a snapshot when the queue backs up
and destroyed when idle, under a count and monthly spend cap
([autoscaling](autoscaling.md)).

## Performance rules

- Python never serves static bytes.
- CPU-heavy work (PBKDF2, large JSON, compression, image rendering, RSA) runs
  in a thread, never on the event loop.
- Warm up before `/readyz`; cache public snapshots in memory and invalidate on
  republish.
- A route that cannot meet its budget in Python moves into the Go daemon.

## Fleet tooling

The `tools/next_*.py` tools and the renderer are mapped in
[fleet tooling](fleet-tooling.md). Instances are labelled `fmnext-*`, tagged
`forkmesh-next`, and never added to the desktop's saved hosts. Installer and
fleet tests sandbox `HOME` and the `XDG_*` folders and drop
`FORKMESH_HOME` / `FORKMESH_PROJECTS_DIR` (AGENTS.md).

pages.markdown:
# Android

The Android app has the iPhone app's features and its look, the same Liquid
Glass theme, and talks to the same endpoints, so the server cannot tell the
two apart. Since 2026-10-28 every phone change ships in both apps in the same
pull request. Back to the [phone apps](README.md).

## Install

1. On the phone, open [forkmesh.com/#downloads](https://forkmesh.com/#downloads)
   and download `forkmesh-android-universal.apk`.
2. Open the file. Android asks once to allow installs from your browser;
   allow it, then **Install**.
3. Open ForkMesh and [sign in](getting-started.md#2-sign-in).

Requires Android 8.0 or later. The APK is signed with ForkMesh's release key;
Android refuses an update signed with any other key.

## Updates

The app is not in a store, so it tells you itself when a newer version is out
and opens the download page (your instance's Android download link, or
`https://forkmesh.com/mobile`). Install the new APK over the old one: the app
id and signing key stay the same, so your sign-in, keys and local repositories
are kept.

## Notifications

Android has no push service in ForkMesh. Instead the app keeps one
**background connection** per signed-in project, shown as a quiet ongoing
notification:

```text
   ForkMesh cores ◄──── one socket per project ──── Android app
                         reconnects with backoff      foreground service,
                         paused by Doze and when      restarted on boot and
                         the network drops            after an update
```

- It carries pings, direct messages and calls. Channel messages do not raise a
  notification on Android.
- With notifications off it still listens for calls only ("Listening for
  calls").
- It holds no wakelock; Doze and network loss pause it, and a 15-minute
  background job revives it if Android stopped it.
- A force-stopped app does not ring until you open it again.

## ↔️ Differences kept on purpose

| On Android | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| Background connection instead of push | The app uses no Google push service; see [Notifications](#notifications) |
| Approving from a notification opens the app | The screen lock needs an on-screen dialog to fall back to |
| Dictation is `/dictate` in the prompt composer, with no mic button | A quiet stop after words sends the prompt |
| Chat and ping times use a 12-hour clock | Agent prompts keep 24-hour stamps |
| Calls run in the app's call page | One-to-one and group calls, with the voice changer, call backgrounds and face changer; Android rings through its own call notification |
| No dictation during a call | A second microphone capture could take the microphone from the call |

iPhone features that need an Apple-only API and so are not on Android: Eye
Control and Spider Room (ARKit), the on-device Gemma model (MLX), CallKit's
system call screen, 3D face tracking in the face changer (TrueDepth), the
Cloud Dragon mascot and the App Store update gate. The full list, with
reasons, is in [docs/native/ANDROID.md](../native/ANDROID.md#11-differences-kept-on-purpose).

## Keys and AutoFill

Your device key and the Password Vault's device keys live in the Android
Keystore. The vault can be chosen as Android's **AutoFill service** in system
settings. More in [privacy and security](privacy-and-security.md).

Related: [getting started](getting-started.md) ·
[Android internals](../native/ANDROID.md) · [phone apps](README.md)

pages.description: Part of Phone apps.
pages.markdown:
# Apple Health on iPhone

Part of [Phone apps](README.md).

The ForkMesh iPhone app works with Apple Health. It uses Apple's HealthKit
framework to connect seven optional tools to the Health app: Pedometer, Water
Intake, Calorie Counter, Sleep, Sugar Break, Stretch Break and Food Guide. This
page lists
what each tool reads and writes, what reaches your ForkMesh account, and how
to turn it off.

Nothing is read or written until you turn on a tool's Apple Health switch and
allow it in the iOS permission sheet. The rest of ForkMesh does not use
HealthKit.

## Where to find it in the app

- **In each tool.** The Apple Health switch sits in a card marked **Works with
  Apple Health**, with the data that tool reads and writes listed under it and
  a **How ForkMesh uses Apple Health** button.
- **In Settings.** **Settings > Legal > Apple Health** opens the same guide for
  all seven tools, whether or not you have installed them.

The tools are installed from Market in the app. A tool you have not installed
never asks for Apple Health access.

## What each tool reads and writes

| Tool | Reads from Apple Health | Writes to Apple Health | Saved to your ForkMesh account |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Pedometer | Steps, walking and running distance, flights climbed, active energy | Heart rate, only when you tap out your pulse and choose **Save to Apple Health** | One total per day, so your steps show on web and desktop. Heart rate is never sent. |
| Water Intake | Water that other apps logged | Each drink you log, as Water | Water from other apps is added to your drinks log |
| Calorie Counter | The meals ForkMesh wrote, so edits and deletions stay in step | Dietary energy, protein, carbohydrates and fat for the meals you log | Nothing from Apple Health |
| Sleep | Sleep that an Apple Watch or another app recorded | Nights your phone detected, only with **Save detected sleep to Apple Health** on | Each night's sleep |
| Sugar Break | Dietary sugar that other apps logged | Nothing | Nothing. Apple Health sugar never leaves the phone. |
| Stretch Break | Minutes of Flexibility and Mind and Body workouts | Each guided session you finish, as a workout | Nothing from Apple Health |
| Food Guide | The last 14 days of dietary energy, protein, fiber, sugar, saturated fat, sodium, iron, calcium, potassium, magnesium, folate and vitamins C, D and B12 that other apps logged | Nothing | Nothing. The nutrition history and the meal ideas worked out from it stay on the phone. |

Pedometer and Sleep also use the iPhone's motion sensor, which iOS asks about
separately under Motion & Fitness.

## What ForkMesh does with it

- The readings saved to your account are there so a tool shows the same
  numbers on web, desktop and mobile. They are encrypted with a key created
  for your account alone.
- ForkMesh does not use Apple Health data for advertising or marketing, does
  not sell it, and does not share it with data brokers or any other third
  party.
- ForkMesh does not store Apple Health data in iCloud.
- ForkMesh never deletes or changes health data that another app wrote.

The [privacy policy](https://forkmesh.com/privacy#apple-health) says the same.

## Turning it off

- Turn off the Apple Health switch in the tool. Reading and writing stop at
  once. What was already written to Apple Health stays there.
- Or open the iPhone **Settings** app, then **Health > Data Access & Devices >
  ForkMesh**, and turn off any type of data.
- Uninstalling a tool deletes its data from your ForkMesh account on every
  device. Deleting your account does the same for every tool. Apple Health
  keeps its own copy, which you manage in the Health app.

pages.description: Follow, steer and hear your coding agents from your wrist. The watch app is new and still growing. Back to the phone apps.
pages.markdown:
# Apple Watch

Follow, steer and hear your coding agents from your wrist. The watch app is
new and still growing. Back to the [phone apps](README.md).

## How it works

The watch has no ForkMesh session of its own. Your iPhone holds the session
and the keys in its device-only Keychain, unseals your agents' transcripts and
sends the watch a compact summary; the watch's commands go back through the
phone.

```text
   desktop · cloud runners           iPhone                     Apple Watch
   agents run here          ───►     unseals transcripts  ───►  agent list,
                                     with its own key           live view, sound
                            ◄───     sends your command   ◄───  Stop, Continue,
                                                                prompt, Retry
```

So the watch needs the iPhone app installed, signed in and nearby. It runs
watchOS 10 or later.

## What it does

| | Feature | What you get |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 📋 | Agent list | Every active and recent agent with its model, repository, status, turns and tokens; running agents first |
| 👀 | Live view | Watch the agent work, with its last reply on screen |
| ⏯️ | Controls | **Stop**, **Continue** and **Retry**; send a prompt by dictation or Scribble |
| 🔍 | Review changes | Read an agent's diff file by file and mark files as reviewed |
| 🎧 | Listen | Each agent plays as sound and haptics, so you can tell what it is doing without looking; the optional Announcer says short lines such as "run done" or "is waiting for you" |
| 🗣️ | Siri | "Start a new ForkMesh agent": name a repository, or it uses the repository and model you last used on the phone |
| ⌚ | Complications and Smart Stack | The current run at a glance |
| 🔔 | Notifications | The phone's ForkMesh notifications appear on the watch |

There is no Pause: an agent is stopped and continued.

## Next

A standalone mode that signs in on the watch itself, so it works without the
phone nearby. How the watch app is built:
[phone app parity, watchOS](../native/PARITY.md#4-watchos-app-control-agents-see-and-hear-them).

Related: [Siri](siri.md) · [agent access](mobile-agent-access.md) ·
[phone apps](README.md)

pages.title: Editing files and opening pull requests from the phone
pages.description: Part of Phone apps.
pages.markdown:
# Editing files and opening pull requests from the phone

Part of [Phone apps](README.md).

From the repository browser in the iOS or Android app, a person can edit one
text file and propose it as a pull request with no clone, no fork and no push
access. Related: [mobile node contract](mobile-node-contract.md),
[signatures](../encryption.md).

## Why no fork is needed

A ForkMesh pull request is a signed patch, not a pointer to a branch. The
relay verifies only the author's Ed25519 signature over title, base, head,
patch and commits, plus size, inbox depth and per-author quota. The receiving
node merges from the carried patch (`git apply --index --3way`, or `git am
--3way` when commits are included) and never resolves the head branch. So a
contributor needs nowhere to push. A fork on ForkMesh is a durable copy you
keep, not a gate in front of an edit button.

## Every edit opens a pull request

Even with write access, the phone opens a pull request, so nothing merges
unreviewed from a phone. Round one is one file per pull request; multi-file
work goes through a clone.

## Building a patch without a clone

A Git blob id is `sha1("blob " + <byte length> + "\0" + <bytes>)`, so the phone
can compute both sides of an `index` line:

1. Fetch the file's raw bytes for the ref being browsed.
2. `oldId` from those bytes, `newId` from the edited text as UTF-8.
3. Emit one `diff --git` section with `index <oldId>..<newId>` and Myers hunks.
4. Sign and submit.

Rules that keep the patch valid:

- Diff the raw bytes, never a decoded string, so `oldId` is the real blob id
  for the three-way fallback.
- If the server supplies a blob id and it disagrees with the computed one,
  refuse and offer the clone path.
- Omit the mode on the `index` line; the tree API does not expose modes, and
  guessing `100644` would strip an executable bit.
- Refuse bytes that are not valid UTF-8 rather than decoding them lossily,
  because the decoded text becomes the new file content.

## Submission

```json
{"pull": {"title": "…", "base": "main", "head": "<account>:mobile-edit/<label>",
  "patch": "diff --git …", "commits": "", "description": "…",
  "author": "<node pubkey>", "authorName": "<account>", "ts": 0, "sig": "…"}}
```

`base` is the branch being browsed. `head` is informational. `commits` is
empty because there are no local commits. The signature covers
`"\x00".join([title, base, head, patch, commits])` under
`forkmesh-pull-event-v1`. The relay assigns the number outside the signed
bytes.

## Limits

| Condition | Behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| Binary or non-UTF-8 content | Refused, clone path offered |
| File over 512 KB | Refused, clone path offered |
| Served blob id disagrees | Refused, clone path offered |
| Inbox full (`429 inbox_full`) or author quota (`429 author_quota`) | Shown as "not accepting pull requests right now" |
| Upstream moved while editing | Submitted; `--3way` absorbs drift, real conflicts surface at merge |

Because a single-file edit carries no commit mbox, the owner merges it under
their own name and the relay records the contributor.

## Forks from the phone

A phone cannot host, but it can publish. A fork is a clone published as
`<me>/<name>` with `forkedFrom` set in the signed catalog record. The field is
omitted, not empty, when a repository is not a fork, so older catalog
signatures stay valid.

Not built yet: a push-access probe (the signed `info/refs?service=git-receive-pack`
request answers it: `200` yes, `401` no, `503 push_unavailable` unknown),
multi-file edits, file creation and deletion, and a fork button.

pages.title: ForkMesh-Owned Git Engine Specification
pages.description: Part of Phone apps.
pages.markdown:
# ForkMesh-Owned Git Engine Specification

Part of [Phone apps](README.md).

The mobile apps carry their own Git engine: Swift in
`native/ios/ForkMeshCore/Sources/FMGit` and Kotlin in
`native/android/core/src/main/kotlin/com/forkmesh/nativeapp/git`. It treats all
repository and network data as attacker-controlled and is a security boundary.
How the phone uses it is in the [mobile node contract](mobile-node-contract.md).

## Dependency boundary

Runtime code is owned ForkMesh code plus platform standard libraries
(Foundation, system zlib and a pinned SHA1DC detector on iOS; the JDK on
Android). No libgit2, JGit, go-git, other Git library, Git executable, shell or
process fallback. System Git is used only in tests, as fixture generator,
disposable smart-HTTP server and interoperability oracle. A source and runtime
guard fails the build if production code can spawn a process.

## Supported subset

- Non-bare SHA-1 repositories, `core.repositoryformatversion = 0`, app-private
  worktree with `<worktree>/.git`. Bare repositories, linked worktrees,
  `core.worktree`, alternates, grafts, replace refs and extensions other than
  `objectFormat = sha1` are rejected; SHA-256 returns
  `unsupportedRepositoryFormat` without touching disk.
- Objects: blobs, trees, commits; annotated tags parsed. Modes `100644`,
  `100755`, `120000`; gitlinks rejected. Commits are written UTF-8 with no
  `encoding` header.
- Refs: loose refs under `refs/heads/`, `refs/remotes/`, `refs/tags/`, symbolic
  or detached `HEAD`, packed refs read-only. Writes use lock files and atomic
  rename; reflogs only for `HEAD` and `refs/heads/*`.
- Config: only `.git/config`, and only `core.repositoryformatversion`,
  `core.filemode`, `core.bare`, `extensions.objectformat`, `remote.<n>.url`
  (HTTPS, no credentials), `remote.<n>.fetch`, `branch.<n>.remote`,
  `branch.<n>.merge`. Includes, aliases, hooks paths, helpers and external
  commands are rejected.
- Index version 2 only, no extensions written. Pack v2 and index v2 read
  (including `OFS_DELTA` and `REF_DELTA`); non-delta packs written. Thin packs
  rejected.
- Local operations: status, add, remove, branch, checkout, commit, log, read
  tree and blob.

## Transport

HTTPS smart HTTP only; no `git://`, `ssh://`, `http://`, `file://` or URL
user-info. Fetch is protocol v2 only (`Git-Protocol: version=2`) with stateless
negotiation (32 `have` lines per round, at most 8 rounds), no thin packs. Push
uses the receive-pack advertisement with expected-old-OID commands,
`report-status-v2` when offered, and a typed result per ref. Non-fast-forward
and force updates are refused locally before any body is sent; ref deletion is
not expressible. Redirects are never followed. Authentication headers come
from a caller-supplied provider that sees the final method, URL and body; the
engine stores no credentials and sends no cookies. Downloaded packs land in a
quarantine directory and are installed atomically only after every hash and
limit check passes.

## Not supported

SHA-256 repositories, shallow and partial clone, LFS, SSH, submodules, linked
worktrees, merge and rebase, hooks, credential helpers, signature verification,
and server-side hosting. Each fails with a typed error instead of a lossy
approximation.

## Resource limits

Limits are part of the protocol boundary. Callers may lower defaults but never
raise hard caps.

| Resource | Default | Hard cap |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| pkt-line length | 65,520 B | 65,520 B |
| pkt-lines per response | 50,000 | 200,000 |
| refs per advertisement | 25,000 | 100,000 |
| object size | 64 MiB | 256 MiB |
| compressed pack per operation | 512 MiB | 1 GiB |
| inflated pack per operation | 768 MiB | 1 GiB |
| delta chain depth | 32 | 50 |
| delta expansion ratio | 32:1 | 64:1 |
| tree depth / entries per tree | 64 / 25,000 | 128 / 100,000 |
| checkout files / bytes | 100,000 / 512 MiB | 250,000 / 1 GiB |
| path component / path length | 255 B / 1,024 B | 255 B / 4,096 B |
| connect or first byte / idle read | 15 s / 30 s | 30 s / 60 s |
| operation deadline | 5 min | 15 min (30 min if approved) |

Cancellation is checked before every network read and write, every 64 KiB of
body, every inflate append, delta instruction, file write and rename. A
cancelled operation leaves the repository in its prior state.

## SHA-1 policy

Plain SHA-1 is not collision-safe. Complete object frames are screened through
the pinned SHA1DC detector; for untrusted transport the engine fails closed
(`hashScreeningUnavailable`) whenever a clear detector result is unavailable.
Network SHA-1 operations stay gated on collision-corpus evidence and
independent cryptography review.

## Worktree and filesystem policy

Checkout happens only inside an app-private root, one validated path component
at a time. Absolute paths, empty, `.` or `..` components, NUL, backslash,
control characters, trailing dot or space, reserved device names and
platform-ambiguous colons are rejected, as are case or normalization
collisions. A checkout is built in a sibling staging directory, verified to
stay below its root, then promoted atomically. Repository-controlled symlinks
are never followed; a symlink is written only if its target cannot escape.

## API and errors

`GitRepository` exposes open/init, `status`, `add`, `remove`, `commit`,
`createBranch`, `checkout`, `clone`, `fetch`, `push`, `readTree`, `readBlob`
and `log`. Network operations report bounded, redacted progress to a
`GitProgressListener` and honour a `GitCancellationToken`. Errors are typed:
`invalidRepository`, `unsupportedRepositoryFormat`, `invalidObject`,
`objectHashMismatch`, `invalidTree`, `invalidRef`, `refLocked`, `indexCorrupt`,
`packCorrupt`, `packChecksumMismatch`, `deltaDepthExceeded`,
`resourceLimitExceeded`, `pathEscapesWorktree`, `symlinkEscape`,
`networkUnavailable`, `tlsRejected`, `authenticationFailed`,
`protocolUnsupported`, `remoteRejected`, `nonFastForward`, `cancelled`,
`operationInterrupted`. Callers never parse message text.

## Atomicity and recovery

Every mutation writes a bounded journal in `.git/forkmesh-journal/` (operation,
staging paths, expected old and new refs) with no credentials or content.
Objects and packs are written to private temporary paths, verified, then
renamed; index, config, reflog and ref changes go through lock files in a fixed
order. On open, recovery removes uncommitted staging or completes an idempotent
rename; if preconditions cannot be proven, the repository opens read-only with
`operationInterrupted`. A partial clone never produces a valid-looking `HEAD`.

## Threat model

The protocol-wide model is in [threat model](../protocol/threat-model.md).

| Threat | Mitigation |
| --- | --- |
| Path traversal, symlink escape, case-folding overwrite | Component validation, staging-root containment, no symlink traversal |
| Malformed objects, zlib or delta bombs | Checked cursors, declared-size checks, streamed inflate, depth and ratio caps, hash verification |
| Pack or index corruption | Signature, count, CRC, checksum and ordering checks before use |
| Ref injection, lock races, stale push | Ref grammar, lock files, expected-old-OID commands, no force |
| Credential disclosure | No URL user-info, redaction, request-scoped memory only |
| TLS downgrade or redirect to another host | HTTPS only, strict validation, zero redirects, no trust-all API |
| Protocol desync | Exact pkt-line framing, MIME checks, capability allowlist, count caps |
| Crash or cancellation mid-operation | Quarantine, journal, idempotent recovery, read-only fail-closed |
| SHA-1 collision | Full-frame screening, fail closed without a detector result |
| Executable fallback | No third-party runtime dependencies, process guard |

Interrupted operations surface `operationInterrupted` rather than inferred
success, and recovery preserves a diagnostic copy instead of deleting a
repository.

## Testing

Published vectors for SHA-1, SHA-256, zlib, framing, tree order and refs;
bidirectional fixtures against system Git for local authoring; packs from
several Git versions plus malformed corpora, delta bombs and cancellation;
disposable smart-HTTP remotes for credentials, TLS, rejection and stale push;
fuzz and property tests for every parser.
